title: Stats don't support Flock's claim of solving 1 million crimes
summary: Flock has made unsupported or inconsistent statistical claims in the past, according to a CBS News review and criminal justice experts.
story: Faced with recent questions about the privacy costs of its technology, the surveillance camera startup Flock Safety and its CEO have deployed a tidy statistic to tout its benefits.
"Last year we helped clear just over a million crimes in America," Flock CEO Garrett Langley said in a March 2026 podcast interview.
"Over a million cases were solved last year with this technology," Langley told the auto industry publication The Drive, "and the level of abuse is incredibly low relative to that."
"Today, Flock technology assists your officers in more than one million crimes solved annually," Langley said in a blog post last month announcing new privacy updates.
But a CBS News review finds the claim that Flock helped solve a million crimes in 2025 is not supported by the available evidence.

In a statement for this report, Flock spokesman Paris Lewbel cast the statistic in a different framing. In addition to case clearances, he said, it includes "investigative leads, cross-jurisdictional assistance, searches conducted during active investigations, and other Flock deployments."
"The most precise way to describe our 2025 national estimate is that Flock technology supported approximately 1 million investigations and incidents," Lewbel said.
The company did not answer whether Langley had been imprecise in claiming Flock solved one million crimes in 2025, and did not provide CBS News with underlying data supporting that claim.

Flock first explained the source of its claims of one million crimes solved in a May 2026 blog post announcing the results of its 2025 Impact Census, in which about 700 law enforcement agencies that use Flock's system participated. Flock says agencies that formally tracked outcomes supplied raw counts, while others provided percentage estimates. The blog post also said the study found 20% of cleared cases in customer jurisdictions in 2025 were assisted by Flock technology.
In explaining the 20% finding, the company said 307 agencies supplied percentage estimates. Those responses were then referenced with FBI crime and clearance data for each responding agency.

The "one million crimes" statistic was a separate and broader calculation. "Across all use cases — direct case clearances, investigative leads, cross-jurisdictional assists, and field deployments — Flock supported approximately 1 million investigations and incidents during the year," the company said in the blog post.
Experts in crime data say the company's crime-solving statistical claims are not reliable.

"It's worth about the paper it's printed on," said Charles Fain Lehman, a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute who is a proponent of the technology. "...But I think if you look under the hood of the academic research, that still points you in a direction of there's an effect — it's just a smaller effect."

Footnotes and caveats on Flock's blog post regarding its 2025 Impact Census say these figures are "directional estimates rather than audited totals" and that its methodology is "not a finished product."
The company's claims have surfaced in local government documents and deliberations as municipalities grapple with the costs and benefits of the surveillance technology.

When the city council in Costa Mesa, California, considered whether to continue its contract with Flock this summer at an annual cost of $151,800, city records show, its police department issued a positive recommendation that cited in part the claim that "Flock technology assisted in solving an estimated 20% of cleared cases" in 2025.
On July 21, Costa Mesa City Council voted 6-1 to keep the cameras but renegotiate the city's contract with Flock.
Even if its CEO described Flock's statistical claims with all the caveats included on its website, criminologists say there are bigger issues with its methodology.

A major issue with Flock's study is that even if Flock is used to help with a case, "it doesn't necessarily mean in a counterfactual world where Flock cameras didn't exist, the case wouldn't have been solved," said Andrew Wheeler, a criminologist and data scientist at Gainwell Technologies who has published research on automated license plate technology.
Flock's study of 2025 crime, he said, did not use established empirical methods to account for this counterfactual.
"The 'a million crimes solved' is probably a gross over-estimate based on that particular work," Wheeler said.
Disputed statistical claims
It is not the first time Flock's statistics have come under scrutiny.

In 2024, the company began claiming that its technology "is instrumental in solving 10% of reported crimes in the U.S." (This is distinct from its later claim that an estimated 20% of cleared cases in 2025 were assisted by Flock technology in customer jurisdictions.)
The 10% claim was promoted publicly in a February 2024 press release connected to the release of a white paper authored by two Flock employees.
However, that 10% claim is not actually contained within the text of the Flock-authored white paper.
Rather, the paper concludes that every additional camera per sworn officer is associated with a 9.1-percentage-point increase in the agency's license plate reader-assisted clearance rate.
The white paper says it was "created with the consultation" of two academics — Johnny Nhan of Texas Christian University and Richard Helfers of the University of Texas at Tyler.

The white paper is an analysis based on survey responses Flock received from 477 agencies, 123 of which supplied data used in the final model. Because the agencies were not randomly selected, it was not established that they were representative of the 18,000 law enforcement agencies in the United States.
Wheeler, in a blog post at the time, criticized the white paper's methodology and called the conclusion that Flock helped solve 10% of crimes nationwide "ridiculous."

Nhan, one of the two consultants for the white paper, told 404 Media in 2024 that he and Helfers helped with statistical calculations and formatting, but regarding the conclusions, he said he "personally would have done things much differently."
In response to questions from CBS News, Nhan similarly backed away from the 2024 paper's conclusions.

"I did get to look at a version of the paper and did discuss a little bit, but the methods and data sources were not known to us so we didn't dive into it," he said. "I personally didn't want to delve into its effectiveness or impact on crime rates, which is a very complex topic for any criminologist."
By contrast, Flock's 2024 release attributed a quotation to Nhan praising the company as "fully transparent and accessible during every stage of the research process."
Asked in a CBS News interview in August if Flock's national crime-solving claims are supported by peer-reviewed studies, Langley said peer-reviewed research was not part of the company's claims.
"No, there's no peer-reviewed study, and we're not articulating that it was peer-reviewed," Langley said.
He added that there was "one indisputable data point" from the prior month's data.
"In July of this year, just last month, 1,025 missing people detected, 22,000 stolen cars detected," he said. "Those detections lead to results."

The detection of a vehicle associated with a missing person case, however, is different from the detection of a missing person. Flock has said its license plate cameras do not use facial recognition technology.

Asked for underlying data supporting the "indisputable" July figures, Lewbel told CBS News those two statistics "are based on unique vehicle detections involving vehicles associated with records in the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database and the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children's AMBER Alert database."
Internal inconsistencies
As of late August, Flock's website featured a series of crime-solving statistics that could not easily be reconciled. Several of those statistics were removed following an inquiry from CBS News.

"Flock technology is currently being used to solve approximately 2,000+ crimes per day, accounting for over 10% of all reported crime in the United States," the company said on the third page of a 2026 Company Fact Sheet that was, until recently, part of a media kit available on its website.
A separate page of the same fact sheet provided an entirely different figure: "2,800+ crimes solved weekly with the help of Flock Technology." (That's about 400 crimes per day.)

Elsewhere, the company's FAQ page stated both "On average, 1,000+ crimes solved per day with the help of Flock Technology" and "On average, 2,200+ crimes solved per week with the help of Flock technology." (The latter figure is about 314 crimes per day.)

"The statistics cited in your questions come from materials published at different points in time and reflect different time periods, datasets, and methodologies," Lewbel said in written response to questions about the inconsistencies.

Following questions from CBS News earlier this month, Flock's 2026 Company Fact Sheet and other documents which had been stored in a publicly-viewable Google Drive folder linked from the "Media Kit" section of the company's website became unavailable.
The company's FAQ page also changed, removing the claim of "1,000+ crimes solved per day."
"A trade-off that I can make"

Flock's crime-solving claims have coincided with a period of rapid growth and investment. The company has raised more than $1 billion from Silicon Valley and, according to an article in Inc., is valued at approximately $8.4 billion.
In different public statements, Langley has altered the framing around the million-crimes statistic. At times, he has cited it without any context at all.
"We never would have guessed, just like the sheer impact we've had, right?"  Langley said in his recent interview with CBS News. "So last year alone, over a million criminal cases."
In an April 2026 TED Talk that has now been viewed more than 5 million times, a host asked Langley about instances in which Flock's technology has been abused.
Langley conceded there have been instances of privacy abuse before pivoting to Flock's benefits.
"I look at the million-plus cases and go, OK, this is a trade-off that I can make," Langley said in reply, without providing any further description of the one-million figure. "But that's my choice."
With that, the TED Talk host thanked Langley and the audience applauded as the CEO walked off stage.

Flock cameras

title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan to be executed by firing squad, Pentagon says
summary: The Trump administration has approved a plan to execute former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan — who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood — by firing squad, the Pentagon said.
story: The Trump administration has approved a plan to execute former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan — who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood — by firing squad, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said late Monday.
Parnell said on social media the plan to use an Army firing squad was recommended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and approved by President Trump.
"The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote.
CBS News has reached out to Hasan's attorney for comment.

According to an email sent to the families of the victims and obtained by CBS News Texas on Tuesday, the execution has been scheduled for Dec. 3. When CBS News Texas reached out to Fort Hood for comment, it was directed to Army headquarters.

A former Army psychiatrist, Hasan was convicted of murdering 13 people and injuring more than 30 in a 2013 court-martial. Hasan acknowledged at trial that he was responsible for the shooting, claiming he opened fire on fellow members of the Army in an attempt to protect Islamic insurgents from U.S. military forces. He was sentenced to death.
Hasan's case could mark the military's first execution of an American service member since 1961, when a soldier was hanged for raping and attempting to murder an 11-year-old girl.
It would also mark a rare use of a firing squad. The method was used in South Carolina three times last year, marking the first firing squad executions since 2010.

The federal government typically uses lethal injection for civilian death penalty cases. Earlier this year, the Justice Department said federal officials should consider other methods, including firing squads, electrocution and lethal gas.

The decision by Hegseth comes after a lengthy appeals process for Hasan. He chose to represent himself at trial, and in an unusual course of events, he clashed with his own court-appointed standby attorneys, who worried that Hasan was intentionally seeking the death penalty.

Hasan asked the Supreme Court to review his case in 2024, arguing the judge violated his right to a public trial by clearing the public from the courtroom before discussing some of his issues with the attorneys. The high court declined to take up the issue last year.

title: Storm brewing off Mexico could impact Gulf Coast as hurricane this weekend
summary: Tropical Depression Nine formed in the Gulf, and it's expected to become a hurricane later this week.
story: With less than two months remaining in the 2026 hurricane season, the potential for a ninth named tropical storm in the Atlantic basin is brewing in the southern Gulf.
Since the Atlantic's season began on June 1, it has only seen eight named storms this year, while El Niño continues to bring a more active season in the Pacific. The season ends Nov. 30.
What we know about the possible path

Tropical Depression Nine formed in the Gulf on Tuesday. As the storm brews over the warmer waters off Mexico, it's expected to become a tropical storm by early Wednesday and a hurricane on Thursday, according to the National Hurricane Center.
If it does become a tropical storm, it would receive the name Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs."
Forecast models are beginning to come to agreement that the northward motion of this tropical system brings it to the Gulf Coast this weekend.

Regardless of its name or if it develops into a tropical storm, we do know that it will bring moderate to heavy rainfall to the Gulf Coast and into the rest of the Southeast this weekend into early next week.
Some longer-range forecast models also see this moisture eventually reaching the Ohio Valley and Northeast by midweek next week.
What we do not know
Timing, storm intensity and severity of impacts to land with this tropical system are what remain unknown.
While some models have impacts starting Friday evening, others show it beginning later in the weekend.
Beware the "I"-named storm
While tropical storm and hurricane formation and frequency vary throughout the season, the "I"-named systems tend to be the most retired names within the Atlantic basin.
The most commonly known retired "I"-named storms are Ian (2022), Ida (2021), Irma (2017), and Irene (2011).
When Ike was retired in 2008, Isaias replaced the "I" name on the Atlantic tropical cyclones list, which rotates every six years.

title: California couple at center of surrogacy scandal arrested
summary: Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang, who had at least 25 children via surrogates, were arrested at their home in Arcadia, California.
story: A California couple at the center of a surrogacy scandal was arrested on Tuesday. A law enforcement source confirmed the arrests to CBS News shortly before officials held a news conference to announce the latest developments.
Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang are being charged with multiple counts, including conspiracy to commit child abuse and dissuading a witness, Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman said.
The couple drew national headlines last year after authorities raided their Arcadia mansion in July 2025 and took 21 kids, mostly surrogate-born, into state custody.

Tuesday morning, detectives from the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department arrested the couple at their residence. They were then transferred to the Pasadena courthouse to be arraigned, Sheriff Robert Luna said. A judge confirmed each will be held on a $20 million bond.
A neighbor said Tuesday that helicopters and police could be seen at the couple's mansion and the entire block is taped off.
"What has been publicly filed in the complaint today is incredibly disturbing. It involves horrific punishment and beatings and child abuse," Hochman said at the news conference.
Officials said the investigation began in May 2025 when Zhang brought a 2-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury.

"She appeared to be untruthful with hospital staff about how the injury was sustained and the hospital staff notified law enforcement authorities," Luna said, adding that when Arcadia police went to the home, "what they discovered raised even more serious concerns."

The district attorney said Tuesday that the children were seated for hours a day in three different rooms called "Learning Centers" under the supervision of various nannies at the couple's home, which he called a "house of horrors." The couple kept a system of 32 motion-activated cameras in the various rooms in the Arcadia mansion, he said. Footage from these cameras went to a television near their desk that the couple used to monitor the discipline given by the nannies.

Hochman said the nannies were caught on video spanking, slapping or hitting the children. One nanny, Chunmei Li,  allegedly struck the 2-month-old baby in the head, the district attorney said. A $105,000 warrant for her arrest was previously issued, but she remains on the run, he said.
Xuan's attorney, Mitchell Krems, said: "My client is innocent. It is the nanny's wrongdoing who went on the run. He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family."

Melissa Brisman, an attorney for two of the surrogates involved in the case, told CBS News, "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system."
Brisman added that it's important surrogacy remains an option for those who need the help to become parents, but said there must "be adequate protections for those who enter the surrogacy system."
"We need to make sure bad actors don't ruin it for everyone else," she said.

On Tuesday, officials said the Arcadia Police Department requested assistance from the LA County Sheriff's Department in early September. A Los Angeles FBI spokesperson confirmed the FBI served a search warrant at the home, separate from a search conducted by the sheriff's department.
"We will continue to work together to pursue justice for all 21 children involved in this case," Luna said.

Maria Castellanos, a surrogate who carried two children for Zhang and Xuan, said after learning of their arrest, "I'm mad that everyone involved couldn't stop this so the kids wouldn't go through everything they went through. I'm just mad with the whole process, the whole thing. It's not just them."
"I trusted Silvia," she said.

Josh  Boswell
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Christa Pike is conscious, speaking after botched execution, attorneys say
summary: Christa Pike, a death row inmate who was subject​ to a failed execution attempt in Tennessee last week, is conscious and speaking from her hospital bed, her attorneys said Tuesday.
story: Christa Pike, a death row inmate who was subject to a failed execution attempt in Tennessee last week, is conscious and speaking from her hospital bed, her attorneys said Tuesday.
Pike survived the state's Sept. 30 attempt to execute her by lethal injection at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. She has been hospitalized since.

In a statement Tuesday, her attorneys said that she was "conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care," but noted that "her prognosis remains unclear" and "at a minimum" they "expect a long recovery."
They also said that "despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed."

Pike was given two lethal doses of pentobarbital, but according to media witnesses, the execution was canceled when it was determined she had not lost consciousness and still had a heartbeat. One media witness noted that she could be heard loudly snoring about one hour after the procedure had started. She was then taken by ambulance to an area hospital.
One of her attorneys, Steve Ferrell, told "CBS Mornings" on Monday that doctors were working to clear her body of the pentobarbital and that she was on a ventilator.
Pike was convicted in the 1995 murder of a former classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 at the time of the crime, and 20 when she was sentenced in 1996.
Pike's execution was allowed to move forward last week after the Supreme Court denied a last-minute effort to halt it. She was set to be the first woman executed in the state in about two centuries.

In the wake of the failed execution, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said the state's prison chief, Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, will resign. Lee also said that all remaining scheduled executions in the state this year have been canceled amid what he said would be a "third-party review" of the botched execution. Pike's attorneys have also filed a motion in Davidson County court requesting that all evidence related to the failed execution be preserved.

In that motion, her attorneys also claimed that during the execution, the corrections department team failed to realize that the IV lines had not been correctly placed "or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering" Pike's body.
Ferrell told "CBS Mornings" that her legal team would like to see her sentence commuted.
"The least that could happen now is that we at least take death off the table and start looking for what the future could be for her," Ferrell said.

Emily Mae  Czachor and 
                                                  
                                  Kerry  Breen
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: 2026 midterm election races to watch
summary: CBS News has identified 10 key Senate and 42 House races that will likely decide the majority — all of which can change during the midterm campaign.
story: CBS News' Battleground Tracker polling is back for 2026, capturing what's on voters' minds and the key groups to watch coast to coast, as well as what it means for districts, seat estimates and control of the U.S. House of Representatives.
Every district and state matters, but CBS News also identifies 10 key Senate and 42 House races that will likely decide the majority — all of which can change as the campaign rolls on.
Democrats and Republicans are focusing on a small number of races in the House and the Senate as they fight for control of Congress in the midterm elections this fall.
Republicans, who currently have the majority in both chambers, are vulnerable primarily because of the unpopular Iran war and continuing cost-of-living economic pressure.
Senate

Republicans have 53 seats, and Democrats have 47. Most of the 22 seats the GOP is defending are in states Mr. Trump easily won in 2024. Democrats must add a net total of four seats to take the majority while also defending a few seats against GOP challenges.
Here are the ten 2026 Senate races to watch:
Alaska

GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola are the front-runners in Alaska's top-four primary, where another candidate by the same name as the incumbent is also on the ballot. Alaska hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, but the party is eyeing the race as a pickup opportunity.
Iowa

GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and state Rep. Josh Turek are facing off in Iowa after Sen. Joni Ernst decided not to seek reelection. The race has grown surprisingly competitive in a state that's shifted to the right in recent years, as affordability issues and the Trump tariff policies weigh on Iowans.
Maine

GOP Sen. Susan Collins is defending her seat against Troy Jackson, who became the Democratic nominee after Graham Platner bowed out of the race in July following a sexual assault allegation. Collins has survived challenges in previous reelection fights, but Democrats are optimistic about their chances in a state that Kamala Harris won in 2024 by almost 7 points.
Michigan

Former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed are vying for an open seat in Michigan after Sen. Gary Peters decided to retire from Congress. El-Sayed is a progressive former Michigan health official who defeated a more moderate opponent in a divisive Democratic primary, while Rogers is seeking the seat after losing a bid to Sen. Elissa Slotkin last cycle.
Ohio

GOP Sen. Jon Husted is defending his seat against a comeback bid by former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his reelection bid in Ohio's other Senate seat last cycle. Democrats are hoping Brown's working-class brand will propel him to victory against Husted, the former lieutenant governor who was appointed to JD Vance's seat last year after Vance became vice president.
Texas

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and state Rep. James Talarico are competing in a closely watched contest in the Lone Star State. Democrats saw their chances of flipping the seat improve after Paxton defeated incumbent GOP Sen. John Cornyn, given Paxton's history of personal controversies and more conservative positions. But Republicans remain confident in their chances of holding onto the seat, though some concede that the race will be tough — and expensive.
Kansas

GOP Sen. Roger Marshall is aiming to prevent pastor Adam Hamilton from becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Kansas since 1932. Hamilton — a former Republican who leads the state's largest United Methodist church — has sought to capitalize on discontent around the cost of living, the Iran war and energy prices, which have hit Kansas farmers hard. Recent polls indicate a tight race, and national Republicans have poured millions into defending Marshall, who has cast Hamilton as a progressive in centrist's clothing.
Georgia

GOP Rep. Mike Collins is taking on Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia in a competitive race that was once expected to be the easiest pickup opportunity for Republicans. But a messy Republican primary slowed the launch of Republicans' general election fight to unseat the first-term senator.
North Carolina

Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper and former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley are jockeying for a seat representing North Carolina in the Senate after GOP Sen. Thom Tillis announced he wouldn't seek reelection. Democrats see the seat in the Tar Heel State as a key prize, representing their best chance at flipping a seat this cycle.
New Hampshire

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas and former GOP Sen. John Sununu are running for an open Senate seat in New Hampshire to fill Sen. Jeanne Shaheen's seat upon her retirement. New Hampshire hasn't elected a Republican to the Senate since 2010, but Republicans are hopeful about the prospects for Sununu, whose family has been dominant in Granite State politics.
House

All 435 House seats are up for election, with 218 as the threshold for the majority. The House is currently very narrowly divided, with 218 Republicans, plus an independent who caucuses with the GOP, and 214 Democrats. Two seats are vacant.
These are the 42 House races to watch:
Arizona's 1st Congressional District

Republican Jay Feely and Democrat Amish Shah are vying to replace eight-term GOP Rep. David Schweikert, who ran unsuccessfully for governor. Feely, an NFL veteran and former analyst for CBS Sports, initially ran in another district, but he switched at the urging of President Trump. Shah failed to unseat Schweikert in 2024.
Arizona's 6th Congressional District

Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani is up against Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza in the district that stretches from the Tucson-area suburbs down to the southeastern corner of the state along the U.S.-Mexico border.
California's 13th Congressional District

The seat held by Democratic Rep. Adam Gray is one of the House Republicans' campaign arm's top targets. Gray flipped the seat in 2024, narrowly winning by fewer than 200 votes. In 2022, he lost by fewer than 600 votes. In June's nonpartisan primary, he had a significant advantage over Republican Kevin Lincoln, a Marine veteran.
California's 22nd Congressional District

GOP Rep. David Valadao is one of two remaining House Republicans in Congress who voted to impeach President Trump in 2021 over the Capitol riot. He is the last one running for reelection, since Washington Rep. Dan Newhouse is retiring. Valadao is running against Democrat Randy Villegas in the newly redrawn district.
California's 45th Congressional District

Democratic Rep. Derek Tran's district was redrawn as part of Gov. Gavin Newsom's redistricting push, making his new district one that Vice President Kamala Harris won by only 4 points. The House Republicans' campaign arm is backing former Cerritos Mayor Chuong Vo in its effort to target the Orange County-area district.
California's 48th Congressional District
Republican Jim Desmond and Democrat Marni Von Wilpert are on the ballot to replace outgoing GOP Rep. Darrell Issa in a newly redrawn Southern California district.
Colorado's 8th Congressional District

GOP Rep. Gabe Evans, who flipped a seat held by a Democrat in 2025, is running for reelection against Democrat Manny Rutinel, a progressive state representative. The district, which is north of Denver, has a sizable Latino population.
Florida's 14th Congressional District

Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor's Tampa-area district has been redrawn to be more friendly to Republican, but it is still rated as Lean Democratic. Former state Rep. Mike Beltran won the crowded GOP primary to take on Castor in the fall.
Florida's 22nd Congressional District

After this district was gerrymandered to be more GOP-friendly, its congresswoman, Democrat Lois Frankel, opted instead to run in the 23rd District. Democrat Pia Dandiya won the August primary, and Republican Casey Askar prevailed in the crowded GOP primary. Both parties' campaign arms are targeting the district, which includes Palm Beach County.
Florida's 25th Congressional District

Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz is running for reelection here, though the Boca Raton-area district's boundaries were altered to be more favorable to Republicans. Moskowitz faces former Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer on the ballot.
Iowa's 1st Congressional District
Democrat Christina Bohannan is trying for a third time to unseat Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks. Miller-Meeks has won several close races since 2020.
Iowa's 2nd Congressional District
Republican Joe Mitchell and Democrat Lindsay James are on the ballot to replace GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Senate.
Iowa's 3rd Congressional District
GOP Rep. Zach Nunn is defending his seat against Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott. Nunn, who has represented the Des Moines-area district since 2023, won reelection in 2024 by less than 4 points.
Michigan's 4th Congressional District
Longtime GOP Rep. Bill Huizenga is trying to fend off a challenge from Democrat Sean McCann, a state senator.
Michigan's 7th Congressional District

GOP Rep. Tom Barrett, who was first elected in 2024, is one of a handful of Republicans who have supported Democratic-led war powers resolutions to rein in President Trump on Iran. He's facing Democrat William Lawrence, who cofounded the Sunrise Movement and is a former member of the Democratic Socialists of America.
Michigan's 8th Congressional District

After suspending his campaign, Thomas Smith defeated a Trump-backed candidate to win the GOP primary and take on Democratic Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet. Though the district elected McDonald Rivet in 2024, it also voted for President Trump.
Michigan's 10th Congressional District
Republican Michael Bouchard and Democrat Christina Hines are competing for the open seat, which is currently held by GOP Rep. John James, who is running for Michigan governor.
Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District

Republican Brinker Harding and Democrat Denise Powell are hoping to replace retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon in the Omaha-area district. Though the seat has been in GOP hands for all but two years in the last three decades, the district has voted for a Democrat in three of the last five presidential elections.
Nevada's 3rd Congressional District
Video game music composer Marty O'Donnell is hoping to unseat Democratic Rep. Susie Lee in the 3rd District, which touches parts of Las Vegas.
New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas opted to run for Senate this year, leaving the swingy seat open. Pappas has held the seat since 2017, but before that, it flipped five times between Republican and Democrats. Democrat Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, will face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo.
New Jersey's 7th Congressional District

GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr. is defending his seat against Democrat Rebecca Bennett, after his lengthy absence from Congress earlier this year. Upon his return to work in June, he disclosed he had been diagnosed with depression and was hospitalized for treatment.
New Mexico's 2nd Congressional District

Marine veteran Greg Cunningham is challenging Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez in the district, which spans the southern half of the state and includes part of Albuquerque. Vasquez was elected to the House in 2022, flipping the seat.
New York's 3rd Congressional District

Democratic Rep. Tom Suozzi is defending his seat against former New York state Rep. Mike LePetri in the Long Island district. The longtime Democratic district flipped Republican in 2022, but after former Rep. George Santos was expelled from Congress, Suozzi won the special election for the seat. He was reelected in 2024, though Mr. Trump won the district.
New York's 4th Congressional District

In 2024, Democratic Rep. Laura Gillen defeated the Republican incumbent, Rep. Anthony D'Esposito, after he beat her in the race for the open Long Island seat in 2022. She'll face local tax receiver and GOP candidate Jeanine Driscoll.
New York's 17th Congressional District

GOP Rep. Mike Lawler has held the lower Hudson Valley seat since 2023, casting himself as a moderate who can work across the aisle. Democrat Cait Conley, a national security expert and Army combat veteran, moved to the district shortly before announcing her candidacy, though she grew up in the region. Harris narrowly won the district against Mr. Trump in 2024.
New York's 19th Congressional District
Democratic Rep. Josh Riley is trying for a second term in a district that has been competitive. GOP state Sen. Peter Oberacker is his opponent.
North Carolina's 1st Congressional District

The race is a rematch between Republican Laurie Buckhout and Democratic Rep. Don Davis. Davis is facing a tough reelection bid in a district that has leaned further to the right after several rounds of gerrymandering by state Republicans.
North Carolina's 11th Congressional District

GOP Rep. Chuck Edwards dropped his reelection bid after a House Ethics Committee investigation concluded he engaged in "persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct" toward two young women who worked for him. Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkom replaced Edwards on the ballot and will face Democrat Jamie Ager.
Ohio's 1st Congressional District

With Ohio's new court-approved congressional map, Republicans are targeting the 1st District, represented by Democratic Rep. Greg Landsman since 2023. Air Force veteran and former CIA case officer Eric Conroy won the crowded GOP primary with Mr. Trump's backing. Although Mr. Trump won the new district under its new boundaries, CBS News rates the district as Lean Democratic.
Ohio's 9th Congressional District

Voters have another chance to pick between longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur and Republican Derek Merrin. title: Cornell taps Sally Yates to lead review of its response to sexual misconduct claims
summary: Cornell University said Tuesday it is bringing on a former Justice Department official to review its handling of sexual misconduct claims, including the alleged 2024 sexual assault of a former student at a fraternity house​.
story: Cornell University said Tuesday it is bringing on a former Justice Department official to review its handling of sexual misconduct claims, including the alleged 2024 sexual assault of a former student at a fraternity house.
The review will look not just at that specific incident, but also more broadly at "how the University prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus."
Sally Yates tapped to review Cornell's policies, response
Former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates will lead what the university is calling a "comprehensive independent review," the university said in its announcement.
The university said Yates' review will cover "Cornell's policies, practices and resources across the full range of prevention and response."
That includes:

how reports are received and investigatedstudent support systemslooking into how hearings, disciplinary decisions are handled the role and response of campus policehow coordination takes place with other law enforcement agencies and prosecutorsfraternity and sorority oversight
how reports are received and investigated
student support systems
looking into how hearings, disciplinary decisions are handled
the role and response of campus police
how coordination takes place with other law enforcement agencies and prosecutors
fraternity and sorority oversight

"Sally Yates brings extraordinary experience, independence and judgment to this work," said Anne Meinig Smalling, chair of Cornell's Board of Trustees. "The questions raised by the Jane Doe matter warrant a rigorous examination of Cornell's response to that case, but our responsibility is broader. We have asked Ms. Yates and her team to examine Cornell's overall approach to preventing and responding to sexual misconduct, identify where we are doing things well and where we can do better, and recommend changes that will help make our community safer."

Yates and her review will report their findings to a special committee of the Board of Trustees, which then expects to share the results and recommendations with the broader Cornell community, according to the university.
About Sally Yates

Yates served in the Justice Department for decades and as deputy U.S. attorney general under President Obama. She was acting U.S. attorney general for 10 days during President Trump's first term before she was fired for "refusing to enforce a legal order designed to protect the citizens of the United States," the White House said at the time. Yates' firing came after she said she was "not convinced" an immigration order by Mr. Trump was "lawful," and that the Justice Department would not defend it in court "until I become convinced that it is appropriate to do so."
In private practice, she investigated allegations of abuse, misconduct and harassment at the National Women's Soccer League.
Yates and Letitia James will conduct different investigations
Yates' review is separate from Letitia James' criminal investigation as special prosecutor.

A spokesperson for James' office said New York's attorney general has already spoken with several of the key people involved, including "the Tompkins County District Attorney, Jane Doe's attorney, and several candidates for outside counsel to support the investigation. The DA has agreed to cooperate, and OAG remains committed to a thorough and independent investigation guided only by the facts and the law."
University's president meets with students
The announcement comes as Cornell is facing intense scrutiny and on-campus protests over how the school responded to the alleged gang rape in which nobody was criminally charged.

CBS News New York has learned Cornell's President Michael Kotlikoff met with the graduate and professional student assembly Monday. He fielded questions from students about the school's Title IX procedures and the future of Greek life on campus.
One student present at the meeting said Kotlikoff spoke of forthcoming short-term and long-term actions to mitigate party culture at the university.
"We stand with Jane Doe, but also we stand with taking more measures to prevent this from happening in the future," student Emma McDermott said.
Faculty considers no-confidence vote
Some professors are now calling for Kotlikoff's resignation.
"I hope it can be a truly impartial and external investigation," professor Ariana Kim said.

Monday night, Kim introduced a resolution of no confidence in the ability of the administration to effectively address sexual assault at the university. The Faculty Senate, made up of dozens of Cornell professors including Kim, will vote on the resolution next week.

"It would be a massive statement to the upper administration and hopefully signal to them you need to resign, step down, make room for new leadership who can better understand and more holistically lead this institution," Kim said.

"We understand the frustration and concern being expressed by members of our community, and we are listening and engaging directly with them. Shared governance is an important part of Cornell, and President Kotlikoff and members of the administration are scheduled to meet with the Faculty Senate next week. We look forward to that conversation and to continuing to engage constructively with faculty and others across the Cornell community," a Cornell spokesperson said.

"It is imperative that Cornell be willing to examine itself with the same rigor we expect of others. We want to understand not just what happened in 2024, but how Cornell can become a leader in preventing sexual violence, supporting those who come forward and responding to allegations rigorously, fairly and compassionately," Smalling said.
Attorney for one of the accused supports independent review
Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney for one of the men named in Jane Doe's lawsuit, says he welcomes the review.

"Sally Yates has tremendous experience as a prosecutor and investigator, and she and her team should have access to the full record and the freedom to follow the facts wherever they lead," Miltenberg said. "There has been a tremendous amount of public discussion and pressure surrounding this case. That makes it even more important that the review focus on the evidence and take an honest look at what happened, how Cornell handled it, and whether its policies and procedures were followed. Cornell should be held to the same standard it expects of its students: a process that is rigorous, fair and consistent with due process.
"At the end of the day, the facts should speak for themselves," Miltenberg added.
CBS News has reached out to all seven of the men named in the lawsuit. Two of their attorneys have responded, saying their clients deny the allegations.

title: Eva Marie Saint, "North by Northwest" star, dies at 102
summary: Eva Marie Saint won an Oscar for her film debut opposite Marlon Brando in "On the Waterfront." She bucked many Hollywood conventions throughout her lengthy career.
story: Academy Award-winning actor Eva Marie Saint, who starred in such classics as "On the Waterfront" and "North by Northwest," but also bucked Hollywood conventions throughout her lengthy career, has died. She was 102.
Her publicist, Jeff Sanderson, said she died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles, surrounded by family and loved ones.

A regal-looking blonde who ricocheted from playing sultry spies to Southern belles and Superman's stepmother, Saint made her motion picture debut opposite Marlon Brando in Elia Kazan's "On the Waterfront" (1954). Saint played Edie Doyle, whose brother was murdered by thugs working for a mob boss running a longshoremen's union; her character becomes involved with Brando's pugilistic dockworker Terry Malloy.

Her performance earned Saint one of the film's eight Academy Awards. (She was only the fourth person to win a best supporting actress Oscar for their film debut.) On the night she received her award, she was visibly pregnant. "I may have the baby right here!" she said. (Her son, Darrell, was born two days later.)

Saint married director-producer Jeffrey Hayden in 1951, and the couple stayed together for 65 years until his death in 2016. They had two children. Saint had made it clear that family was more important to her than her career.

"I had an agent once who wanted me to make many more movies," she told CBS' "Sunday Morning" in 2014. "I said, 'I can't. I can only do one a year, if that. I have children, young children.' And he said, 'Well, I guess you won't be a superstar.' And I said, 'Well, I guess not.'"
And what happened to that agent? "Fired him," she said.

She kept up her self-imposed limit on films; she also brought her extended family to the set of Otto Preminger's "Exodus" while filming in Cyprus and Israel. Despite not cranking out movies, Saint followed her Oscar win by appearing in many prestige projects, including "A Hatful of Rain," "Raintree County," "All Fall Down," "The Russians Are Coming, the Russians Are Coming," "Grand Prix," and the eponymous TV miniseries based on "How the West Was Won." She also received five Emmy nominations, and won for the 1990 TV movie "People Like Us." At age 97, she appeared on a podcast series.

But perhaps her most memorable performance was as Eve Kendall, a mysterious blonde who crosses paths with Cary Grant's Roger Thornhill as he runs from murderous spies in the 1959 Alfred Hitchcock thriller "North by Northwest." Little does Thornhill realize that Kendall herself is a secret agent.
Saint said Hitchcock's direction to her playing a sexy spy was simple: "Three things: Lower your voice. Don't use your hands. And look directly into Cary Grant's eyes at all times," she recalled.

Hitchcock had a reputation for being tough on young female actors, but not Saint. "I found that he was such a wonderful director, gentleman, funny, courteous, but there are other actresses who don't feel the same way. I don't even want to hear stories about him," she said.
Though playing a femme fatale was new to her, Saint said she wasn't surprised upon watching her performance. "No. I don't think actors are surprised," she said. "I mean, that's what we do."
"Too innocent" looking

Born on July 4, 1924, in Newark, New Jersey, Saint grew up in upstate New York, and attended Bowling Green State University in Ohio (where she was "Sweater Queen"). Originally planning to become a teacher, Saint began acting in student productions, and changed her career focus.

Moving to New York City, she trained at the Actors Studio with famed acting coach Lee Strasberg, and was hired for a production of "Mister Roberts" alongside Henry Fonda. But she was let go by director Joshua Logan; she found out it was because she was deemed "too innocent" looking. The actor who took her place was Jocelyn Brando (Marlon's sister).
Crushed, she was nonetheless determined not to let it dissuade her from pursuing an acting career.

When she was starting out, she told Variety in 2021, Saint and a fellow female actor would talk in a made-up language while riding the subway. "We were so frustrated about not getting jobs, so I suggested that we do something so people would notice us," she said. "When we'd start gabbing, we'd get a little audience. People would put down their papers and wonder, what language is that?"

Saint established herself in the early days of live television as a dramatic actor in plays on "Studio One," "Goodyear Television Playhouse," "GE True Theater" and "Philco Television Playhouse." She starred in the first TV production of Horton Foote's "The Trip to Bountiful," and repeated her role on Broadway, where she was spotted by Kazan, the "Waterfront" director.

He asked Saint to audition opposite Brando in an improvised scene. Upon entering the room, Brando put on a radio, and the two started dancing. "He did something to flip my skirt, and I was so embarrassed I cried a little bit afterward," Saint told the Santa Barbara Independent in 2010. "But Kazan saw the chemistry, and he could see that it could work for the movie."
She said Brando was wonderful to work with.

"What was a little scary about him, which worked for me in the movie, was his perception of people that was so keen," she said. "He could look at somebody or talk with them and hone into what that person was all about. And he would mention it about people around us. So sometimes I would sit there and think, 'If he knows that about that person, he must know more about me than I know about myself.' It made me a little self-conscious, but I used that in the movie. He'd been out in the world and I had been at home protected, so I used that."
Following "Waterfont," Saint appeared on TV in a musical version of Thornton Wilder's "Our Town" with Paul Newman and Frank Sinatra, and also appeared onstage numerous theater productions.

But Hollywood beckoned, and the Oscar winner starred opposite such actors as Montgomery Clift and Elizabeth Taylor ("Raintree County"), Paul Newman ("Exodus"), Warren Beatty ("All Fall Down"), James Garner ("36 Hours"), Richard Burton and Taylor ("The Sandpiper"), Yves Montand ("Grand Prix"), Gregory Peck ("The Stalking Moon"), Bob Hope ("That Certain Feeling," "Cancel My Reservation"), and Tom Hanks ("Nothing in Common").
Other film credits included "Because of Winn-Dixie," "Don't Come Knocking" (with Sam Shepard), "Superman Returns" (as Martha Kent), and "Winter's Tale."

On TV she appeared in "The Best Little Girl in the World," "Moonlighting," the two-hander "Taxi!!" (opposite Martin Sheen), "The Last Days of Patton" (with George C. Scott), "I'll be Home for Christmas," "My Antonia," the 1996 TV miniseries "Titanic," and "Frasier."

And in recent years, Saint podcasted. She played Marisa Tomei's aunt in "The Bus Ride," a short play streamed on "The Pack Podcast." She said the feisty character, written by Eugene Pack, was compelling, calling his work "so honest."
"I've lived long enough to know what's honest and what isn't, and Eugene's plays are," she said. "They're charming, they're positive, but they're not saccharine."
Saint is survived by her two children, Darrell and Laurette, four grandchildren and two great grandchildren, Sanderson's statement said.

title: Former Cornell frat members ask university to clear their names
summary: Some former Cornell University students say they are being falsely connected to a 2024 sexual assault​​ and targeted online.
story: A group of former Cornell University students say they are being falsely connected to the alleged 2024 fraternity house rape, and smeared and targeted online, and they want the college to say explicitly that they were not among men accused in the incident.

The former students, members of the Chi Phi fraternity who graduated in 2022 and 2023, say online sleuths have wrongly pegged them for harassment, leading to negative personal and professional consequences.
A lawyer for the group asked the school in a letter on Oct. 3 to clear them and others who graduated prior to the alleged assault.

"We understand that federal privacy law limits what Cornell may say about individual students, and we are not asking Cornell to identify anyone who was in the group chat," wrote attorney Adam Ford, referring to a Snapchat message thread from the night of the October 2024 incident. "We are asking for the opposite: a public confirmation as to who was not."

A woman identified as Jane Doe sued Cornell, the fraternity and several men who she says pressured her into taking the drug ketamine and sexually assaulted her. According to the suit, which was filed in September, a fraternity member sent a crude message to a Chi Phi Snapchat group chat suggesting that a woman was available for sex in a room in the frat house, leading to hours of assault.
The local district attorney did not bring criminal charges against anyone at the time. New York Attorney General Letitia James has now been appointed special counsel to investigate the case.

Ford's letter says none of the men he represents were in the group chat. While all had been previous members of Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity, they were not students at the time of the alleged assault.

Ford wrote that the men have been harassed in the days since a website devoted to exposing people associated with the rape posted their names under a list of former Chi Phi members. The messages they received, according to Ford, included threats like "I will find you," "you will never know peace" and "all 57 men of the fraternity deserve public execution."

The men's names have been removed from the website following a cease-and-desist letter sent on Oct. 2. A podcaster who indicated in a tweet that they were in the group chat also appears to have deleted the post after receiving a letter from Ford.
"Most of them have had their employers and higher education institutions take

adverse actions against them, including being placed on leave," Ford wrote in the letter, which was addressed to Brian White, Cornell's vice president and general counsel. "We believe Cornell is uniquely situated to correct the public record with a clear and unambiguous public statement that members of the Chi Phi fraternity who were not enrolled at Cornell during the fall of 2024 were not on the relevant 'Chi Phi Actives' Snapchat group chat."
A spokesperson for the school did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.
The men have also asked for individualized private letters "confirming that the University has information proving they were not members of the Chi Phi Actives group chat."

title: Hearing over effort to deport Kilmar Abrego Garcia to Liberia abruptly canceled
summary: A hearing before a federal judge over whether Kilmar Abrego Garcia can be deported to Liberia was abruptly canceled on Tuesday.
story: Greenbelt, Maryland — A hearing before a federal judge over whether Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran man wrongfully deported by the Trump administration last year, can be sent to Liberia was abruptly canceled on Tuesday, leaving the matter unresolved for now.
Abrego Garcia's legal team was set to ask a federal judge to block his deportation to the West African country, where the administration has attempted to send him in his ongoing legal saga.

But the hearing before U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis in federal court in Maryland was delayed for 15 minutes before a court official informed the public that it was canceled. The courtroom was emptied shortly afterwards.
Abrego Garcia's attorney Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg told reporters the hearing was "unable to go forward" but did not comment on why. Justice Department attorneys also did not comment.

Abrego Garcia, who had been living in Maryland with his family, was mistakenly deported to El Salvador in March 2025, despite a judge's 2019 order that blocked his deportation to the country on the grounds that he could be harmed by local gangs. The Trump administration had said Abrego Garcia was a member of the gang MS-13, which he has denied.
He was initially held at the Salvadoran mega-prison CECOT and was eventually returned to the U.S. in June 2025 to face criminal human smuggling charges.

In March, the Trump administration said that it was ready to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia, and asked Xinis to dissolve her order that is currently blocking that, or any other removal of Abrego Garcia, from happening.

In court filings, the Trump administration said that Liberia's government was willing to accept Abrego Garcia and that Immigration and Customs Enforcement could arrange a charter plane to send him to the West African country in a matter of days.

Liberia is among the countries that have agreed to accept non-native immigrants from the U.S., and the Trump administration began sending deportees from Latin America there in August. CBS News traveled to Liberia last month and interviewed a number of them. They described being in limbo and feeling stateless. They are unable to return to the U.S., where many have spouses and children, and said they are scared of being persecuted if they go back to their homelands.

Abrego Garcia has said he is willing to go to Costa Rica and designated the country as his preferred country of removal, and Costa Rica has indicated it would provide him refugee status or residency. But at a hearing last year, a Justice Department lawyer said there had not been discussions about deporting him there.

Tuesday's hearing would have been the first since a federal judge in Tennessee tossed out the criminal indictment charging Abrego Garcia with the alleged crimes, finding that the Justice Department's prosecution of him was vindictive. The government appealed that order in August.

In court filings ahead of the scheduled hearing, Abrego Garcia's lawyers said that the Trump administration is "trying to abuse its immigration powers to punish" him because their client had the "audacity" to challenge his removal to El Salvador.

"Just as the Government unlawfully wielded its criminal powers against Abrego Garcia, so it seeks to unlawfully exploit its immigration powers against him," they wrote in a motion for relief in May. "The record leaves no mystery about what is going on. If the Government truly wanted to remove Abrego Garcia from the United States, it would have sent him to Costa Rica in August 2025 when he designated it [as his country of removal]."
The Trump administration has also attempted to re-deport Abrego Garcia to the African nations of Uganda, Eswatini and Ghana, but none of the countries agreed to accept him.
The Justice Department said in court filings that Xinis should deny Abrego Garcia's motions because "his claims fail as a matter of law."
Abrego Garcia has remained free from ICE custody as his case has proceeded.

title: Olympian accused of damaging Reflecting Pool seeks probe of potential misconduct
summary: David Hearn is asking the Justice and Interior Dept. inspectors general to investigate his arrest and the dismissal of the case against him.
story: Attorneys for Olympic canoeist David Hearn asked the internal watchdogs at the Justice and Interior departments on Tuesday to investigate the circumstances surrounding his arrest, indictment and the dismissal of the case, according to a letter seen by CBS News.

Hearn's case garnered national attention, after he was falsely accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and subsequently indicted on a charge of felony destruction of government property.

Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, later moved to dismiss the case after she said new information had come to light showing the damage had been caused by a contractor's "botched installation," not vandalism.

"Because of the actions of various DOJ and DOI employees, Mr. Hearn was deprived of his liberty, indicted for a crime he did not commit, threatened with incarceration of up to 10 years, and endured the defaming of his name and reputation by high-ranking government officials," Hearn's attorneys wrote in the letter to DOJ Inspector General Don Berthiaume and DOI Inspector General Caryl Brzymialkiewicz.
Those officials, they pointed out, included Pirro, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and President Trump.

"The DOJ OIG and the DOI OIG must conduct detailed and comprehensive investigations to determine what happened inside their agencies that led to the shocking and indefensible treatment of Mr. Hearn," they wrote. "Anything less than a full and fair review would be a betrayal of your mission and perpetuate the outrageous mistreatment of Mr. Hearn."

Hearn was initially detained in jail for five hours on June 19, after he stopped by the Reflecting Pool during a bike ride. He put his hand into the water and touched a piece of the liner that had already come loose before he was asked by a member of the National Park Police to remove his hand from the water.

His lawyers said that during his five-hour detention, he was never read his Miranda rights or permitted to make a phone call, and that he only learned he was initially facing misdemeanor charges when he found two citations stuffed into a brown paper bag with his other belongings shortly after his release from custody.
A grand jury in the D.C. Superior Court later indicted him on the felony count on July 2.

Despite a request from Hearn's attorneys to preserve the physical evidence in the case, his lawyers said the government fenced off the area around the Reflecting Pool in question and undertook repairs to the section of the liner that was at the heart of the indictment.

By the end of July, Pirro moved to dismiss the case altogether, alleging that the Interior Department had delayed producing materials to prosecutors that undermined the evidentiary basis for the case.

"The record reflects an indictment obtained through unusual haste and a prosecution shaped from the outset by political pressure and built on an inadequate investigation," Hearn's lawyers wrote in the letter to the inspectors general.

Pirro was later spotted toting a large box into the White House that sources later confirmed to CBS News contained evidence from the case that she presented to Mr. Trump, after he lashed out at her for dismissing the case against Hearn.

The White House has since held meetings with prosecutors to explore whether other charges could be brought. But a Superior Court Judge foreclosed that possibility on Oct. 1, after he ruled that the case had to be dismissed with prejudice — meaning it cannot be brought again.

"Should the Court dismiss this case in a fashion that allows the government to reinitiate prosecution in the future, the Court would be exposing him to the risk that, due to pressure from the President Of the United States apparently motivated at least in part by Mr. Hearn's political views, he would again be charged with a crime that prosecutors have determined he did not commit," the judge wrote in the opinion dismissing the case.

The letter alleges that prosecutors had exculpatory evidence in hand before they sought an indictment against Hearn. It also alleges that Pirro improperly approached one of the defense's expert witnesses who was inspecting the Reflecting Pool and peppered the expert with questions.

"Defense counsel was given no notice that the encounter would take place and was not present for it, and the government has never produced any report, note, or record of the exchange," Hearn's attorneys wrote.

They continued, "A U.S. Attorney who personally interrogates a represented defendant's testifying expert, in the field, surrounded by her own staff and without notice to counsel, is not gathering evidence—she is testing how the defense intends to prove its case."

They also accused Pirro of running afoul of the rules of professional conduct for attorneys when she spoke publicly about the case during a press conference, and questioned whether the sole grand jury witness in the case had been recalled in order to "manufacture" a damages estimate to help support the felony charge.
Hearn's lawyers also complained that Pirro's statements announcing the indictment "extended well beyond the bare fact of the charge."

"[S]he previewed anticipated witness testimony, vouched for the credibility of government witnesses, opined directly on Mr. Hearn's guilt, and characterized the alleged conduct as 'anarchy' and 'criminal behavior' — conduct implicating the trial-publicity and prosecutorial-conduct constraints of D.C. Rules of Professional Conduct," Hearn's attorneys wrote.
A Justice Department spokesperson said, "The Office of the Inspector General operates independently and makes its own decisions about what to review."

title: ABC asks judge to block FCC early license review
summary: An ABC lawyer argued the FCC was effectively forcing the broadcast company to sit with its "head on a guillotine" while it awaits a decision about its license renewals.
story: An attorney for Disney's ABC asked a federal judge on Tuesday to block the Federal Communications Commission from conducting an early review of the network's broadcast licenses, saying the regulatory proceeding was initiated to retaliate against ABC over content that offended the Trump administration.

During a roughly two-hour hearing in federal court in Washington, D.C., ABC argued that comments from President Trump and FCC Chair Brendan Carr laid bare the true reasons behind why the regulatory agency took the unprecedented step in April of ordering eight television stations owned by ABC and its parent company to submit renewal applications for their broadcast licenses years ahead of schedule.
Those licenses were originally scheduled for renewal between 2028 and 2031.
"They are retaliating with their government power to stop ABC from exercising their protected First Amendment speech," said Beth Wilkinson, an attorney for the company.

Wilkinson at one point used the French Revolution to illustrate the FCC's actions, arguing the agency was effectively forcing the broadcast company to sit with its "head on a guillotine" while it awaits a decision about the licenses.

As the process plays out, she said, the regulatory action is having an immediate chilling effect on how ABC makes editorial decisions. Some of those decisions could in turn lead the FCC to "give us the corporate death penalty and take away our licenses," she said.

In her remarks, she highlighted a speech that Mr. Trump made at the White House in July, in which he chastised ABC and NBC for not broadcasting the speech and called for their licenses to be revoked. Those remarks, she said, represented a "direct threat" to her client.
"People may not like some of ABC's coverage and the president is entitled to it, but the public has the right to be exposed to different speech and viewpoints," she said.

The Justice Department, which is defending the FCC, has argued that the agency's decision in April to order an early license review was triggered by Disney's failure to adequately respond to an ongoing investigation into the company's diversity, equity and inclusion practices.

ABC "refused to adequately respond" to the FCC's anti-discrimination probe, said Dimitar Georgiev-Remme, one of the Justice Department's attorneys representing the FCC in the case. "The commission decided to look for information that it needed by calling for early renewal of plaintiffs' broadcast license."
Tuesday's legal arguments centered primarily on whether Disney and ABC have legal authority to challenge the FCC's early license renewal process in the district court.

The Justice Department argues that the regulatory process that governs license renewals would require a company to appeal an FCC order to the full commission. After that, any adverse decision can only be heard by a federal appellate court — and not a U.S. district court.

ABC, however, alleges that the type of retaliatory conduct it is facing in this case falls outside the scope of the regulatory appeals process prescribed by Congress, and this is the only way the company can seek relief to address the immediate harm it is facing.

In one such example of harm, Wilkinson said the network has changed the ways in which it covers political topics, noting that the talk show "The View" has changed how it selects the clips it uses in the show.

Comedian Jimmy Kimmel, a longstanding critic of Trump, also separately posted his interview with Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico on YouTube rather than airing it with the network, she added.
Wilkinson said that even if the company had sought to appeal the April decision to initiate an early license renewal, the commission has the power to sit on the matter indefinitely.
She also noted that if the FCC ultimately decides to renew the licenses at the end of the process, ABC will have no effective legal remedy to address the harm it has suffered.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan, a Biden appointee, at times appeared skeptical at the government's claim that the FCC initiated the early license renewal process in order to get more information for its anti-discrimination investigation.

When she asked the Justice Department what other llegal tools it has at its disposal to compel ABC to provide the requested data, Georgiev-Remme could not provide an immediate answer, prompting the judge to ask the government to file a brief addressing her question by Oct. 9.

title: Ex-CIA official found with $40 million in gold bars admits to sprawling scheme
summary: A former CIA official admitted to inventing fake classified programs to divert nearly $200 million in government money that was used to buy Florida mansions and gold bars.
story: Washington — A former CIA official who was found with $40 million in gold bars in his home in May pleaded guilty on Tuesday, admitting he invented fake classified programs to divert nearly $200 million in government money that he used to buy Florida mansions and gold.
David Rush entered a guilty plea on a single count of wire fraud during a hearing in federal court in Virginia.
As part of his plea agreement, Rush agreed to forfeit at least $194 million, including 298 gold bars, two BMWs, 35 luxury watches and four luxury homes in Florida. He faces up to 20 years in prison.

In a filing known as a criminal information detailing the allegations Rush admitted to, prosecutors said he invented a fake classified program to steer $145 million in government funds through a front company, using the money to purchase the homes in Florida that he intended to resell for profit. Separately, he "fabricated a separate purported sensitive government activity to justify the acquisition of gold bars," prosecutors said.

"Although the real estate and gold acquisitions involved different transactions and intermediaries, they were executions of the same overarching scheme — RUSH created false classified authorities, directed and approved the associated expenditures, caused contractors and subcontractors to carry out the transactions, and thereafter exercised possession or control over the acquired assets," the filing said.

Prosecutors said Rush had access to "highly sensitive and classified government programs," although the filing does not name the CIA as his former employer. The spy agency and FBI said previously that the investigation began when the CIA referred the matter to the bureau. In the affidavit supporting the original criminal complaint against him, he was described as a "former Senior Executive Service level employee" at a government agency in eastern Virginia.

The document said Rush caused an unidentified contractor known as Company 1 to transfer about $145 million to a holding company set up at his direction. He then instructed employees at that company and a subcontractor to route that money to a holding company that he controlled, and used the funds to purchase four properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound, Florida.

Rush was arrested in May. FBI agents found the gold bars, $2 million in cash and luxury watches when executing a search warrant at his home. Prosecutors said Tuesday that the holding company had about $38.6 million left in its account.

The gold bars were purchased after Rush told the unnamed contractors "that he was working on a Top-Secret project in which he had to deliver high-value commodities to unnamed individuals," the information said. One of the contractors wired $45 million to the holding company in January, a transaction that forms the basis of the wire fraud charge.

Rush was originally charged with one count of stealing public money, with investigators saying he had provided false information about his education and military service on his government application, and fraudulently took military leave after his service ended.
In June, a federal judge ordered Rush to remain in custody as the case proceeded, determining that he posed a severe flight risk.

At his detention hearing, government lawyers called Rush a "master manipulator" who lied to his neighbors about being a pilot, lied to his co-workers and leveraged his "access to seniority." A Justice Department lawyer said Rush "cannot be trusted" and is "fully willing and able to skirt the rules."

Callie  Teitelbaum
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Trump temporarily expands use of red-dyed diesel. Will it lower costs?
summary: Experts say the new executive order will have a limited impact on farmers and truckers who rely on diesel.
story: President Trump's new executive order allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways is aimed at lowering costs for truckers and farmers grappling with diesel prices that remain near record highs. But experts say they are skeptical that the order could deliver sweeping savings.
"It might lead to savings for some, but there are a lot of details that will prevent this from having widespread relief," Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at GasBuddy, told CBS News.

Mr. Trump announced the executive order on Tuesday during a midterm rally in Nebraska, saying the move will "officially waive the off-road requirement and allow anyone to purchase tax-free red-dye diesel for any reason." Red-dyed diesel is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel used to fuel trucks and other on-road vehicles.

The EO comes as diesel prices remain high, although they've eased slightly after reaching a record high last month of $6.53 a gallon. High diesel prices are placing financial strains on the nation's transportation, construction and agricultural industries, which rely heavily on the fuel to move goods.
On Tuesday, the national average for a gallon of diesel stood at $6.32, according to AAA, compared to $3.76 before the war in Iran started.
The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Read on to learn more about red-dyed diesel.
What is red-dyed diesel?
Red-dyed diesel is tax-free diesel intended for off-road vehicles, including farm and construction equipment.

The fuel is dyed red because it allows state law enforcement to easily spot it if drivers are using it on roads and highways in an effort to skirt taxes. Violators may face large fines or penalties, including tax evasion.

Mr. Trump's executive order temporarily removes the limits on red-dyed diesel, allowing all drivers to use it without incurring taxes or penalties. However, it doesn't entirely eliminate taxes on red-dyed diesel.

Instead, it defers the federal excise tax for the remainder of 2026 and directs the Treasury secretary to explore ways to eliminate the requirement to pay the taxes, according to the White House. That means drivers could potentially be on the hook for a payment down the road, experts said.
"Whether anyone who makes the switch to dyed diesel suddenly gets a tax bill is the most unanswered question I have," De Haan said in a post on X.
Will the Trump administration's EO lead to cost savings?
According to a White House fact sheet on the executive order, drivers who rely on diesel could save more than $100 each time they fill up.
However, many states also have bans on using red-dyed diesel on roads and highways. The White House said it is working with states to encourage them to also waive the ban.

But if some states don't waive their bans, it could lead to a "convoluted patchwork" of enforcement, which may ultimately deter trucks that need to cross state lines from using red-dyed diesel, De Haan added.

"If one state is enforcing red-dyed diesel and a trucker crosses over with dyed diesel, that could spell trouble, and [lead to] enforcement issues," he said. "Most of the large end users that could stand to benefit from lower prices probably won't get much of the benefit behind this."
The impact on farmers will also be muted, given that they already get tax-free diesel in most states, De Haan noted.
"Most of them have thousands of liters that they've been buying at tax-free, at scheduled intervals, I should say, and so it's not really any huge advantage," he told CBS News.

The EO will allow farmers to use red-dyed diesel in personal vehicles, but it will yield only minimal savings, he added. "I don't think that any farmer is going to be jumping for joy at the prospect of saving, you know, 50 or 60 cents a gallon on their personal vehicle."
Fails to address the supply issue
Experts noted that the EO doesn't address the lack of diesel supply, the key issue keeping prices elevated.
"The U.S. has about 105 million barrels of diesel in  inventory," Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, told CBS News in an email. "This move doesn't increase or decrease that level."
In theory, the EO should still put downward pressure on diesel prices; however, swings in the diesel market could blunt progress toward lower prices, Kloza added.
Lowering prices without increasing supply could also stimulate demand, which could have the unintended consequence of driving up costs, De Haan pointed out.
"Part of the reason why we have these high prices is because economics is telling us that there are imbalances," he said. "So to ignore them and go ahead with this risks exacerbating the issue."
