title: Paramount closes $110 billion deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery
summary: The merger unites two major movie studios, news operations CBS News and CNN and cable networks including Comedy Central and TNT.
story: Paramount Skydance on Tuesday completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, uniting the movie studios behind "The Godfather" and the "Harry Potter" films into a media colossus rebranded as Skydance.
The merger also brings together the news outlets CBS News and CNN, major cable networks such as Comedy Central, Nickelodeon, TBS and TNT and the streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max.
David Ellison, who orchestrated the merger as CEO of Paramount Skydance, will lead the new company along with co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, who was previously CEO of toy company Mattel.
In an email to employees, Ellison and Kreiz said the merger will allow the company to create a "stronger competitor, one with the scale to take on the biggest players in our industry."
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," Ellison said in a separate statement from Skydance.
As part of the deal, Warner Bros. shareholders will receive the cash equivalent of roughly $31 per share, the company said.

The deal came together after Paramount settled a July lawsuit from a coalition of 12 state attorneys general and a separate lawsuit from the Writers Guild of America (WGA). Both had sued to block it on antitrust grounds.

Under the settlement agreement, Paramount pledged to produce 30 films in each of the first two years after the merger and is barred from selling or closing the Paramount or Warner Bros. studio lots in Los Angeles for at least five years.

Paramount has also agreed to establish an editorial board to "help CNN and CBS maintain editorial independence," according to California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office. WGA agreed to settle its lawsuit after Paramount reached a deal with the states.
Ellison and Kreiz said the company is targeting $6 billion in cost savings, a move that some in the media industry are concerned could lead to job losses.
"Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce," the co-CEOs said in the email to Skydance employees.

title: Amelia Earhart investigators to study mysterious object in Pacific
summary: Investigators have begun an expedition to study a mysterious "visual anomaly" that they say may be Amelia Earhart's long-lost plane.
story: A team searching for Amelia Earhart's lost plane has begun its expedition to the Pacific, where it plans to study a mysterious object that researchers say may be her aircraft.

The item, known as the Taraia Object, has been visible in photos dating back to 1938, the year after Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared over the Pacific Ocean during Earhart's attempt to become the first female pilot to circle the world. Earhart, Noonan and their Electra 10E plane were never found.

Researchers identified the "visual anomaly" in a lagoon on Nikumaroro, a small island in Kiribati about halfway between Australia and Hawaii. The island is about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, where Earhart and Noonan were planning to travel.

Now, a team of researchers from Purdue University and the Oregon-based Archaeological Legacy Institute are traveling to Nikumaroro to examine the object. The research team previously said in a news release that there is "very strong" evidence that the object is Earhart's lost plane.

The team previously said they will take photos and videos of the lagoon and Taraia Object. Then, they will use magnetometers and sonar devices to scan the area before dredging the item from the water so researchers can attempt to identify it. The process will be documented by the Archealogy Channel, with short vlogs on their streaming platform, Heritage Broadcasting Service.

Richard Pettigrew, from the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said that he believes Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumororo and camped there. He believes they survived on the island for some time, citing 1930s relics and human skeletal remains that were found there but lost over the decades.

"We owe it to Amelia's legacy at Purdue to follow the evidence," Steve Schultz, a senior vice president at Purdue University and field assistant on the expedition, told CBS News. Earhart lectured at the school before embarking on her final flight. Some of her belongings remain on display in the university's archives.

Some experts are skeptical. Ric Gillespie, the executive director of the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, told NBC News in 2025 that he does not think the Taraia Object is related to the Earhart expedition.
"We've looked there in that spot, and there's nothing there," he said.

For nearly a century, researchers have tried to find Earhart's missing plane, believing it will help them answer the question of what happened to the famed aviator. In 2024, another expedition team captured a sonar image that seemed to resemble a plane resting at the bottom of the sea. But the object was later determined to be a rock formation.

Wendy Rover of The Ninety Nines, an international organization for women pilots that Earhart helped establish, said she hopes the mystery of what happened to Earhart can someday be solved. Rover told CBS News that when she is flying and looking for safe places to land, she imagines Earhart doing the same while over the Pacific.
"Amelia Earhart was out there. She was going through that exact same thing," Rover said. "So yeah - what happened? What did happen? I would love to know."

title: Why you just got a $90 Social Security check — and who missed out
summary: Millions of seniors are getting $90 direct deposits from Social Security this week, prompting questions about the source of the money.
story: Millions of seniors are receiving $90 deposits from the Social Security Administration this week, prompting some to question the source of the money. The checks are tied to the Trump administration's announcement that it would send checks to about 20 million Medicare enrollees to lower healthcare costs.

President Trump on Friday announced that the administration would send the money to some participants in the healthcare plan's Part B, which pays for doctor visits, outpatient care and preventive screenings. About one-third of Medicare Part B's 62.9 million enrollees are eligible, with about 40 million not qualifying for the payments.

The payments are funded by the Medicare Improvement Fund, which was set up by Congress to improve and support the original Medicare fee-for-service program. Experts say the $90, while helpful, won't fully offset higher costs facing Medicare recipients.
Premiums for Part B rose by more than $200 annually in 2026 and are projected to increase by nearly $80 in 2027, according to the Medicare trustees' most recent annual report.
Americans of all ages are grappling with rising healthcare costs, which they cite as a top financial concern, according to polling from nonprofit health policy research organization KFF.
Who qualifies for the $90 checks?

Seniors enrolled in Part B under traditional Medicare and who don't pay income-related premiums or receive premium assistance from Medicaid are eligible for the one-time payment. Beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Advantage are ineligible for the payments.
That leaves more than 20 million Part B enrollees who are eligible, according to a CMS fact sheet.

"People who are paying the income-related premium have higher incomes to begin with, so the thinking is that they may be better able to absorb higher costs and wouldn't benefit as much from the $90 payment as people with lower incomes," Juliette Cubanski, vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, told CBS News.
Medicare Advantage isn't the same as traditional Medicare, which is likely why those enrollees don't qualify for the payments, she added.
The agency said the initiative improves Medicare and makes coverage more affordable by putting "healthcare dollars back where they belong – in the hands of our Medicare beneficiaries."
How will the money be sent?

Most eligible beneficiaries will receive the $90 rebate through a direct deposit from the Social Security Administration on or around Oct. 8, according to the CMS fact sheet. Some seniors reported receiving the payments or pending deposits on Tuesday, according to social media reports.

Some beneficiaries will receive a $90 paper check from the U.S. Department of the Treasury later in October. It will include the following message: "Medicare Improvement Fund Payment; $90 Payment to Offset October Premium."
Some advocates say the paper payments could go unnoticed by seniors, especially given the volume of mail many receive from insurers during open enrollment season.
Why are 40 million people left out?
About 40 million Medicare Part B enrollees are ineligible for the $90 payment. They include:
Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plansThose who pay an income-related adjusted premiumPeople who do not live in the U.S.Beneficiaries who receive premium assistance
Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans
Those who pay an income-related adjusted premium
People who do not live in the U.S.
Beneficiaries who receive premium assistance

Eligible beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Part B can call 1-800-MEDICARE to determine whether or not they qualify for the one-time check. Beneficiaries who want to check on the status of their payment can call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213 beginning on Oct. 15.

title: Jim Bakker, who co-founded "The PTL Club" but fell into disgrace, dies at 86
summary: Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around "The PTL Club" TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died at 86.
story: Branson, Mo. — Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful "The PTL Club" TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86.
Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. His cause of death was not immediately clear.
The pair lived near the Missouri entertainment town of Branson and filmed their TV show, "The Jim Bakker Show," there since it launched in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020.

"He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry," Lori Bakker said in a statement. "Jim loved people deeply. He loved this ministry, and he loved the friends and partners who stood with him throughout the years. Even in his final days, his heart was still for the work of God and for the Gospel to continue reaching the world."

But it was another evangelical program that made Jim and his first wife, Tammy Faye Bakker, cultural icons - so much so that they were often skewered in the 1980s and 1990s by late-night comedians and parodied on "Saturday Night Live." A theatrical movie on their lives, "The Eyes of Tammy Faye," was released in September 2021.

At its peak in the mid-1980s, the Bakkers' ministry included not only the TV show, which drew up to 13 million nightly viewers, but also the Christian-based Heritage USA theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry — he preached, she sang and played the accordion as they crossed the country visiting churches and tent revivals.

They caught the attention of televangelist Pat Robertson, and in 1965 launched a children's show on Robertson's Christian Broadcasting Network. By 1966, he was hosting "The 700 Club," a Christian talk show.
Bakker left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. "The PTL Club" — PTL stands for "Praise the Lord" — became its signature show.
In its heyday in the 1980s, "The PTL Club" was drawing millions of viewers - and bringing in millions of dollars annually from followers.

Sort of a Christian version of "The Tonight Show," it featured chats with guests and Christian entertainers. Bakker offered upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye - charismatic and always wearing her trademark heavy mascara - sang. Most episodes were taped at their sprawling complex just south of Charlotte, North Carolina.
The couple was so famous that they were often parodied by TV comedians for their lavish lifestyle and Tammy Faye's abundant makeup.
Jim Bakker gets caught up in scandals

In March 1987, their empire began to crack when Bakker admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Bakker was forced to resign from his own empire, turning over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell.
Tammy Faye stuck by Bakker, often with tears running down her mascara, even as many saw his downfall as a fitting symbol of the greed and hypocrisy of the 1980s.
Things only got worse.

In 1988, Bakker was indicted for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL's finances. He was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison, though the sentence was later reduced to eight years.
At a news conference after Bakker was found guilty, Tammy Faye stood in front of the microphones and sang the hymn, "On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand."

Their marriage crumbled and Tammy Faye divorced Bakker in 1992, just short of their 31st anniversary, while he was still in prison. She later married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995 and spent about two years in prison.
Tammy Faye died of colon cancer in 2007.
Bakker was released on parole in 1994. He married his second wife, Lori, in 1998. The couple launched "The Jim Bakker Show" on the PTL Satellite Network five years later.

In June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic.
The lawsuit said Bakker and a guest made the cure claim during 11 episodes in February and March of 2020.
Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and his second wife adopted five children in 2002.

title: Alleged Chinese agent makes federal court appearance
summary: CBS News was first to report​ that the FBI arrested Wanying "Heather" Zhang on Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China.
story: A suspected Chinese agent appeared in a Los Angeles federal court Monday after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's son near Seattle last year.

Orange County, California, realtor Wanying "Heather" Zhang, 34, appeared calm, dressed in a tailored, white zip-up jacket, sweatpants and white sneakers, with shackles on her wrists and ankles. CBS News was first to report that the FBI arrested Zhang on Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China.
In court, she spoke only to confirm her name and that she understood the charge against her of working as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government.
Zhang was represented by a public defender at the hearing.
Judge Steve Kim rescheduled her detention hearing to Wednesday to give Zhang more time to hire a private criminal defense attorney.
Zhang was remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals until her Wednesday hearing.
The public defender, Chad Pennington, told the judge he believed Zhang intended to hire private counsel.
Her husband, Edric Ding, watched the proceedings, flanked by his sister, attorney Elaine Lori.
Standing at the podium, Zhang looked back at her husband briefly, but showed no emotion.

Lori and Ding declined to comment inside the courthouse and remained silent as they were questioned by reporters as they walked to their car after the hearing. When reached by phone on Sunday, Ding told CBS News, "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.

Three prosecutors represented the Justice Department: Scott Lara of the National Security Division's Counterintelligence and Export Control Section, and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Amanda Elbogen and Colin Scott. They said they were not authorized to comment.

U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli posted a video on X of Zhang being frogmarched through the airport by federal law enforcement on Sunday, wearing the same outfit she wore in court on Monday.

A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of allegedly traveling to Seattle in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.

Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.
The FBI agent's affidavit claimed the government obtained text messages between Zhang and Chinese government officials evidencing the alleged surveillance.

In one exchange, Zhang allegedly texted her supposed Chinese government handler on the day of her alleged Seattle trip, "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," while footage from Ting-Yu's neighbor's security camera showed her "appearing to film" the president's son, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening, according to the affidavit.
As well as arresting Zhang on Sunday, FBI agents also searched her home in an upscale suburb of Irvine, California.
A resident of the neighborhood said she saw about 10 FBI agents searching Zhang's home on Sunday morning.

"Several of them were sitting at a table inside the garage," said the neighbor, who asked to remain anonymous due to safety concerns. "Even the ones standing guard were wearing gloves. They told us there was a search going on."
Zhang appears to have been renting the home, after selling her 6,030-square-foot, six-bed house a mile away for $6 million in June, according to property records.
A former neighbor told CBS News he was surprised that the young realtor couple could afford such an expensive property.
"She introduced herself as Heather," said the neighbor, who also asked to remain anonymous due to safety concerns. "She was super friendly.

"Usually, the people here, they're a little bit older, because the price of the homes is from $3 million to $10 million. But they were very young," the neighbor continued. "They did a lot of upgrades. Even though the house was almost brand new, they started changing so many things."
"Two years later, they only sold it for a little bit higher than what they purchased. It didn't make sense why would they want to lose money after spending all of that money," the neighbor added.

The Justice Department claims Zhang was working as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government from June 2025 to September 2025, and plotted her surveillance mission with Beijing officials during a trip to China in June 2025.

"The complaint in this case lays bare a brazen plot directed by the Chinese government to conduct a covert surveillance mission on U.S. soil targeting close relatives of a Taiwanese government official," Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division said in a statement released Monday.

"Wanying Zhang's arrest for allegedly acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government makes clear how far China's authoritarian regime will go to advance its goals. However, this case also demonstrates the FBI's unwavering commitment to defending the sovereignty of our democratic allies and combating all attempts by the Chinese government - and any foreign adversary - to conduct transnational repression within our borders," Rozhavsky said.
The Chinese and Taiwanese governments have not responded to requests for comment.

title: FBI arrests woman at LAX accused of being Chinese agent
summary: Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was arrested on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
story: The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News.

Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.
It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney.

A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.

Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.

"If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint.

Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades. It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured.
CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment.
The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home.
Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening.
CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu.
Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.
The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account.
"Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote.

The complaint claims  Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security.
Holt's affidavit claims  Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission.
She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint.
On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said.
Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties.

Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications.

Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA, Taiwan's national news agency.
Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S.

Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang, 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent.
Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents.

The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime.

New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China.

In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China.

title: British Airways flight drops 27,000 feet, returns to London
summary: A spokesperson for British Airways said there was a technical issue and that the aircraft later landed safely.
story: A British Airways flight dropped about 27,000 feet in 10 minutes while en route from London to Chicago on Monday, according to flight data.
The plane started the descent from 36,000 feet to 9,000 feet about 30 minutes after it departed London, tracking data from FlightAware shows. It appeared to be a controlled descent.
A spokesperson for British Airways said there was a technical issue and that the aircraft later landed safely.
Flight data shows the plane turned around over Ireland and circled for a few hours, apparently to burn off fuel.
It lfinally landed back at Heathrow Airport Monday evening local time. Video of the landing was captured by an automatic tracking camera streaming live to the Flightradar24 YouTube channel.
"Customers disembarked the aircraft normally and our teams are working to get their travel plans back on track as quickly as possible," the airline spokesperson said.

title: Coca-Cola reveals new flavors for Coke, Powerade and other brands
summary: Coca-Cola said it will roll out the new flavors, all fruit-inspired, in 2027. Here's what the beverage giant is planning.
story: Coca-Cola is refreshing its beverage lineup with a series of new fruit flavors.

The company said Monday that it will roll out "innovations" for its Coca-Cola, Fairlife, Mr. Pibb, Powerade and Topo Chico brands starting in 2027. Coca-Cola will showcase the new products at the National Association of Convenience Stores event in Las Vegas, Nevada, this week.

A Coca-Cola spokesperson said the company is also testing several new products in New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania to gauge consumer interest in a prebiotic version of Coca-Cola Zero Sugar, Sprite Zero Sugar and Fresca.
Coca-Cola fans will have two new flavors to try next year: Coca-Cola Cherry Lime is scheduled to debut in February, and Coca-Cola Strawberry Float will make its premiere in the summer.

The cherry lime product is a new spin on Coca-Cola Cherry, while the strawberry float version appears to be a nod to the popular dessert that blends soda and ice cream. Both come in sugar and zero-sugar options.

Other Coca-Cola beverage brands are also set to get a fruit-inspired refresh next year. Powerade will add watermelon and lemon-lime zero-sugar options in January 2027. Mr. Pibb, a spicy cherry soft drink, will debut "Mr. Pibb Black-Current" in the spring, while a "berry-forward" flavor will be offered for a limited time.

Topo Chico, a carbonated mineral water product, will launch a pineapple-coconut flavor in February, building on its existing lineup of fruit flavors, which include raspberry with lemon, passionfruit and tropical mango, among others.

Core Power protein shakes, sold under the Fairlife brand, will be available in banana and strawberry beginning in January, the first new flavors in almost a decade. Both will contain 26 grams of protein, while the banana flavor will also be available in a 42-gram version.

title: What to know about plague amid reports of Russian lab worker's death
summary: Reports of a lab worker dying in Russia after allegedly being exposed to plague have raised concerns, even as the WHO says the public health risk is low.
story: U.S. and world health officials are calling on Russia to share more information after Russian media reports said a scientist at an infectious disease research facility in Siberia died after possibly contracting plague during a lab accident.
The reports have caused concern, even as the World Health Organization says "the public health risk to the general population appears to be low," based on the current information.
Dr. Céline Gounder, a CBS News medical contributor and editor-at-large for public health at KFF Health News, echoed that belief on "CBS Mornings" on Tuesday.
"The American public does not need to be worried," she said.
Still, an official cause of death has not been made public and a lack of transparency from Russia has led some experts to question if the lab worker had the plague.

"The response doesn't fit plague. It's not congruent with plague," Dr. Amesh Adalja, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, told CBS News. "Plague is something, in the 21st century, that's treatable with antibiotics."
Here's what to know.
Concern about situation in Russia

Russian media has reported that a female researcher, identified as Darya Shipilova, 28, died after being exposed to the plague in a lab accident at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute. Initial reports said that Shipilova broke a test tube containing the plague bacteria Yersinia pestis in late September, came down with severe pneumonia and died of her illness.
The World Health Organization said Shipilova died of severe pneumonia overnight into Oct. 2.
Russian officials have since cast doubt on those reports. Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said there was no accident and that Shipilova had died of "pneumonia of unknown origin."

The WHO said it was told by Russia on Oct. 6 that no plague was detected. The global health agency said it asked Russian authorities to provide information about which pathogen caused Shipilova's illness.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday called on Russia to be more transparent, and said the nation should "share more information with the world."

A State Department spokesperson later told CBS News that the U.S. Embassy in Moscow had "engaged Russian authorities about the reported death" and "asked for additional information," which it has encouraged Russia to share "quickly and transparently."
The WHO said it is following the situation closely and requesting further information from Russian authorities.
What is plague?
Plague is caused by the Yersinia pestis bacteria. There are three main types of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.
Bubonic plague is the most common form of plague. Infected people may have painfully swollen lymph nodes known as buboes, along with fever and chills, a severe headache, body aches and exhaustion.

Septicemic plague happens when the Yersinia pestis bacteria enters the bloodstream. Patients may develop fever, chills, extreme weakness, abdominal pain, shock and possible internal bleeding. Some skin may turn black and die.

Pneumonic plague typically occurs when the other forms of plague are not treated and the Yersinia pestis bacteria infects the lungs. Patients develop pneumonia and may show fever, headache, weakness, shortness of breath, chest pain, cough and bloody or watery mucus. The pneumonia could cause respiratory failure. This is considered the most serious version of plague, and is always fatal if left untreated.
Russian media reports indicated that Shipilova may have died of pneumonic plague.
How does plague spread?

Plague is most commonly spread through the bite of fleas carried by infected rodents. Animals, including cats and dogs, can also become infected from eating smaller animals that were carrying those fleas.
Pneumonic plague can be spread between people. In cases of pneumonic plague, droplets emitted when a sick person coughs can lead to others becoming infected.
Russia's health watchdog said that nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shipilova before her death were tested, and none had plague.
How is plague treated?
Plague can be successfully treated with antibiotics, health organizations and doctors say. Patients need to be treated as soon as possible.
Researchers who regularly work with plague can also be vaccinated for it, Gounder noted.
Plague outbreaks in the Middle Ages killed millions, due to widespread, common flea and rat infestations and less understanding of how to prevent disease from spreading.

About seven plague cases are reported each year in the United States, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. More than 80% of the cases in the U.S. are bubonic plague, the agency said.
Most U.S. cases occur in the West and Southwest. Cases are usually treated successfully, according to CDC data. The last fatal case of plague in the U.S. was recorded in 2021.

title: U.K. arrests 7th man on suspicion of terrorism over air base incident
summary: Police have now detained seven people, and released six on bail, in connection with the incident near an air base used by U.S. warplanes that President Trump and Britain's leader say has Iran links.
story: British police on Tuesday arrested a 22-year-old man in London on suspicion of a terror offense over a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that authorities have linked to Iran. It was the seventh arrest in connection with a suspected plot against RAF Fairford, 100 miles west of London, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran during the ongoing war.
The U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing force said the man, a British national, was detained in the Westminster area of central London on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.

The six other men who were arrested as part of the investigation have been released on bail, under investigation and monitoring. The decision to bail them drew criticism last week from President Trump.
Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said detectives "continue to pursue multiple lines of enquiry" and "remain committed to investigating all possible angles."

Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base early on Sept. 27 as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swooped on the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline —   in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the U.K. sees "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident, without saying why or what the nature of the suspected plot was.

Mr. Trump had previously said Iran "might be" involved, telling reporters on Sept. 28 that U.S. and British authorities worked "very closely" on the matter and "we know everything about them. We would not have released them" from custody.
Iran has denied involvement, but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

The U.S. moved its B-52 and B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford on Sunday, though it's unclear whether or how the move was connected to the arrests. Mr. Trump told reporters on Monday he didn't want to tempt "the enemy" by having the bombers there.

"We had a threat, and if we're going to be threatened, we would just move them, and that sort of alleviates that," he said in Washington, adding that the people behind the unspecified threat "would be linked to Iran," without offering details.

title: Amelia Earhart investigators to study mysterious object in Pacific
summary: Investigators have begun an expedition to study a mysterious "visual anomaly" that they say may be Amelia Earhart's long-lost plane.
story: A team searching for Amelia Earhart's lost plane has begun its expedition to the Pacific, where it plans to study a mysterious object that researchers say may be her aircraft.

The item, known as the Taraia Object, has been visible in photos dating back to 1938, the year after Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared over the Pacific Ocean during Earhart's attempt to become the first female pilot to circle the world. Earhart, Noonan and their Electra 10E plane were never found.

Researchers identified the "visual anomaly" in a lagoon on Nikumaroro, a small island in Kiribati about halfway between Australia and Hawaii. The island is about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, where Earhart and Noonan were planning to travel.

Now, a team of researchers from Purdue University and the Oregon-based Archaeological Legacy Institute are traveling to Nikumaroro to examine the object. The research team previously said in a news release that there is "very strong" evidence that the object is Earhart's lost plane.

The team previously said they will take photos and videos of the lagoon and Taraia Object. Then, they will use magnetometers and sonar devices to scan the area before dredging the item from the water so researchers can attempt to identify it. The process will be documented by the Archealogy Channel, with short vlogs on their streaming platform, Heritage Broadcasting Service.

Richard Pettigrew, from the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said that he believes Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumororo and camped there. He believes they survived on the island for some time, citing 1930s relics and human skeletal remains that were found there but lost over the decades.

"We owe it to Amelia's legacy at Purdue to follow the evidence," Steve Schultz, a senior vice president at Purdue University and field assistant on the expedition, told CBS News. Earhart lectured at the school before embarking on her final flight. Some of her belongings remain on display in the university's archives.

Some experts are skeptical. Ric Gillespie, the executive director of the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, told NBC News in 2025 that he does not think the Taraia Object is related to the Earhart expedition.
"We've looked there in that spot, and there's nothing there," he said.

For nearly a century, researchers have tried to find Earhart's missing plane, believing it will help them answer the question of what happened to the famed aviator. In 2024, another expedition team captured a sonar image that seemed to resemble a plane resting at the bottom of the sea. But the object was later determined to be a rock formation.

Wendy Rover of The Ninety Nines, an international organization for women pilots that Earhart helped establish, said she hopes the mystery of what happened to Earhart can someday be solved. Rover told CBS News that when she is flying and looking for safe places to land, she imagines Earhart doing the same while over the Pacific.
"Amelia Earhart was out there. She was going through that exact same thing," Rover said. "So yeah - what happened? What did happen? I would love to know."

title: How beavers are protecting West London from flooding
summary: Five Eurasian beavers were released into the town of Greenford in October 2023. Then, they got to work, felling trees, gathering branches and building dams.
story: To find a little wilderness in West London, take a left at the shopping mall and head under the highway. Near a McDonald's and within reach of the city's busy transport network, a family of beavers is reshaping a wetland and helping protect nearby streets and a Tube station from flooding.

Five Eurasian beavers were released into the town of Greenford in October 2023. They were the first to return to West London in about 400 years, part of an effort to bring back a species hunted to extinction centuries ago. The animals live within a fenced site that remains accessible to the public.
Veterinarian and conservationist Dr. Sean McCormack, one of the driving forces behind the Ealing Beaver Project, puts the chances of spotting one during a recent visit at 90%.
"Anytime from now you could see a beaver swimming across the lagoon here," he said.
But these animals were brought here to do more than draw an audience. They were offered a job.

The area around nearby Greenford Station had suffered repeated flooding during heavy rainfall. Local authorities were considering engineering works to hold back water before it reached the urban area downstream. McCormack and his fellow conservationists proposed a different approach: let beavers help manage it.
"They had planned a lot of expensive engineering works to create reservoirs to hold more water," he said. "And we said beavers could do that at a fraction of the cost and maybe more effectively."
The beavers got to work, felling trees, gathering branches and building dams. By July this year, they had constructed seven dams and created three ponds that help retain water.
Their engineering changes how rainfall moves through the landscape. Instead of rushing downstream, water is held in ponds, spread across the wetland and released more slowly.
The results came sooner than expected, McCormack said.

"By the second winter they were here — no flooding at all," he said of the downstream area the project was intended to help. "So we knew it would work in theory, we didn't realize they would do it so fast."
The project also reports that the dams have helped prevent flooding in Greenford Station's lobby and the surrounding residential area.

The transformation extends beyond flood protection. The beavers have built a lodge roughly 6 feet high, with an underwater entrance connecting it to the lagoon. Around it, their work is creating opportunities for other wildlife.
Beside a fallen tree, McCormack points out how a beaver chewed more deeply into one side of the trunk, bringing it down into the water.
"And then all that dead wood is going to provide habitat for beetles and woodpeckers and bats and all sorts of things," he says.
For visitors joining a guided evening beaver safari, the attraction is often simpler: catching sight of an animal going about its business in an unexpected corner of the capital.
Sometimes, baby beavers, called kits, make an appearance.

The breeding success has become another sign that the animals are settling in. The project reported that the parents, Willow and Woody, welcomed two more kits in 2026, their third consecutive year of breeding. McCormack has described their continued success as "nature's report card."
The lessons could reach beyond this patch of London: learning to live alongside beavers and harness their benefits could help communities facing the challenges of climate change, McCormack said.
And there is another benefit, harder to measure in flood levels or species counts.
"They make people smile," he said.

title: Democrats see White House "pay for play" scheme with Balkan gas project
summary: Democratic lawmakers accuse the Trump administration of lifting sanctions against a Bosnian Serb separatist leader in a bid to help enrich the president's allies.
story: London — The involvement of a small American firm linked to associates of President Trump in an energy project in Bosnia and Herzegovina worth more than $1.5 billion has raised questions about how the White House could be using its leverage in the fragile Balkan state.

U.S. lawmakers accuse the Trump administration of lifting sanctions on Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik in an effort to enrich and empower allies of Mr. Trump, and of undermining longstanding U.S. foreign policy interests in the region in the process.

On Sunday, Mr. Trump was hailed by Dodik after his Serb nationalist party won one of Bosnia and Herzegovina's three presidency seats, which are split between Bosnia's Muslim, Serb and Croat ethnic groups under the country's complex power-sharing electoral system.

"If it had not been for Donald Trump's magnificent victory … we would probably be political corpses today," Dodik told supporters in a speech, in which he also thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for his support.
Company with links to Trump poised to build gas pipeline

AAFS Infrastructure & Energy, a company incorporated in the U.S. last year and headed by President Trump's former personal attorney Jesse Binnall and Joseph Flynn, the brother of Trump ally General Michael Flynn, is close to securing a contract to develop the Southern Interconnection Gas Pipeline.

The pipeline project has been discussed by Bosnian officials for years, but long opposed by Dodik, who has close ties with the Kremlin. But Dodik, whose party has veto power in Bosnia's parliament, said he would not stand in the way of the proposal following the announcement of AAFS' involvement last April. Six months earlier, the Trump administration lifted sanctions against Dodik that were imposed by the U.S. Treasury almost a decade ago.

The pipeline would connect Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia's gas network, allowing Bosnia to import liquefied natural gas (LNG) from its neighbors. The project, which is valued at around $1.7 billion according to the Croatian government, would help make Bosnia and Herzegovina less reliant on Russian gas imports.
On its website, AAFS describes itself as a company focused on "energy security, project structuring, capital alignment, and long-term regional infrastructure development."
The company does not appear to have demonstrable experience in any similar energy projects.

The secessionist leader Dodik, who until recently served as the president of Bosnia's self-governing, Serb-run territory called Republika Srpska, has long been accused of undermining the U.S. brokered Dayton Accords, which ended the bloody sectarian violence between Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia in the 1990s.

The sanctions, which included asset freezes and visa bans, were imposed by the Obama administration in 2017. The Biden administration then imposed further sanctions in 2022, accusing Dodik of corruption, including the charge that he had handed government contracts to close business associates in Republika Srpska.

A congressional report published last month by House Democrats, titled "Pay for Play in the Balkans," alleges that those two decisions — the removal of sanctions on Dodik and his decision to not oppose the pipeline — are directly linked.

"The Trump administration has used its diplomatic influence and connections with shady characters like Michael Flynn … to facilitate the concession contract for the SIC [Southern Interconnection Gas pipeline] to AAFS Infrastructure and Energy LLC, a company owned and operated by Michael Flynn's brother Joseph Flynn and Trump-affiliated lawyer and political activist Jesse Binnall," the report alleges.
AAFS Infrastructure and Energy LLC did not respond to a CBS News request for comment.

Foreign agent registration filings (FARA) cited in the report and reviewed by CBS News show that Michael Flynn, President Trump's former national security adviser, last worked as a paid lobbyist for Republika Srpska in October 2025, the month during which the sanctions against Dodik were lifted.

Those same filings show that Flynn was paid $100,000 for that work by RRB Strategies, a lobbying firm run by Rod Blagojevich, the former Illinois governor who was convicted in 2011 of 18 counts of corruption and spent nearly eight years in a federal prison before being pardoned by President Trump last year.
Flynn provided strategic advice and counsel, analysis and information research, and introductions to the Republika Srpska government, according to the FARA filings.

Blagoyevich's firm originally signed a contract to "provide communications and public affairs support on behalf of the Republic of Srpska" in March 2025, separate FARA filings reviewed by CBS News show.
CBS News sought comment from email aliases associated with Flynn and Blagojevich, but did not receive any response by the time of publication.

On Nov. 13, 2025, the U.S. Embassy in Sarajevo said in a social media post that Chargé d'Affaires John Ginkel had met Bosnian Prime Minister Nermin Niksic to discuss the gas pipeline project and "to support the importation of U.S. gas through Croatia to consumers in Bosnia and Herzegovina."
One week later, the embassy announced a preliminary agreement for an "American company to develop, build, and manage the pipeline."
Four days after that, on Nov. 24, AAFS Infrastructure & Energy was incorporated in the state of Wyoming.
In January, the U.S Embassy in Sarajevo posted again confirming that a meeting had taken place between AAFS leadership, including Joseph Flynn and Binnall, and top Bosnian officials.
AAFS was then granted the status of lead investor and operator on the proposed natural gas pipeline in legislation passed by Bosnia's parliament in April.

Later that month, the Croatian and Bosnian governments signed a contract to construct the pipeline with U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright in attendance for the signing ceremony. At a news conference with Bosnia's energy minister on April 2, Binnall hailed the pipeline project as a "priority" for the Trump administration.
The White House declined to comment on the pipeline project last week, but an administration official said the sanctions against Dodik were lifted to prevent instability in the Balkans.

"This is yet another example of President Trump's pragmatic, farseeing foreign policy that has prevented disasters on perennial issues that his predecessors so often stumbled into," a White House official told CBS News on Friday, without elaborating on the type of disasters the Trump administration was preventing.

A State Department letter published as part of the House Democrat-authored congressional report said the decision to delist Dodik had helped ensure peace and stability in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The official who wrote the letter, Paul Guaglianone, said lifting sanctions against Dodik had led to Bosnian Serb separatists rolling back policies that would have destabilized Bosnia's government.

The lifting of sanctions "advanced U.S. interests in [Bosnia and Herzegovina] and the Western Balkans. On October 18, the Republika Srpska National Assembly (RSNA) withdrew most of the anti-Dayton legislation it had passed in recent years," the letter read. That legislation had included laws that would have blocked Bosnia's national police and judiciary from having any authority in Republika Srpska.

Political scientist and Balkans foreign policy expert Jasmin Mujanović told CBS News the legislation in question had already been struck down prior to the lifting of the sanctions against Dodik, and he was skeptical of the Trump administration's justifications for the move.

"This package of omnibus secessionist laws that the Serb nationalist authorities and the RS [Republika Srpska] entity in Bosnia had unlawfully voted through in the local assembly had already been struck down by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia Herzegovina," he said.

"If the argument is that the Trump administration nevertheless managed to get Dodik and his people to withdraw the laws, it's still unclear what the significance of that is, or for that matter, why, given that the laws are moot," he said, adding that it that would "result in sanctions relief for an entire regime."

title: Mexico arrests alleged cartel leader and fuel smuggler "The Tank"
summary: Authorities say "El Tanque" runs a massive fuel theft network and is linked to homicides, kidnappings and drug trafficking.
story: Security forces in Mexico have arrested an alleged leader of a notorious cartel who is accused by the U.S. of drug trafficking and a large-scale fuel smuggling operation, authorities said Tuesday.
Ivan Cazarin Molina (a.k.a. "El Tanque"—meaning "The Tank"), was captured on Monday in the town of Zapopan in Jalisco state, security minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said in a social media post.

Mexican authorities say Molina, the alleged regional leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), runs a massive fuel theft network and is linked to homicides, kidnappings and drug trafficking. He is accused of being involved in the attack on a Mexican Army helicopter in Jalisco in 2015 that killed members of the Army and the Federal Police.
Harfuch posted several images of Molina being apprehended by National Guard members and being escorted in handcuffs.
The U.S. Treasury sanctioned Molina in September 2024, saying he was part of the inner circle of "El Mencho," the infamous Jalisco cartel leader who was later killed in a military operation.

"Although primarily involved in fuel theft, El Tanque has also engaged in drug trafficking, extortion, and homicide," the Treasury said at the time. "El Tanque's fuel theft generates tens of millions of dollars per year for himself and CJNG."

U.S. authorities allege Molina manages a network of ostensibly legitimate retail gas stations where he sells stolen fuel. He is also accused of selling stolen fuel to third parties in Mexico, who in turn sell it to the U.S. market, often in Texas.
Fuel theft — more commonly known as huachicol in Mexico — has risen to the second most profitable revenue stream for Mexican cartels behind drug trafficking, according to the U.S. Treasury.

"Fuel theft and crude oil smuggling are cash cows for CJNG's narco-terrorist enterprise, providing a lucrative revenue stream for the group and enabling it to wreak havoc in Mexico and the United States," Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said in 2025.

One of Mexico's most powerful criminal organizations, CJNG is among eight cartels designated as foreign terrorist organizations by the U.S. government. In August, the State Department offered a $25 million reward for information leading to the capture of its new leader, Juan Carlos González, the California-born stepson of "El Mencho."

title: French high schools closed in biggest day of student protests in decades
summary: Nationwide protests across France continued for a third week as demonstrators rallied against poor school conditions.
story: Protesters disrupted hundreds of high schools across France on Tuesday in what a student union said was a historic morning.

The union, Union Syndicale Lycéenne, said 2,000 high schools were at a standstill and all universities were mobilized amid the protests by students, parents and teachers against poor school conditions.
The protests are now in their third week, with demonstrators demanding the government address underfunded and under-resourced schools, which many say are falling apart.
A large group of students blocked the entrance to their school Tuesday morning, gathering to waive signs and shout a chorus of chants.
"In Saint-Denis, just right outside of Paris, high schools see the ceilings falling apart, water in the walls, rats," one protester told CBS News.

Protesters have clashed with law enforcement, causing damage and setting school buildings ablaze. Police said they detained more than 5,000 people in connection with the protests, including more than 4,000 teenagers.
Video footage showed protesters screaming and running from officers, who have used various tactics to disperse them, including tear gas and stun grenades.

Amid the demonstrations on Monday, a 15-year-old student lost a hand after picking up a police grenade in the northern French town of Lens, authorities told the French news agency AFP. A police union source said the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand.

Last week, in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, an area in the suburbs of Paris, a 14-year-old suffered a jaw fracture after reportedly being struck in the head with a tear gas grenade, according to CBS partner BBC News, which cited the teen's lawyer.
Local officials have announced investigations into both incidents.
The French government, which is mired in political deadlock ahead of the country's presidential elections next spring, has yet to show protesters any meaningful concessions.
One protester told CBS News, "I'll make noise as long as I'm not getting a response."

title: Rubio calls on Russia to be more open about plague lab worker's death
summary: The World Health Organization says public risks are low after a plague center worker's death, but Marco Rubio says Moscow should "share more information with the world."
story: Geneva — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Russia to be more "transparent" about the recent death of a plague research center scientist and any risks associated with the incident, which Russian authorities have offered conflicting information about this week.

"I think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world," Rubio said Tuesday after arriving in Iceland's capital Reykjavik for a visit. He called on Moscow to be "transparent" a day after Russia's primary national health agency denied earlier reports by local officials that the Siberian lab worker might have died of plague after a lab accident and that anti-plague measures were imposed at multiple health facilities in the wake of her death on Oct. 1 or 2.
The World Health Organization said Tuesday that the public health risk in Russia and Europe was considered low after the incident in Russia's far-eastern Siberia region.

"The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole, and very low for the WHO European region," the United Nations health agency's spokesman Christian Lindmeier told reporters at the agency's Geneva headquarters.

Lindmeier said Russian authorities had identified all people who came into contact with the worker from the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, who has been identified as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, before she died and that none had symptoms associated with plague.
The center where Shipilova worked is situated in a part of Siberia where plague is found naturally in wild animal populations, the WHO spokesman confirmed.
Lindmeier said her "illness initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection," but that Russian authorities "are looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death."
"WHO is following the situation closely, working with headquarters to keep other countries informed," he said, and is ready to help Russian authorities if they seek assistance.

Russia's national health agency, Rospotrebnadzor, played down reports Monday by some officials in the Siberian region —   some of which were quickly removed from online platforms — indicating that Shipilova had died after contracting plague in a lab accident.
The agency said she was not diagnosed with plague, but died of "pneumonia of unknown etiology," suggesting doctors didn't know the exact germ that made her sick.

She died in an Irkutsk hospital two days after contracting the illness. The hospital where she was treated, and where her roughly 200 close recent contacts were evaluated, was then partially shut down under quarantine conditions, Russian authorities said. They rejected reports that several other health facilities in the region were also put under restrictions as a precaution.
Rospotrebnadzor said Monday that an analysis of samples from Shipilova revealed no microorganisms associated with her work, which involved handling dangerous pathogens at the lab.

The agency said Tuesday that many of her close contacts, having been brought in for screening, were allowed to go back home. It said some cold and flu infections, including several COVID-19 cases, were discovered, but nothing more sinister.
President Trump assured reporters on Monday that U.S. officials were watching the case closely and stood ready to help.

"We're looking at it very strongly, we just heard about it," he said. "They call it pneumonia, and pneumonia, you know, years ago you could treat pneumonia easier, and the microbes and the germs have gotten stronger disproportionately. But we'll help them."

title: What to know after U.S. Marine arrested for murder in Japan
summary: Police said they arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel.
story: A woman's murder allegedly committed by a U.S. Marine in Okinawa has triggered public outrage, prompted Japan's premier to slam a "heinous crime" and rekindled controversy over the heavy military presence on the southern island.
Here are five things to know about the latest case and Okinawa's thorny relations with the U.S. military bases.
What happened?

Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media.
Security camera footage showed a man entering the hotel with the woman and later leaving alone.

Ballard was arrested when a patrolling officer saw him walking later Saturday in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 15 miles northeast of Naha. His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo News agency reported.
Why are so many bases concentrated in Okinawa?

Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today Okinawa hosts 70% of America's military facilities and most of the 50,000 U.S. troops based in Japan today, despite comprising just 0.6% of Japan's landmass.
In the wake of World War II, Japan regained its sovereignty under the San Francisco Peace Treaty of 1952, but Okinawa remained under American control, making it a hub of U.S. military build-up.
The 1972 return of Okinawa's sovereignty to Japan did little to diminish the number of US bases on the island, leading to the disproportionate burden it is saddled with today.
Why is it so controversial?

There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military on the island. The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to prefectural police.
The heavy U.S. presence has led to a host of issues, from helicopter crashes and noise pollution to crimes involving servicemen, including the 1995 gang-rape of a local 12-year-old schoolgirl.
That rape by three U.S. soldiers in Okinawa fueled widespread calls for a rethink of a 1960 pact that outlined the legal status of Japan-based U.S. military personnel.
The latest incident has sparked widespread anger.
"I'm outraged and flabbergasted to hear that a suspect came to the (entertainment area) after committing a murder," Kenji Higa, who lives in Okinawa City, told the Okinawa Times.
People in Okinawa have long opposed the heavy U.S. military presence on the island, but some have come to see its strategic value due to what is widely viewed as a growing threat from China.
Some also argue the military bases create jobs and help boost Okinawa's local economy, accounting for around 5% of the region's annual income.
How does jurisdiction work?
The 1960 Japan Status of Forces Agreement is often accused of rendering U.S. military bases virtually extraterritorial and immune to Japan's domestic laws.
Japanese authorities are, for example, hard-pressed to conduct an on-site probe into alleged environmental pollution inside the bases and regulate low-altitude flights of their aircraft.
Among the most contentious is Japan's lack of primary jurisdiction over crimes committed by US military personnel while on duty.

Even if crimes are committed while off-duty, as long as the individual responsible remains on base, their custody won't be handed over to Japan until they are indicted, according to the Japan Federation of Bar Associations.
In this case, Kyodo reported that a police officer questioned and detained the suspect as he walked alone on a street in Naha's entertainment district late Saturday.
Japanese prosecutors started examining the suspect's case on Monday to determine whether to press formal charges in coming weeks.
If convicted, he could face life in prison or the death penalty.
How sensitive is the issue for Japan?

Despite the controversy, Japan -- which has a pacifist constitution -- relies on U.S. military might as a deterrent against any potential attack, stressing the importance of American soldiers being trained and on standby 24/7.
But Japan's safety is not necessarily America's only concern.

Experts say Washington essentially sees Okinawa as its strategic foothold to deploy militarily in the region and beyond, and the island is seen by both countries as important for monitoring China, the Taiwan Strait and the Korean peninsula.
In the past, American troops were mobilized from Okinawa to participate in conflicts such as the 1990 Gulf War and the 2003 Iraq War.

title: Coco Gauff decries "insane" amount of online racism after China match dispute
summary: Coco Gauff said she received an "insane" amount of racist comments on social media following a controversial point in her China Open match against home player Sun Xinran.
story: Beijing — Coco Gauff said she received an "insane" amount of racist comments on social media following a controversial point in her China Open match against home player Sun Xinran.

Gauff requested a video review, prompting some boos from the crowd, after electronic advertising boards lining the court flickered during a point late in the first set of her 7-5, 6-1 third-round victory over Sun, a 16-year-old who recently won the U.S. Open junior title.

"Hey everyone, you can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff, who is Black, said in a reply on X. "The amount of racist comments/dms I've received in the last few hours is insane. Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief."
Sun appeared about to win the point when Gauff stopped playing. The chair umpire then ordered the point to be replayed.
Gauff, a two-time Grand Slam champion ranked No. 4, went on to take control of the match on Monday.
"Xinran is (an) incredible talent and player, I apologized for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood," Gauff added in another post.
Sun, who was given a wild card entry by tournament organizers and was making her WTA Tour debut, appeared distraught after the loss.
Gauff, who reached the fourth round of Wimbledon as a 15-year-old in 2019, sympathized with Sun.

"I did not like to see her so emotional as I've been there and I really understand what it is like but this is just the beginning of an incredible career," Gauff said. "It was an honor to share the court in front of her home crowd."

title: Alleged Chinese agent makes federal court appearance
summary: CBS News was first to report​ that the FBI arrested Wanying "Heather" Zhang on Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China.
story: A suspected Chinese agent appeared in a Los Angeles federal court Monday after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's son near Seattle last year.

Orange County, California, realtor Wanying "Heather" Zhang, 34, appeared calm, dressed in a tailored, white zip-up jacket, sweatpants and white sneakers, with shackles on her wrists and ankles. CBS News was first to report that the FBI arrested Zhang on Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China.
In court, she spoke only to confirm her name and that she understood the charge against her of working as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government.
Zhang was represented by a public defender at the hearing.
Judge Steve Kim rescheduled her detention hearing to Wednesday to give Zhang more time to hire a private criminal defense attorney.
Zhang was remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals until her Wednesday hearing.
The public defender, Chad Pennington, told the judge he believed Zhang intended to hire private counsel.
Her husband, Edric Ding, watched the proceedings, flanked by his sister, attorney Elaine Lori.
Standing at the podium, Zhang looked back at her husband briefly, but showed no emotion.

Lori and Ding declined to comment inside the courthouse and remained silent as they were questioned by reporters as they walked to their car after the hearing. When reached by phone on Sunday, Ding told CBS News, "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.

Three prosecutors represented the Justice Department: Scott Lara of the National Security Division's Counterintelligence and Export Control Section, and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Amanda Elbogen and Colin Scott. They said they were not authorized to comment.

U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli posted a video on X of Zhang being frogmarched through the airport by federal law enforcement on Sunday, wearing the same outfit she wore in court on Monday.

A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of allegedly traveling to Seattle in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.

Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.
The FBI agent's affidavit claimed the government obtained text messages between Zhang and Chinese government officials evidencing the alleged surveillance.

In one exchange, Zhang allegedly texted her supposed Chinese government handler on the day of her alleged Seattle trip, "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," while footage from Ting-Yu's neighbor's security camera showed her "appearing to film" the president's son, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening, according to the affidavit.
As well as arresting Zhang on Sunday, FBI agents also searched her home in an upscale suburb of Irvine, California.
A resident of the neighborhood said she saw about 10 FBI agents searching Zhang's home on Sunday morning.

"Several of them were sitting at a table inside the garage," said the neighbor, who asked to remain anonymous due to safety concerns. "Even the ones standing guard were wearing gloves. They told us there was a search going on."
Zhang appears to have been renting the home, after selling her 6,030-square-foot, six-bed house a mile away for $6 million in June, according to property records.
A former neighbor told CBS News he was surprised that the young realtor couple could afford such an expensive property.
"She introduced herself as Heather," said the neighbor, who also asked to remain anonymous due to safety concerns. "She was super friendly.

"Usually, the people here, they're a little bit older, because the price of the homes is from $3 million to $10 million. But they were very young," the neighbor continued. "They did a lot of upgrades. Even though the house was almost brand new, they started changing so many things."
"Two years later, they only sold it for a little bit higher than what they purchased. It didn't make sense why would they want to lose money after spending all of that money," the neighbor added.

The Justice Department claims Zhang was working as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government from June 2025 to September 2025, and plotted her surveillance mission with Beijing officials during a trip to China in June 2025.

"The complaint in this case lays bare a brazen plot directed by the Chinese government to conduct a covert surveillance mission on U.S. soil targeting close relatives of a Taiwanese government official," Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division said in a statement released Monday.

"Wanying Zhang's arrest for allegedly acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government makes clear how far China's authoritarian regime will go to advance its goals. However, this case also demonstrates the FBI's unwavering commitment to defending the sovereignty of our democratic allies and combating all attempts by the Chinese government - and any foreign adversary - to conduct transnational repression within our borders," Rozhavsky said.
The Chinese and Taiwanese governments have not responded to requests for comment.

title: FBI arrests woman at LAX accused of being Chinese agent
summary: Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was arrested on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
story: The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News.

Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.
It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney.

A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.

Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.

"If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint.

Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades. It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured.
CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment.
The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home.
Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening.
CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu.
Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.
The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account.
"Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote.

The complaint claims  Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security.
Holt's affidavit claims  Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission.
She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint.
On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said.
Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties.

Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications.

Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA, Taiwan's national news agency.
Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S.

Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang, 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent.
Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents.

The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime.

New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China.

In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China.
