title: U.S. military removes bombers from U.K. air base following security incident
summary: All U.S. bombers deployed to RAF Fairford have been returned to their home stations in the United States, a Pentagon spokesperson confirmed to CBS News.
story: The U.S. Air Force has removed all of its bombers from a U.K. air base following a security incident that led to the arrest of five British men and one U.K.-Iranian national last month, a Pentagon spokesperson confirmed to CBS News on Sunday.
All U.S. bombers deployed to RAF Fairford have been returned to their home stations in the United States, the spokesperson said. The Wall Street Journal was first to report on the bombers' return.

"U.S. Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements," the Pentagon spokesperson's statement said. "The Airmen that operate America's bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States — anywhere, anytime."

On Sept. 27, five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
The suspects have since been released on bail.

A dual U.K.-Iranian national was also later arrested on suspicion of plotting a terror attack. The 25-year-old man was taken into custody in London on Thursday, and on Saturday, Counter Terrorism Policing announced he had been released on bail.
The British government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident at the air base, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week.

"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," the prime minister told the BBC.

Iranian officials have said several times since the beginning of the war that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. But the Iranian Embassy in London said in a statement last week that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Asked on Monday by CBS News if the Fairford base was secure, a spokesperson for Prime Minister Burnham insisted it was, and declined to comment on "foreign nations' military operations."
The spokesman noted a remark by Britain's defense secretary last week, about the country having "tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world."
"I would just point you to the president's [Trump's] words last week, where he praised our police, defense and security services in relation to RAF Fairford."
Mr. Trump did laud British authorities' cooperation with the U.S. military in the incident, but he also said he was "surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that."

title: Israel was prepared to shoot down FlyDubai plane, sources say
summary: Israel was ready to implement a long-practiced protocol after the captain of a FlyDubai plane was attacked in the cockpit, Israeli sources told CBS News.
story: Israel was prepared to shoot down a FlyDubai plane after the captain was attacked in the cockpit, even with over 150 Israelis on board, two Israeli sources with direct knowledge of the situation told CBS News.

The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, passengers on board the plane and the flight captain have said.

Israel has a long-practiced procedure for this kind of possible 9/11-style event, according to the sources. After the plane plunged 14,000 feet, the Israeli Air Force tried to contact the cockpit but got no answer. A pre-established committee was quickly roused and a command center established.

Fighter jets were scrambled and Israel's airspace was closed. But Israel called back the jets once it realized that, about 400 miles from Israel, the plane turned toward Saudi Arabia, and the Saudis scrambled their own jets.

The captain of the plane was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. A group of Israeli passengers and FlyDubai staff then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, according to accounts from the plane.
If Flight 1073 had gotten within a certain distance, Israel would have sent jets into Jordanian airspace to investigate, the sources told CBS News.

The Israeli fighter pilots would have gotten as close as possible to inspect the cockpit and try to make visual contact with the pilot to assess the situation, the sources said. They would have then done the same to the cabin to assess the status of the passengers. If there appeared to be panic, they would relay their findings to the Air Force and the pre-established committee.

If it was determined the plane was hijacked, and the potential hijackers maintained radio silence and made no demands, the committee would get the defense minister and the prime minister on a call, the sources said.

The protocol calls for a rogue flight approaching Israel to be shot out of the sky, but only the prime minister could have made that decision. The sources told CBS News that shooting down the passenger jet would be considered better than many hundreds being killed if a rogue plane slammed into Israel's prominent Azrieli buildings, the airport or another "high-value target."

The co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain said during his interrogation in the United Arab Emirates that he had planned the attack even before he was employed by FlyDubai, an Israeli official told CBS News. The co-pilot, identified by sources familiar with the investigation as Omani national Hamam al Hamami, intended to crash the plane at Ben Gurion Airport, the official said, adding that he had flown to Israel in the past.

The attempted hijacking was likely a lone-wolf attack, an early investigation by Israel shows, according to sources familiar with the matter. The investigation is ongoing and all avenues are still being explored, the sources told CBS News.

title: Russia plays down reported plague lab death and says, trust us
summary: A Russian plague lab worker died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," officials say, in response to initial reports that she was exposed to the deadly bacteria during a lab accident.
story: Russia's government played down concerns Monday sparked by media reports that a female scientist in Siberia might have died of exposure to the plague after a lab accident.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov stressed that the state health watchdog known as Rospotrebnadzor was the "lead agency with expertise in this area," and he urged Russians to "listen to official information" from its "highly qualified professionals."
The researcher who died has been identified by Russian reports as Darya Shipilova, 28, who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute more than 2,500 miles east of Moscow.
Russian media initially reported that she broke a test tube containing plague bacteria in late September, came down with severe pneumonia and then died of her illness.
The World Health Organization said she died of severe pneumonia overnight into Oct. 2.

The plague bacterium referred to by the reports is yersinia pestis, the same one that caused the Black Death that swept across Europe in the mid-1300s, killing an estimated 25 million to 50 million people. That pandemic, often referred to as the bubonic plague, was spread by fleas living on rodents and other animals in close proximity to — and in the same grim sanitary conditions as — people.
The pathogen, if untreated, can cause swelling, fever and death.

Shipilova, according to Russian media, died from the pneumonic plague, which is caused by the same bacteria but attacks the lungs and causes a fever and a cough that can turn bloody. Pneumonic plague can be transmitted from person to person, unlike bubonic plague, and can also be fatal.

The head of Russia's eastern Republic of Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, initially said Shipilova died of the plague in a post on the state-backed messaging app MAX. He later edited the post to add the word "possibly," according to an independent regional Russian media outlet that operates in exile, Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal).
He was not the only Russian official to walk back their words on the story.
Local officials initially warned people not to visit the town of Shelekhov, where the scientist was hospitalized and later died, citing "unofficial information" about a human plague case.
The post was deleted less than two hours later, according to both Lyudi Baikala and Astra, another independent news website.
Since then, Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, has said it carried out "anti-epidemic measures" that included testing nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shipilova.

The agency said some people had tested positive for colds or COVID, but that no pathogens causing dangerous infections were found. It also said there had been no accident at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, and it attributed the scientist's death to "pneumonia of unknown origin."
A WHO spokesperson said that based on the unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general public appears to be low.
Speaking with reporters on Monday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the reports of a suspected plague case in Russia were not cause for alarm, but "for focus."

"We know what we know, obviously, about whatever the Russians have provided," he said. "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected, and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread."

But Rubio said, given "very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia," he did not believe it was "cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus, and a cause to just keep an eye on it, and we're doing that."

title: Japanese leader calls woman's murder, allegedly by U.S. Marine, "heinous crime"
summary: A woman's murder allegedly committed by a U.S. Marine​ in Okinawa is a "heinous crime," Japan's premier said on Monday, as the new accusation of violence involving American forces sparked public outrage.
story: A woman's murder allegedly committed by a U.S. Marine in Okinawa is a "heinous crime," Japan's premier said on Monday, as the new accusation of violence involving American forces sparked public outrage.

Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving incidents by U.S. personnel have long sparked protests on the island, which bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of U.S. military facilities in Japan.  The new case involves Lance Cpl.     Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old U.S. Marine stationed at Futenma Air Station in Okinawa, who was arrested on suspicion of killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media.

Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.

A patrolling police officer then found a 20-year-old man, later identified as Ballard, who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 15 miles northeast of Naha. The officer asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station, where he was arrested, NHK reported.
His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo news agency reported.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told lawmakers the government has lodged a strong protest with the United States, urging its "full cooperation with the investigation" and "strict discipline among U.S. military personnel."
"The occurrence of such a heinous crime is extremely regrettable," Takaichi said.
Emotions run high
Around 100 people participated in a rally in Naha on Sunday, holding up placards stating their "strong protest" against the murder, Japanese media reported.
Okinawa native Sorane Sakihama, 24, who organized a similar rally in Tokyo on Sunday, said she cried upon learning about the woman's death.
"We couldn't protect her. That made me so angry and sad," the university student told AFP, adding that she was planning to organize another protest in front of the U.S. Embassy for Tuesday evening.
"I want to ask them — what are these soldiers stationed here for? They might say they are here to protect lives or boost security. But how can they say that when a life was taken by their own?"

Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters on Monday that "the government will work with the United States to thoroughly make sure there will be no recurrence, and reduce burdens on local residents."

News of the Marine's arrest immediately prompted Japan's foreign affairs and defense ministers to summon senior U.S. officials to convey their "extreme disappointment" and "lodge strong protests," Kihara said.

The incident came just a few weeks after Okinawa elected Genta Koja as its new governor, ending the eight-year rule of his predecessor, who had long pushed for a major U.S. military base to be moved off the island.
Koja, 42, accepts a central government plan to keep the U.S. Marine Corps' Futenma air base on Okinawa's main island, but to move it to a less populated location.

Calling the murder-robbery "extremely malicious in nature," Koja told reporters on Sunday it had "hugely shocked residents here who are forced to live side-by-side with the bases, and instilled new fear in them."
"I am infuriated," Koja said.
He said the incident showed U.S. efforts to "educate soldiers and improve their behavior have not been functioning at all."
Koja said he will travel to Tokyo "soon" to lodge a protest with top government officials, including Takaichi.

On Monday, U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass said on social media that he is telling U.S. military commanders this week they need "to hold our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity." He also said that he and Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, discussed the "next steps in strengthening that bond of trust with our Japanese partners and base-hosting communities."
Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today it hosts 70% of America's military facilities and most of the 50,000 U.S. troops based in Japan.

There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military on the island. The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to prefectural police.
A Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison last year.
In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
Under a bilateral status of forces agreement, the case is being handled by the Japanese authorities because the suspect was not on duty and was arrested off base.
Japanese prosecutors started examining the suspect's case on Monday to determine whether to press formal charges in the coming weeks.
If convicted, he could face life in prison or the death penalty.

title: Key Biden aide recalls "draconian measures" being considered against Israel
summary: In a CBS News interview, Biden-era Middle East adviser Brett McGurk recounted the administration's response to the Oct. 7 attack, its handling of the Israel-Hamas war, the role of Iran and the long-sought push to normalize relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
story: President Joe Biden was on the verge of taking "draconian measures" after an Israeli military drone strike killed seven World Central Kitchen aid workers in the Gaza Strip in April 2024, but U.S. intelligence that Iran was about to launch an "unprecedented" aerial attack on Israel prevented Biden from moving forward, according to Brett McGurk, a top Middle East adviser to four presidents.
In an interview with "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" taped Thursday, McGurk described Biden as "fed up" with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's handling of the war in Gaza.

"At that moment, if not for that impending missile attack, which we then had to deploy military forces … I think we would have taken some pretty draconian measures against Israel," he said, adding that cutting off U.S. weapons to Israel "was very much on the table."

The U.S. and its Arab and European partners helped protect Israel from the Iranian attack, which McGurk said included 120 ballistic missiles, 170 drones and 30 cruise missiles that were "all launched to land at the same time."

In his new memoir titled "Brink," which is set to be published Tuesday, McGurk recalled a tense conversation between Biden and Netanyahu around that time in which the U.S. leader warned the prime minister he could end the weapons supply. At the time, the Israeli government said it believed there were more than 130 hostages in Gaza and around 34,000 Gazan deaths, according to the Hamas-run Gaza Ministry of Health.
"You think I'm Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal," McGurk quotes Biden as saying.
McGurk spoke to CBS News ahead of the release of his new book on the Gaza hostage negotiations, "Brink."

The longtime foreign policy aide recounted the Biden administration's initial reaction to Hamas' Oct. 7 terror attack on Israel, its handling of Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza, the efforts to secure an Israel-Hamas ceasefire and hostage release deal, the role of Iran and — starting years earlier — a long-sought push to normalize relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
McGurk is no longer working with the Bidens and is currently a CNN contributor.
McGurk: "If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis"

Biden's handling of the Israel-Hamas war has drawn years of scrutiny — including from within his own party. During the 2024 presidential campaign, the administration faced intense pressure to stop military aid to Israel amid the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

The U.S. is the largest weapons supplier to Israel, and provides billions in aid. A 2023 State Department review of Israel's conduct found that it was "reasonable to assess" that Israeli security forces have used U.S.-made weapons in ways "inconsistent with" international humanitarian law obligations. Casualties in Gaza, "including high levels of civilian casualties," raised "substantial questions as to whether the IDF is using" U.S.-made weapons "effectively in all cases," the report said.

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen told "Face the Nation" in November 2024 that Biden didn't use U.S. leverage effectively, arguing he sent Israel "more bombs and more money" after Netaynahu disregarded his requests, and pointed to U.S. laws blocking arms shipments to military units that violated human rights.

Since then, debates over the future of U.S.-Israel relations have continued to rage. Some of the criticism that the Biden administration was not strong enough in its response to Israeli actions in Gaza has been directed at McGurk, who was the White House National Security Council's coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa and one of his most influential advisers.

McGurk noted that the Biden administration did pause some weapons transfers to Israel, including 2,000-pound bombs but never instituted a weapons halt. He believes some of the calls to go further may not have been effective.

"Israel also has one of the largest arms industries in the world, so the idea that had Biden gone further on a step on that course, it would have stopped the war, I just think the record does not support that," McGurk said.
McGurk also argued that exerting too much public pressure on Israel could have hardened Hamas' stance, ultimately setting back the negotiations to end the war in Gaza and release the hostages.

"I come back to the question: How do you end this crisis?" he said. "And I think the record shows: If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis, it's going to make it worse."

At the same time as the Israel-Hamas war, attacks on U.S. forces by Iranian-backed proxy groups surged. McGurk pushed Biden to punish Iran in an effort to deter the attacks, and expressed some frustration with Biden administration colleagues who were wary of striking Iranian officials in response.
What would've happened if Iran "made a dash" toward weapons-grade uranium
McGurk said part of Biden's goal was to prevent the outbreak of a broader regional war. Meanwhile, periodic aerial attacks between Iran and Israel continued.
In December 2024, McGurk traveled to Israel with national security adviser Jake Sullivan as they worked toward a deal with Hamas to release the remaining Israeli hostages.

During the visit, according to McGurk, Netanyahu talked about taking out nuclear sites in Iran, including at Fordow, a facility built inside a mountain that processed and stored highly enriched uranium. Fordow was one of the three Iranian nuclear sites that President Trump ordered to be bombed  in June 2025, eight months before the Trump administration and Israeli forces launched a wider war against Iran.

McGurk said the Biden administration was concerned in late 2024 that Iran "might make a dash" toward making weapons-grade uranium, and officials were open to carrying out strikes if there were evidence obtained that showed Iran was making a bomb. Netanyahu urged the US not to wait for that step. Iran had been building up a stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium, which is a short step from the material required to build a bomb.

"We actually had a principals committee meeting — that's everybody around the table — what would we do if we see that?" McGurk said. "And as I recall, unanimity on: We would do the strike in Fordow. We didn't see that. We sent a message to Iran, don't even think about it. But yet Netanyahu was clearly contemplating that."

Hamas and Israel struck a ceasefire deal that led to the release of some hostages a month after that, just days before President Trump was inaugurated and the Biden national security team left the White House. McGurk said he and Mr. Trump's Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff "agreed we're going to work in lockstep." He described how the Biden and Trump teams put pressure on both Hamas and Israel.
Hamas released the last living hostages in October 2025, as part of another ceasefire agreement.
U.S. saw no "warning or indicator" of Oct. 7 attack

The circumstances leading up to the Oct. 7 attack have drawn renewed attention in recent weeks, as The New York Times, The Atlantic and the Israeli newspaper Haaretz report on warnings that officials in Egypt and the United Arab Emirates allegedly delivered to Israel that Hamas was planning a major attack. Netanyahu has strongly denied that there were any warnings, but his opponents in Israel's election later this month have expressed outrage.

CBS has confirmed via a former US official and a diplomatic source that Emirati Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed al Nahyan, President of the UAE, did share a warning with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu in the weeks leading up to the attack. The UAE had learned that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major attack but did not have specific intelligence such as a date, time or location.
McGurk told CBS News the U.S. had no intelligence that could have warned about Hamas' Oct. 7 attack.
"We did not have anything in our system that would have been a warning and indicator," he said. "No U.S. intelligence of a warning or indicator."
But he said Israel should launch an official inquiry that probes its own security establishment and political leadership, much like the U.S. did after the 9/11 attacks.

"I think they had an assumption that was deeply ingrained that Hamas was deterred, assuaged, and was not about to do something massive on any scale like this," McGurk said. "I think that was a false assumption in their system, a failure of imagination, and it was tragic."
McGurk on the Biden-MBS fist bump: "I encouraged the president to just shake his hand"

Hours before the Oct. 7 2023 attack, McGurk said he met with the Saudi Arabian Ambassador to the U.S., Princess Reema Bandar,  to discuss a different issue — a potential pathway for Israel and Saudi Arabia to normalize relations.

MB SUGGESTIONED INSERT: Just weeks prior, Prime Minister Netanyahu had stood at the UN General Assembly in New York and predicted a new Middle East to include normalization between the Jewish State and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, birthplace of Islam.
"I believe that we are at the cusp of an even more dramatic breakthrough: an historic peace with Saudi Arabia," Netanyahu said.

The idea of Saudi Arabia establishing formal diplomatic ties with Israel had been floated to McGurk by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman nearly two years earlier, in January 2021, shortly after Biden took office, McGurk said, a deal that would have included a pathway to a Palestinian peace agreement. McGurk said he reported that extraordinary offer back to the President, but the U.S. did not act on it.

Biden was skeptical of Saudi Arabia, vowing in the 2020 Democratic primaries to treat the kingdom as a "pariah" due to U.S. intelligence indicating that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was linked to the murder of Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi.

McGurk also explained that Biden did not want to focus on the Middle East, and only reached out to the Gulf States after the chaotic August 2021 U.S. exit from Afghanistan caused the emergency need for the U.S. to ask those governments to take in Afghan allies fleeing the Taliban. The U.S. needed another favor in 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine, and turned again to the Gulf states, specifically Saudi Arabia, asking them to pump more oil to alleviate a spike in prices.

Rebuilding frayed relations because a necessity for U.S. national security. McGurk said it was a "mistake" that administration officials did not engage with Saudi Arabia more frequently early in Biden's term. He convinced him to visit in 2022.

McGurk offered rare criticism of Biden over his 2022 visit to Saudi Arabia, which came during a global spike in energy prices. He recounts that for 18 minutes Air Force One sat on the tarmac in the Kingdom as Biden argued with aides over how he would greet the Crown Price at his palace.
Rather than shaking bin Salman's hand, Biden famously gave him a fist bump.

"He was concerned about the optics and the imagery," McGurk told CBS News, and "I encouraged the president to just shake his hand." He later said: "We were asking some very hard things to the Saudis that we needed for our core interests, and so I think the fist bump set us back."

By 2023, the U.S., Israel and Saudi Arabia were working toward a normalization agreement, a complicated deal that likely would have involved the U.S. offering Saudi Arabia a civil nuclear program and Israel agreeing to concessions around the Palestinian territories. The Oct. 7 attack derailed those talks — and President Biden often openly theorized that Hamas may have sought to prevent normalization.
McGurk said he "never saw anything to tie a direct connection," but didn't rule out that idea.

"Hamas, of course, does not recognize Israel, wants to destroy Israel, and I would not be surprised if one of the motivations on October 7th was to knock this agenda off the table," McGurk said, calling the prospect of Saudi-Israeli normalization "one of the biggest deals since the Cold War."

President Trump has revived the terms of that U.S.-Saudi arrangement, including the pledge to develop a civil nuclear program. However, the current Israel government has refused to discuss a Palestinian state in the wake of Oct 7 attacks, and the civilian death toll in Gaza from the war makes normalization more politically difficult for Saudi leaders.

Michael Douglas is letting go of all his secrets in his new memoir.

According to Page Six, the 82-year-old actor disclosed in his new book, "One Helluva Ride, that he had an affair with a co-star almost 20 years his junior while filming the 1992 movie, "Basic Instinct."

While many at the time believed Douglas and his on-screen love interest, Sharon Stone, were having an affair in real life, the actor admitted in the memoir that it was actually actress Jeanne Tripplehorn with whom he was having the affair.
"The truth is, I fell very hard for Jeanne despite our nearly 20-year age difference," he said in the book. "In fact, I was ready to officially leave my wife for Jeanne. I was crazy about her."
Douglas admitted to engaging in an on-set affair with "Basic Instinct" co-star, Jeanne Tripplehorn. (Pool ARNAL/GARCIA/PICOT/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)
MICHAEL DOUGLAS CONFIRMS SECRET AFFAIR WITH KATHLEEN TURNER ON 'ROMANCING THE STONE' SET
At the time, Douglas was still married to his first wife, Diandra Luker, although he has said they were separated and living separate lives. Luker eventually filed for divorce in 1995.
He went on to say that his "relationship with Jeanne lasted through production," but that they "went our separate ways" once they were done making the film.
"But I will always think of her as an amazing actress and a truly terrific woman that I was very fortunate to spend time with," he added.

"Basic Instinct" follows Douglas' character, homicide detective Nick Curran, as he is seduced by a crime novelist and prime murder suspect, played by Sharon Stone. Tripplehorn portrayed police psychologist Dr. Beth Garner, who was also Curran's lover.
Douglas wrote that his relationship with Tripplehorn lasted throughout production on the film and then they ended it. (TriStar Pictures/courtesy Everett Collection)

"The truth is that during the production of Romancing the Stone, Kathleen and I fell hard for each other and began a relationship," he wrote in an excerpt obtained by People. "It wasn’t a fly-by night affair; it grew naturally from how closely we were working together, how much pressure we were under, how much we respected and cared for one another, and how attracted we were to each other. Like every other guy in the world at the time, I was knocked sideways by Kathleen."

He wrote that when he left home to film the movie, he and Luker were "still technically married, but separated," and that while audiences were "certain for years that we were in a relationship together" while making the movie, they denied it, even through the making of the sequel and years later when they reunited on "The Kominsky Method."

Anson Williams is feeling better than ever at 77.
The actor, best known for playing Potsie Weber on the beloved sitcom "Happy Days," shared a shirtless selfie Saturday while celebrating his health, creativity and continued career.
"My yearly reminder to every Boomer: NEVER let anyone diminish us because of our age," Williams wrote in the Instagram caption.

He added that there are "mountains still worth climbing," and lastly gave "the absolute refusal to let anyone else decide my worth" as a reason for why he's thriving.
Williams also encouraged his followers to continue pursuing their goals.
"We didn’t come this far to become invisible," he wrote. "We came this far to become unstoppable. We’re not winding down. We’re still winning — and we haven’t even played our best hand yet."

summary: Robert Kelker-Kelly, the soap opera actor who played Bo Brady on "Days of Our Lives," has died at 62 in St. Peters, Missouri, after a reported medical event.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Robert Kelker-Kelly, the actor best known for playing Bo Brady on the long-running daytime soap opera "Days of Our Lives," has died. He was 62.
Kelker-Kelly died Oct. 3, a Missouri medical examiner's office told Fox News Digital.
Local police said officers were dispatched at approximately 8:16 p.m. that day after receiving a report that Kelker-Kelly was unconscious and not breathing.
HOLLYWOOD STARS WHO DIED IN 2026: PHOTOS
Robert Kelker-Kelly is seen as Bo Brady on set during a wedding scene.  (Gary Null / NBCU Photo Bank via Getty Images)
"Our officers arrived on scene along with the St. Charles County Ambulance District, and life-saving measures were administered but were unsuccessful," police told Fox News Digital.

"There was nothing suspicious noted at the scene," police noted. "Mr. Kelly had reportedly complained of chest pain shortly before becoming unresponsive, and the circumstances appeared consistent with a medical event."
Police said Kelker-Kelly’s body was released by the medical examiner to a local funeral home.
An official cause of death has not been disclosed.
Robert Kelker-Kelly has died at 62. (Paul Drinkwater / NBCU Photo Bank via Getty Images)
Born April 18, 1964, in Wichita, Kansas, Kelker-Kelly built a career spanning several of daytime television’s most recognizable shows.

He originated the role of Sam Fowler on "Another World" in 1987 and later returned to the soap opera to play other roles, including Bobby Reno and Dr. Shane Roberts.
Kelker-Kelly became widely known to "Days of Our Lives" viewers when he took over the role of Bo Brady in 1992, replacing original portrayer Peter Reckell. He remained with the soap opera until 1995.
Robert Kelker-Kelly and Lisa Rinna pose as their characters from "Days of Our Lives." (Joseph Del Valle / NBCU Photo Bank)
His work on the show earned him the 1994 Soap Opera Digest Award for outstanding lead actor. He also shared the 1995 hottest soap couple honor with Lisa Rinna.
He later joined the cast of "General Hospital," where he played the villainous Stavros Cassadine from 2001 to 2003 before returning to the role in 2013 and 2014.

In addition to acting, Kelker-Kelly was a professional pilot.
He was married to Linda Rattner from 1988 to 1992 and later married actress Miriam Parrish. Their marriage lasted from 1997 until 2013.

title: Pete Davidson takes fresh aim at Zohran Mamdani with biting critique
summary: Pete Davidson questioned whether NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani has any real ties to Staten Island, calling the borough "violently red" in politics.
story: Pete Davidson takes another shot at New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, questioning his Staten Island credentials and criticizing the long-delayed BQE project. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
Pete Davidson questioned Mayor Zohran Mamdani's affiliation with his beloved hometown of Staten Island.
Davidson – a loud and proud local – wondered if the mayor had any connection to the borough during a recent sit-down with Variety.
"Zohran Mamdani ... is he Staten Island? I don't know," Davidson said. "I don't think he's from Staten Island."
PETE DAVIDSON CALLS OUT NYC MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI OVER HIGHWAY MESS
Pete Davidson called out New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani over long-delayed construction on a major highway. (Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images; Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
The "Saturday Night Live" comedian debated if Mamdani had "Staten Island's heart," before admitting, "I don't think he's Staten Island."
He added, "I don't have a problem with the guy, but I definitely don't think he's Staten Island at all. Staten Island's the only red place in New York, and it's violently red."

Davidson, 32, explained, "You know, most of my family is, you know, on the red side. It's not that, like, storm the capital vibe. It's more just like, '[Trump is] funny. Like, I don't care. I just need something different.'"

He continued, "Like, it's not like a racist, misogynistic sort of thing, it's just like ... it's 1985 over there. You are not a real Staten Island politician unless you have a secret family and know one mobster."
Pete Davidson appeared on "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" on Monday, Sept. 28, alongside New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and musical guest TV on the Radio. (Disney via Getty Images)

Last week, Davidson pleaded with the New York City mayor to make a few improvements around his neck of the woods during an appearance on "Jimmy Kimmel Live!"

The BQE, short for the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, is a major New York City highway that runs through Brooklyn and Queens and has long been criticized for traffic congestion and aging infrastructure.
Davidson's request was immediately met with cheers and thunderous applause from the studio audience.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani was sworn into office in January. (Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo)

He added, "So I don't know what mob front or whatever, who's getting money from whatever, but just fix it, please."

"Pete Davidson wants to know what's going on in the BQE," Kimmel said. "He says he drives by it and he sees nobody doing anything. He said it's been like since before he was born."

title: Richard Gere confronts Hollywood fame, ego and greed as 'dark clouds' that threaten inner peace
summary: Richard Gere reveals how more than 40 years of practicing Buddhism helps him battle ego, greed and jealousy in his decades-long Hollywood career.
story: Richard Gere reflects on the values that shaped his life and explains why kindness, compassion and being of service to others can lead to greater happiness. The actor serves as executive producer of the documentary "Wisdom of Happiness."
Richard Gere has spent decades in Hollywood, but he hasn’t let fame go to his head — at least not without a fight.

The actor serves as an executive producer of the documentary "Wisdom of Happiness," which explores the Dalai Lama’s teachings and the pursuit of lasting joy. Gere has practiced Buddhism for more than 40 years.
Asked how he keeps fame and ego in check after decades in Hollywood, Gere admitted he isn’t immune.
TIM ROBBINS TURNS TO AYAHUASCA AFTER FEELING 'CONSUMED BY ANGER' OVER CANCEL CULTURE
Richard Gere attends the screening of the film "Wisdom of Happiness" during the BCN Film Festival at Cinemes Verdi on April 29, 2025, in Barcelona, Spain. (2025 Xavi Torrent)

"Everyone goes through that," the 77-year-old told Fox News Digital. "Everyone has the forces of greed, anger, self-cherishing, impatience, jealousy, the whole gamut. Everyone has that. So I think from Buddhist training and looking at these afflictive emotions and seeing where they’re coming from, they’re not innate in me. They’re kind of add-ons to basic clarity of the mind."

"It’s said that the mind is clear and knowing, so clear, vast, no limits," he said. "It has a sense of knowing, wisdom. The other stuff is just kind of add-ons, like dark clouds coming through. They come, and they go."
Richard Gere wears a tuxedo in New York, circa 1970. (Getty Images)
Gere also isn’t looking to Hollywood for happiness. The longtime leading man has learned that the perks only go so far.
WATCH: RICHARD GERE SHARES THE LIFE LESSON THAT BRINGS HIM HAPPINESS

"Well, clearly, happiness and peace [don’t] come from the outside," he explained. "It comes from inside all of us, and it’s there. You don’t have to create that. But I think it’s removing the bad habits, removing the causes that make us feel bad ultimately. But we’re in control of our experience for sure. We’re responsible for it. If you don’t like the way things are, you change it. And all things are changeable. They’re changing all the time anyhow. Probably when we fight the change is when we feel the worst."
For Gere, that also means questioning how much material success really matters.
Richard Gere prays during a visit to the Chogye Buddhist temple in Seoul on June 21, 2011. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
"Well, what’s really important? Is it what I own or what I am?" Gere said. "I’m not going to get anything from the outside that is permanently going to make me happy."
The Dalai Lama and actor Richard Gere stand following a press conference at Yale College. (Getty Images)
"Momentarily, yes, like a piece of chocolate, but that’s not permanent, is it?" he joked.
Gere has also found happiness far from the spotlight. These days, the star splits his time between Spain and upstate New York.
Alejandra Gere, Richard Gere and his son Homer Gere attend "The Agency" premiere in New York City on Nov. 21, 2024. (Getty Images for Paramount+)

"Well, Spain is my wife’s country, so she gets super happy there," he said with a smile. "And I’ll tell you when my wife’s super happy, I’m super happy. And I grew up in the Northeast. I feel very close to that. And my early family memories, and my grandfather’s farm in Pennsylvania, I think, had a huge impact. It still does."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Alejandra Silva and Richard Gere attend Paramount+'s "The Agency" New York premiere at the Museum of Modern Art on Nov. 21, 2024. (WireImage)
Gere and his wife, Spanish publicist Alejandra Silva, have two sons together. Silva also has a son from a previous relationship, while Gere shares his eldest son, Homer, with ex-wife Carey Lowell.

"My first son is 26 now," Gere said. "And I talked to him about what he’s going through right now. And I remember myself as a 25-year-old, 26-year-old person. Of course, my concerns were different. I certainly was more susceptible to what people said and thought about me and about anything else. And frankly, I don’t care that much about it right now, what anyone thinks or says."

Richard Gere and his mother, Doris Gere, attend the 19th annual American Museum of the Moving Image Benefit at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel in New York City. (WireImage for NBC Universal Photo Department)

Looking back, Gere recalled growing up in "an extraordinary Christian family" with roots in a small town in Pennsylvania. His father, Homer Gere, spent his childhood milking cows, and both his parents instilled in him the importance of helping others — values he carried with him when he discovered Buddhism in his 20s.
Richard Gere and Vicki Sue Robinson appear on Broadway in November 1971. (Getty Images)

"I grew up with that imprint, I think, from my dad and my mom, but there was something about Buddhism that kind of went beyond that and was willing to explore the larger questions," Gere said. "What is reality? What am I? What is a human being?"
"Am I capable of much greater things than just worrying about myself?" he continued. "And certainly, Buddhism wanted to engage those things [for me]."
Richard Gere and Julia Roberts on the set of "Pretty Woman," directed by Garry Marshall. (Touchstone Pictures/Silver Screen Partners IV/Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
But the lessons Gere learned from farmers have never left him.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Actor Richard Gere and his father, Homer George Gere, attend the premiere of "Three Christs" during the Toronto International Film Festival on Sept. 14, 2017, in Toronto, Ontario. (AFP via Getty Images)

"I think that farmers have a balanced sense of the universe," he said. "When the rain doesn’t come, who are you going to complain to? It’s about acceptance of things. It doesn’t make you happy when the rain doesn’t come, or it comes too much, but the forces of the universe are just the way they are. And along with it, hard work."
"Farmers work really hard," Gere said. "I still have the kerosene lantern that my grandfather used. He would get up at four o’clock in the morning and go do the first milking of the cows."

Richard Gere kisses the Dalai Lama's hand during a prayer ceremony celebrating his 90th birth anniversary at the Main Tibetan Temple in McLeod Ganj, near Dharamsala, on July 6, 2025. (AFP via Getty Images)
Gere said he sees that same work ethic in the Dalai Lama.

The Dalai Lama of Tibet presents actor Richard Gere with a traditional Buddhist prayer shawl during ceremonies on the West Front Plaza of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 17, 2007. (Getty Images)
"He still gets up at 3:30 in the morning, does his practice, works on his mind, works on his heart, works on his motivation, purifies himself every day," Gere said.

"He’s a human being, and he continues, as I said, to work on himself," he continued. "If we want to achieve what he’s achieved, to become really such an extraordinary, genuine person, we’ve got to do the work."
Richard Gere discovered Buddhism in his 20s. (Getty Images)
Gere said his connection to "Wisdom of Happiness" became deeply personal after he and Silva first watched the film together in New York.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Richard Gere and Alejandra Silva married in April 2018. (Pablo Cuadra/Getty Images)
"My wife was in tears," he recalled. "And I thought for his 90th birthday, this would be a great summation of an extraordinary life, well-lived, a meaningful life dedicated to others."
But as the film came together, Gere said its message began to feel increasingly urgent.
Richard Gere receives the International Award during the 39th Goya Awards ceremony at the Granada Conference and Exhibition Center in Granada, Spain, on Feb. 8, 2025. (AFP via Getty Images)
"In the time it took to finish the editing and finish the film, I think the world continued to fall apart in a very challenging, dark way," he said.
Richard Gere attends the 20th Anniversary Gala of the Prince Albert II of Monaco Foundation photocall at Opera Garnier in Monaco on Sept. 18, 2026. (WireImage)
Gere said he hopes the documentary reminds people they have the capacity for compassion.
"The beginning point, and maybe the end point, is basic kindness, a warm heart and generosity of spirit," he said.

Richard Gere and Alejandra Silva attend the ELLE for Future photocall at the Four Seasons Hotel in Madrid, Spain, on Nov. 27, 2024. (Getty Images)

title: Dolph Lundgren says he 'always understood' Sylvester Stallone due to similar abusive childhood
summary: Dolph Lundgren says a shared abusive childhood helped him understand Sylvester Stallone in ways few others could across their 40-year friendship.
story: Lundgren reflects on his longtime bond with Stallone, crediting his 'Expendables' role with reviving his career and saying their shared experiences helped them understand each other.
Dolph Lundgren believes his shared abusive childhood helped him better understand Sylvester Stallone throughout their 40-year friendship.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, Lundgren – who recently released his documentary "Dolph: Unbreakable" – explained the gratitude he has for the "Rocky" star after he "resurrected" his career.

"I think part of what's kept it going is I always have been very grateful to him and loving towards him. We've had our ups and downs, but I think, you know, he's discovered a lot of new talent and I think some of them perhaps haven't been as grateful maybe as some others, and I've always paid my respects to him because he's responsible not just for 'Rocky IV' but 'The Expendables.' I did four of those movies, which resurrected my career," Lundgren began.
Sylvester Stallone and Dolph Lundgren have had a friendship that has spanned four decades. (Kiyoshi Ota/Getty Images)
He continued, "I hadn't been on the big screen for 25 years when I did 'Expendables.'"
SYLVESTER STALLONE SHARES HARROWING NEW DETAILS ABOUT ABUSIVE CHILDHOOD
Lundgren went on to share that Stallone is a "complicated guy," but he understands him.
WATCH: Dolph Lundgren opens up about the ‘ups and downs’ in his friendship with Sylvester Stallone

"I've always appreciated him. I always understood him. I know he's a complicated guy, but we have a similar background, so I always knew where he was coming from, which I think he knows. And I think also, it got more emotional, and I believe that I have a feeling that you know, he's also opened up like I have over the years about his upbringing and what he's gone through," Lundgren said.
Dolph Lundgren and Sylvester Stallone on the set of "Rocky IV." (Getty Images)
The actor said the parallels in their lives go deeper than a shared abusive childhood.

"We have daughters; he has three, I got two. And you know if you think about it, who can you ... if you're an action star, who had an abusive childhood, who has three daughters, who has a ton of injuries ... Who can understand you? There's not that many people you can talk to," Lundgren said.
The star explained that there is only Arnold Schwarzenegger left that could possibly understand his and Stallone's upbringing and life story.
"I know he's a complicated guy, but we have a similar background, so I always knew where he was coming from, which I think he knows."

Stallone and Lundgren's friendship has had its share of ups and downs since they met while making "Rocky IV." Stallone told Jimmy Fallon in 2019 on "The Tonight Show" that he initially disliked Lundgren because he seemed "too perfect," but the two eventually became friends and worked together again on "The Expendables" films.

In a September interview with Los Angeles Magazine, Lundgren said they had a "little falling out" over the proposed "Drago" spin-off, but Stallone reached out after learning Lundgren had cancer, and they are now close again.
Sylvester Stallone and Dolph Lundgren attended the world premiere of "Rocky Balboa" in 2006. (E. Charbonneau/WireImage for MGM)
After beating cancer and surviving childhood abuse, Lundgren is now turning his sights on his own documentary.

Speaking to Fox News Digital, Lundgren explained that his newly released documentary is an ability for fans to see the man underneath the armor.

"I wanted people to see, to put together the puzzle of how, why did I play those characters and why did I end up being unbreakable, or at least appear to be unbreakable," he began. "It was all my personal journey. And I think hopefully other people may be able to relate to some of that."

Stallone, Schwarzenegger and Jean Claude Van Damme will be making appearances in the new documentary. According to a synopsis, "Dolph: Unbreakable" will include interviews with the three men, as well as home videos and archival photos, to show a "a raw and revealing portrait" of Lundgren.

title: Former Prince Andrew's historic police showdown could put seized evidence in jeopardy: expert
summary: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's legal challenge targets Thames Valley Police searches of his homes, potentially undermining key evidence in the Epstein probe.
story: Andrew Lownie, author of "Entitled," argues Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor worsened his own crisis and believes new Epstein-related details could still emerge.
Former Prince Andrew isn't waiting quietly for the police investigation into him to play out.
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor launched a legal challenge over searches of his homes following his February arrest.

Mountbatten-Windsor asked the court to rule on whether Thames Valley Police lawfully searched his homes near Windsor Castle and on King Charles III's Sandringham estate, according to The Daily Telegraph. A hearing will be held Thursday.
PRINCE WILLIAM SEES DISGRACED ANDREW AS ‘A TROUBLED SOUL’ BUT EPSTEIN FALLOUT LEAVES ‘NO COMING BACK’: AUTHOR
Former Prince Andrew launched a legal challenge questioning whether police lawfully searched his royal residences following his February arrest. (Kirsty Wigglesworth/WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"Whilst our investigation into misconduct in public office continues, we are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court," a spokesperson for the Thames Valley Police told Fox News Digital. "As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further."
Fox News Digital reached out to Andrew's attorney for comment.
The legal challenge could have significant consequences for the investigation, particularly if the court finds fault with how police obtained evidence.

"He is fighting the police process rather than waiting for the investigation to conclude," Richard Fitzwilliams, royal commentator, told Fox News Digital. "If he wins, it might affect evidence obtained through the searches which he is claiming were not lawfully conducted."

"The background to this is that the police have reportedly not obtained access to the unredacted Epstein files, which has reportedly affected their ability to investigate links between Andrew and Epstein," Fitzwilliams added. "The investigation has been widened from misconduct in public office to include potential sexual misconduct. It is the first time a member of the royal family has challenged the legal process since Charles 1 in 1649."

title: Prince William ‘incandescent with anger’ at Prince Harry as Diana anniversary deepens royal rift: Piers Morgan

Prince William isn't expected to reunite with his brother, Prince Harry, for a potential new documentary about their late mother. Asked about the reports, Piers Morgan argued the brothers' long-running rift makes any reunion unlikely.
"Well, they don't speak to each other and haven't done so for years," the host of "Piers Morgan Uncensored" told Fox News Digital.

Morgan went on to say that William is "absolutely incandescent with anger about what his little brother did in trashing the royal family," including "writing books, doing Netflix documentary shows, doing podcasts, always dumping on the family and attacking his wife, Catherine, attacking Camilla, attacking King Charles."

"Harry took out the spray gun," said Morgan. "And when you do that, then family members who are on the receiving end aren't going to like it. My sympathies are entirely with Prince William, who's a thoroughly honorable, decent young man who's just had it with his brother and wants nothing to do with him."
Fox News Digital reached out to Kensington Palace for comment.

Meanwhile, Prince Harry is considering several projects to mark the 30th anniversary of Diana's death, People magazine reported. According to the outlet, the Duke of Sussex has been exploring how he can "most meaningfully" honor his mother and her legacy ahead of the milestone on Aug. 31, 2027.

While various ideas are under discussion, People reported that no documentary has been finalized or confirmed. Harry has reached out to family members and friends connected to his late mother, multiple sources told the outlet.

Friends of William told The Times that next year is "a difficult situation for him" and that he remains "really emotional" about his mother's death.

The book, about Diana, is highly critical of King Charles III, who is receiving treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer.

story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

title: Matthew McConaughey says Woody Harrelson’s wild antics include 2 am visits, inviting strangers on vacations
summary: Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson share outrageous stories from their decades-long friendship, including a possible DNA test revelation.
story: McConaughey said his "hands couldn't keep up with my mouth" as he tried to sing and play music at the same time in his new film, "The Rivals of Amziah King."
Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson's friendship has put both of them in some wild situations.
While promoting their new show, "Brothers," the two actors, and close friends, have shared many anecdotes from their years-long friendship, which have sent the internet buzzing.

Whether it be finding out they might be brothers to Harrelson surprising McConaughey in bed in the middle of the night, these two Hollywood icons have made it clear they have an interesting friendship.
Harrelson and McConaughey have shared many crazy stories from their years-long friendship. (Eric Charbonneau/Apple TV via Getty Images)
Here are some of the most outrageous stories the two shared during recent interviews.
MATTHEW MCCONAUGHEY'S PIECE OF RELATIONSHIP ADVICE THAT KEEPS HIS MARRIAGE TO CAMILA ALVES STRONG
Late-night surprise
McConaughey shared Harrelson once climbed into his bed at 2 in the morning. (Shea Kastriner/USTA via Getty Images)
During an appearance on the "Glass Half Full" podcast, McConaughey described some of the oddities that come with being Harrelson's friend, saying "he's never gone through a front door in his life."
He explained that no matter how long it has been since they last saw each other, Harrelson has "never called or sent a message" to make plans, adding, "he just shows up."

"We hadn't seen each other for a year at the time when I was living out in LA. I hadn't seen him for a year. Guess my introduction to him," he said. "My wife goes 'ah.' And I go, 'Woah.' Two in the morning, wake up, Woody's in between us in bed! He had jumped the fence, picked the window, snuck in, and got in bed with us."
When host Craig Melvin told Harrelson that "people have been shot for less," the actor replied, "Well, I was hoping he didn't have a gun."
"But what a good way to wake up a friend, you know what I mean, and get to be next to Camila [Alves, McConaughey's wife]," Harrelson added. "Like, that was nice. She was warm to me."
Anniversary confusion
Harrelson and McConaughey have different accounts of when they first met. (David M. Benett/Dave Benett/Getty Images)
When speaking to Melvin, the celebrity duo also shared how they first met, although they admit they have different recollections.
McConaughey admits Harrelson "believes we've known each other one year longer" than he does, because "I don't remember the first time we met."
He blames it on the idea that they began taking shots together at 1 p.m., but when Harrelson corrected him on a detail in the story, McConaughey told him, "I don't remember. You tell me."

"I already knew of him and I liked him from a distance," Harrelson said. "And then I met him, and I'm like, 'Hey, let's do a shot,' and he's like, 'Man, I got a lot of work to do today.' I said, 'One shot's gonna stop you from all the work you got?'"
McConaughey then chimed in adding, "Hence, I don't remember meeting that day. It doesn't sound like that was the beginning and the end of the story."
Living on the edge
McConaughey once witnessed Harrelson do a handstand on the edge of a canyon. (Gary Miller/FilmMagic)
While telling Melvin about Harrelson's many talents, McConaughey casually mentioned that the actor once "did a handstand 18 inches away from the edge of the Grand Canyon."

"The stuff this guy pulls off because he didn't know better is still amazing," McConaughey said. "Most people do that stuff when they're a kid, and they lose it as they get older, because you know better. This kid, what are you, 60 what now... 65 and he's still doing handstands on the edge of the Grand Canyon."
While Harrelson tried to downplay the achievement by saying he was farther away than McConaughey is saying and that it wasn't the Grand Canyon, the "Dallas Buyers Club" star continued to praise him.
"I'm probably exaggerating less than from the edge on his hand, the Grand Canyon," McConaughey said. "The photographer freaks out. Never got a picture of it."
He added that had the photographer been able to take a photo, "it would have been the most epic shot."
Vacation antics
Harrelson once invited strangers to join him and McConaughey on vacation. (Chloe Kern/FilmMagic)
While promoting the new show, the two actors also sat down with Conan O'Brien on his podcast, "Conan O'Brien Needs A Friend."

During the interview, McConaughey shared an unbelievable story about the time Harrelson met a couple on their honeymoon while waiting for his luggage at baggage claim in Greece, and invited them to stay with him and McConaughey in the house McConaughey had rented for them and their families.

"You have a consistent habit of having an open heart and inviting people into your future life or yours or mine," McConaughey told Harrelson during the interview. "He's doing this routinely. He's, he's very consistent. We go on a Greek holiday and my family… we rent the place... We rent the place and they… we fly over, but they get there before us and we show up and there's two people sitting on the tailgate of a truck right in front of our rental."

He went on to say that at first he thought it was Harrelson and his wife Laura, but soon found out it was two strangers who told him, "We met Woody and Laura at the airport getting our luggage and… they're great."
When he confronted Harrelson, who had already claimed the primary bedroom in the rental, he told him, "They're great, man. They're going to be with us for a week."
Break-in
McConaughey shared that Harrelson would often break into his home and sometimes stay for months at a time. (Todd Williamson/NBC via Getty Images)
When speaking with People, McConaughey expanded on the idea that Harrelson would show up at his home "unannounced," calling it "one of Woody's great traits."

"He never comes through a front door. And he’ll swing by for an hour to say, ‘Howdy!’" McConaughey said. "It might turn into, ‘I’ve moved in for three months.’ It’s a beautiful trait how he makes himself at home."

Harrelson confirmed he does make a habit of making McConaughey's house his own, noting, McConaughey "tolerates it."

"There are times when I’m like, ‘Man, Woody, I need some space,’ and my whole family’s like, ‘No, don’t let Woody go. We’ve been staying up later having more milkshakes,’ whatever," McConaughey said. "The laughter’s been in the house a while."

"In Greece a few years ago, we’re sitting around talking about how close we are and our families and et cetera and my mom is there. And she says, ‘Woody, I knew your dad,’" McConaughey told Kelly Ripa on her podcast in 2023.
McConaughey explained to Ripa that his mother and father were divorced before he was born, so there is a possibility that she and Harrelson's father met during that time period.

title: Robert Blake’s son returns to restaurant tied to family tragedy for new murder mystery
summary: Noah Blake opens "A Killer Night in Studio City" at Vitello's, confronting decades of pain tied to his father Robert Blake's infamous trial.
story: Actor Noah Blake returns to Vitello’s with a new murder mystery show. The "Teen Witch" alum says it marks a personal step toward healing and forging an identity beyond his family’s past.

Twenty-five years after Vitello's became part of a painful chapter in his family's history, Noah Blake has returned to the restaurant to direct and star in a fictional murder mystery, describing the production as part of his healing journey.
The "Teen Witch" alum's "A Killer Night in Studio City," a noir-inspired immersive theater production set in 1958, opened at the famed Italian restaurant on Sept. 15.

"When I was first approached about this, of course, there was this little bit of ... and then I was like, 'Wait, what am I doing? Of course, I should do this,'" Blake told Fox News Digital. "This is a chance for me to, not rewrite history, but to create a new page and to create a new connection and a new relationship for me with this place, for my name with this place, for my family with this place."
ROBERT BLAKE DEAD AT 89

Noah Blake (right) stars in "A Killer Night in Studio City," which is described as "an immersive murder mystery where classic Hollywood glamour collides with scandal, ambition, romance, and murder." (Wes Chappell)

"I've got a four-year-old son," Blake said. "I want him to be able to go there and enjoy Vitello's as he's grown up, God willing, as long as Vitello's is there. And I don't want him to ever feel funny. I want him to think about, 'Oh, Vitello's, that's the place where daddy did that fun show.' Not this other stuff. I'm not trying to minimize that tragedy, but it wasn't my tragedy, and it was a cross that I've had to bear and still will probably for the rest of my life."
"A Killer Night in Studio City" is held inside The Velvet Martini Lounge inside Vitello's. (Wes Chappell)

Blake said Vitello's was a regular gathering place for his family while he was growing up, but he stayed away for decades. He eventually returned and agreed to stage the production there, saying he wanted to reclaim positive memories of a place he had loved.
Vitello's Restaurant in Los Angeles is seen here on May 5, 2001. (Getty Images)

"I want to go and do something in this space that is creative, that is fun, that is exciting, where people come and laugh and gasp and have a great time," he explained. "Some people may not even know [what happened] and the people who do might be curious and go, 'Oh, that has nothing to do with anything, and I had a great time.'"
WATCH: NOAH BLAKE SAYS RETURN TO SITE TIED TO FAMILY TRAGEDY IS ‘FULL CIRCLE’
The history Blake is trying to move beyond dates back to 2001, when his father Robert Blake's wife, Bonny Lee Bakley, was killed after the couple had dinner at Vitello's.

The actor was acquitted of murder in 2005 in connection with Bakley's killing. Bakley was shot and killed while sitting in Robert's car near the restaurant. A civil jury later found him liable for her death and ordered him to pay Bakley's family $30 million, prompting him to file for bankruptcy, according to The Associated Press.
Robert Blake in a scene from the 1967 movie "In Cold Blood." (Dukas/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
An appeals court later reduced the award to $15 million, after which the parties reached a confidential settlement. Robert died in 2023 at 89.

Robert Blake, star of the 1970s show "Baretta," stands in court with his attorney M. Gerald Schwartzback on Sept. 17, 2004, for a pretrial conference. Blake was accused of murdering his wife, Bonny Lee Bakley, who was found shot dead in her car in Los Angeles in May 2001. (Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)
Rose Lenore, Bakley's daughter with Robert, feels differently about the production. She told Fox News Digital that Vitello's remains too painful for her and others who loved her mother.

"I think him doing it at Vitello's is upsetting for me and anyone who loved Bonny," she said. "And there were quite a few people who did. She left behind three children, plus me. She also left behind a sister, my aunt, who misses her dearly. And so, to have Robert Blake's son do any show at Vitello's, let alone a murder mystery show, I find that to be insensitive and upsetting."
Bonny Lee Bakley, 44, was murdered on May 4, 2001. (ZUMA Press/ZUMA Archive / Shutterstock)

"I don't even care what the show is about," Lenore said. "I'm also not here to invalidate anyone's healing journey, if that's what this is for him. But I also think it's my moral obligation to stand up for what I believe in. I would still be upset if he was doing anything else. And for Noah to be doing a happy, fun show — I think it's in poor taste."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Rose Lenore Blake attends the Los Angeles screening of "Happy Anniversary" at LOOK Dine-In Cinemas Glendale in Glendale, California, on Jan. 29, 2025. (Getty Images)

"I'm not wishing any harm on Noah," Lenore continued. "I wish him well in his life and career. But it would be hard for me to stay silent on something like this. It would be hard for me to stay silent about my mother."

Responding to Lenore's criticism, Blake wrote in a statement to Fox News Digital, "I have my own deeply personal reasons for doing this play. Vitello's was a place that I loved my entire life. Over time, that place became the physical embodiment for me of a much larger and devastating chapter of my life — one thing that I had nothing to do with, but whose consequences I have had to endure for years."
Noah Blake is seen here with his father Robert Blake during happier times. (Courtesy of Noah Blake)

"Choosing to walk back into that space now and create something uniquely mine — something lighthearted and entertaining that people are enjoying — is part of my own healing journey," he wrote. "It's about taking a place that had come to represent something painfully dark in my life and allowing it to represent something else. I'm not erasing history or rewriting it. I'm simply adding a new page to it, and I don't ask or expect anyone else to sign off on what I need to do to heal."

Actor Robert Blake and his son Noah Blake pause in front of the coffin bearing Bonny Lee Bakley on May 25, 2001, during a funeral ceremony in Los Angeles. Behind them are Robert Blake's assistant, Earle Caldwell, and an unidentified woman. (Getty Images)

"Rose is absolutely entitled to her feelings," Blake continued. "I've been there for her many times over the years, and I care for her. She chose to express her feelings about this publicly, which certainly wouldn't have been my choice and still isn't. I would much rather have had a private conversation with her. I've reached out and asked her to call me so that we could talk about this, and that conversation has yet to happen. But that door remains open for her."
Blake said returning to Vitello's has also forced him to revisit his complicated relationship with his late father.

Noah Blake (left) told Fox News Digital he hopes to one day make a documentary exploring his father Robert Blake's case, sitting down with those who knew the actor in an effort to better understand what happened the night his wife, Bonny Lee Bakley, was killed. (WireImage)

"I don't think people really realize when something like that happens, how many lives are impacted in such a profound way," he explained. "I had to wrestle with who my father really was for everything I thought he was or knew or saw him as. Did he do this thing? Was he really capable of this? Was he that far gone? Was my father this monster?"
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Actor Robert Blake speaks exclusively to Barbara Walters from the Los Angeles County Jail, where he is being held without bail on charges of killing his wife, Bonnie Lee Bakley. Blake said he did the interview for his then-3-year-old daughter, Rosie. His first and only televised interview from jail aired on "20/20" on Wednesday, Feb. 26, 2003. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"It's tough because it makes you question a lot. 'What is my genetic makeup?' It was years of intense scrutiny, and it was impossible to live my life, and for other people as well. It's not cool to know that this guy's son had a nervous breakdown and couldn't leave his house for six months and was having panic attacks and night sweats and was incapable of functioning."
Robert Blake poses with his children Delinah and Noah at the Emmy Awards in Pasadena, California, in September 1977. (Getty Images)

"There were moments my father could be a very loving, kind, decent, generous human being," he said. "And there were times when he could just be an absolute f---ing monster and just the worst kind of selfish and menacing and threatening."

"A Killer Night in Studio City" is running through Halloween. (Wes Chappell)
Before his death, Robert fiercely denied murdering Bakley.

For Blake, returning to the restaurant carries a meaning beyond the fictional story he says he wants to tell. While he recognizes the connection others may make to his family's past, Blake stressed he does not want that history to define him.
Noah Blake told Fox News Digital he wants to create new memories at Vitello's. (Wes Chappell)

"... I live my life as me," he said.

title: Phil Collins gets frank on marriage failures and life regrets: 'I regret my marriages falling apart'
summary: Phil Collins told Piers Morgan his Genesis touring schedule destroyed his first marriage and revealed deep regrets about all three marriages falling apart.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Phil Collins is opening up about his biggest regret throughout the course of his career.
During a recent interview on "Piers Morgan Uncensored," the 75-year-old musician reflected on the toll his career took on his relationships with his children and how it affected his three marriages.

"To some extent, I have to say I regret my marriages falling apart," he explained. "Sometimes I jumped. Well, one time I jumped, two times I was pushed. But I wouldn't have written it like that. But on the other hand, I've got five fantastic kids that I wouldn't have if that hadn't happened. So I have to balance it."
The famous drummer was married to his first wife, Andrea Bertorelli, from 1975 to 1980. Collins adopted Bertorelli's daughter, Joely, and the couple welcomed son Simon.
PHIL COLLINS' BRUSH WITH DEATH LEFT HIS CHILDREN PREPARING FOR THE UNTHINKABLE
Collins shared his biggest regret over the course of his career. (Gina Wetzler/Redferns)

He also shares daughter Lily with his second wife, Jill Tavelman, whom he was married to from 1984 to 1996, and sons Nicholas and Mathew with his third wife, Orianne Cevey, whom he was married to from 1999 to 2006.
When looking back on his first marriage, Collins admitted it broke down because he wasn't around, as he was touring with his band, Genesis, and couldn't be home.

"Genesis did, in one year, I think, three American tours, two European tours, and a tour of Japan. And when I ended up getting separated from my first wife, the guys in the band said, ‘Well, why didn’t you tell us? We’d have stopped it.’ But that’s easy to say in retrospect," he said. "I was gone, and we grew apart."

Despite his failure to make his relationships with his wives work, Collins said he "always tried to be there for the kids," and that he never planned on getting married three times, noting, "You don't go into life thinking that."

title: 'Caddyshack' star Michael O'Keefe claims cocaine was budgeted on set, admits filming scenes high
summary: Michael O'Keefe opens up about rampant cocaine use on the "Caddyshack" set, saying people treated the drug "like it was toothpaste" in the '70s.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Michael O'Keefe is getting candid about what it was like on the set of the hit 1980 movie "Caddyshack."

During a recent interview with Page Six, the 71-year-old actor shared that there was a lot of cocaine on the set of the classic comedy and claimed the drug was even accounted for in the movie's budget, with the actor noting, "there was some miscellaneous item."
"It was the 70s," he said. "That’s what was happening back then. People were just treating it like it was toothpaste, and you had to do it twice a day to stay healthy."
The movie was filmed in 1979 and released in 1980, and also starred Ted Knight, Chevy Chase, Bill Murray and Rodney Dangerfield and was set at the fictional Bushwood Country Club.
O'Keefe recalled doing cocaine before filming certain scenes in "Caddyshack." (Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images)
TOM HARDY'S 'MOBLAND' DRAMA TOPS HOLLYWOOD'S MOST NOTORIOUS ON-SET MELTDOWNS AND FEUDS

When reflecting on the drug use on set, O'Keefe recalled doing cocaine before filming certain scenes, telling Page Six that when he watches those scenes now, "it was not my favorite memory," and that he is "not too happy about them."

"But I can report to you that right after that movie, during that movie, was the last time I ever did anything like cocaine," he said. "I realized that it was a terrible thing to get involved [with], and like so many things in the drug world, it looked like fun, but in reality, it wasn’t."
Part of the reason he decided to take a step back from drugs was the death of Doug Kenney, who co-wrote and produced "Caddyshack."
He called Kenney's death "a huge wake-up call." Kenney died at 33 after falling from a cliff in Hawaii in 1980.

title: Chris Rock shreds 'woke 1.0' era, compares modern outrage to Salem witch hunts
summary: Chris Rock compares cancel culture to Salem witch hunts and the Old Testament, arguing wokeness also needs to come with a willingness to forgive.
story: Former Superman star says the industry is emerging from its 'woke era,' explains why filmmakers are fleeing California, and reveals what comes next
Chris Rock is getting candid about the importance of forgiveness in a world so quick to cancel others.

During a recent appearance on "The Daily" podcast, the 61-year-old comedian discussed his issues with "wokeness," saying that while advocating for marginalized people and giving them a voice is great, it needs to come with forgiveness.

"The problem with wokeness is we're in the Old Testament right now," he said. "And the Old Testament has no forgiveness. The Old Testament didn't work. So they had to write a remix called the New Testament."

Host David Marchese then asked if he thought there was "anything redeeming" that came out of the post-George Floyd era, which he referred to as "woke 1.0," since Democratic politicians now seem to be straying further from that ideology now.
Rock compared wokeness to the Salem witch trials. (Jemal Countess/WireImage)
SKILLET'S JOHN COOPER SAYS WOKE ACTIVISTS HAVE 'BIG HEARTS' BUT ARE 'HURTING THEMSELVES'
The "Grown Ups" star reiterated his position that "it's great to help those that need help," but noted the problem comes "when you institutionalize it."

"The Salem witch hunts. I'm sure the first three witches they caught were actually f- - -ing witches," he said. "But then you open up a witch office and now you've got to start lying. Now you've gotta f- - - ing make s- - - up because you've got overhead. You've got to justify the witch hunters f - - -ing pensions and s- - -."

He explained that just because he advocates for forgiveness, it "doesn't mean condoning abusive behavior. You can reprimand your friends," adding that holding them accountable is "also part of friendship."
"If you’re only friends with your friends when they’re good, they’re not your friends," he said.
Rock said part of friendship is holding each other accountable. (Leon Bennett/EveryStory2026/WireImage)

While he admits there is room for improvement when it comes to cancel culture and wokeness, he noted he is "glad that all of this stuff happened," as it allowed for certain voices to be heard which otherwise may not have been.
Kaivan Shroff — a former Hillary Clinton campaign staffer – disagreed with Rock, telling Fox News Digital the comedian "is oversimplifying this in a way that is pretty self-serving."

"Sometimes the problem is not that people ‘took a joke out of context.’ Often the context is perfectly clear and the comedian knows exactly who the joke is aimed at, knows a lot of people will find it offensive, and is counting on that discomfort to make the material feel edgy or viral," Shroff said. "You don’t get to use outrage as part of the act and then act shocked when the outrage follows."
Rock is currently promoting his new film, "Misty Green," which he wrote and directed in addition to starring in it.
Rock is currently promoting his new film, "Misty Green." (Rosalind O'Connor/NBC via Getty Images)
