The film follows an award-winning actress, Misty Green, who is working hard to make a comeback after years of watching her career slowly fade away, with Rock portraying a casting director who once worked with the actress.

"I'm really into expiration dates. I have a lot of friends who are in their 50s or whatever and there's this thing everybody tells you, ‘You can do art forever.’ And that's just not true," he said. "And a lot of show business has, like you've got to reach certain plateaus by a certain time or else you're going to be in trouble. So yeah, Misty is turning 40 and there's a little bit of an expiration date happening here. I wanted to do a movie about Hollywood. I wanted to do a movie about the expiration dates we all have."

title: Miranda Lambert says she and Ella Langley clashed while making hit record
summary: Miranda Lambert called herself "scrappy" while detailing her studio disagreements with Ella Langley during their record-making collaboration.
story: Ella Langley speaks about her deep appreciation for supporters and how their connection transformed her path during an interview at the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards March 26, 2026, in Los Angeles.
Making a hit record wasn't all harmony for Miranda Lambert and Ella Langley.
The country superstar revealed she and the "Choosin' Texas" singer butted heads while working together, and Lambert said the disagreements were actually a sign they were on the right track.
"If we don't fight by the end of this, we probably didn't do it right," Lambert recalled telling Langley during an appearance on The New York Times' "Popcast."
MIRANDA LAMBERT DELIVERS STRAIGHT-SHOOTING ADVICE TO RISING COUNTRY STAR IN SURPRISE BATHROOM ENCOUNTER
Langley and Lambert worked together as co-writers on the song "Choosin' Texas." Lambert also produced Langley's album "Dandelion." (John Shearer/Getty Images for ACM)
The candid admission came while Lambert discussed the emotional process of creating a record with the rising country star.
"There was hard parts of it. Creating a record is not — I mean, it's a long journey, you know what I mean? And it's a lot of emotions," Lambert said.
ELLA LANGLEY ADDRESSES CRITICISM IN EMOTIONAL CONCERT SPEECH AS 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS' DOMINATES CHARTS
"We did a lot," she admitted when asked if she and Langley were "butting heads" during the process. "And I think that's important because we needed to."
Miranda Lambert and Ella Langley pose in the winner's walk during the 61st Academy of Country Music Awards. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for ACM)
Lambert, who has built a career on songs about heartbreak, independence and life in the country, said she welcomed disagreements as long as they were constructive.
When asked if she enjoys a good argument, the country star didn't hesitate.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
"Yeah, I'm scrappy. … I wanted it to be right, you know what I mean?" she said.
Miranda Lambert said she and Ella Langley weren't afraid to disagree while working together on the record featuring "Choosin' Texas." (Mary Kouw/CBS via Getty Images)
The country star was also asked if she ever let Langley win one of their disagreements. She laughed off the question.

"Yeah. I mean … it's her name. But, yeah, it was a good balance, I felt like, of bouncing songs off each other, saying like, 'That's too far one way,' or 'That doesn't fit the record,' whatever it was. And I love that she trusted me with that. I really do."
"Choosin' Texas" has become a record-breaking hit for Langley.
On that track, Lambert said, there wasn't much fighting to do.

Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas" made Billboard history after the singer teamed up with Miranda Lambert on the hit song. (Getty Images)
"That one is just like — it's like a piece of our DNA. So, no. It's like there's this nostalgia to it, and it's like her love for country and my love for country.
"That one, whether it was the writing of it, just fell out of the production. It was just like, 'This is what it's supposed to be. Let's let it be.'"

Langley celebrated a Billboard record in September after "Choosin' Texas" reached its 23rd week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, surpassing Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" for the longest reign at the top of the chart.
ELLA LANGLEY JOINS MUSIC ROYALTY WITH 'INSANE' MILESTONE FOR 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS'

I'm running out of hyperboles to describe how I feel. So, I will just let my dog in the background show you his excitement," she continued as her dog barked.
Ella Langley posted a video to thank her fans after breaking the Billboard record for longest-running No. 1 on the Hot 100 chart. (Taylor Hill/FilmMagic)

title: Zach Bryan sparks debate after wearing 'Free Palestine' shirt at venue that barred Macklemore
summary: Zach Bryan took the stage in a "Free Palestine" shirt at Robert Kraft's Gillette Stadium, just weeks after Kraft barred Macklemore from the venue.
story: Fox News contributor Joe Concha discusses Robert Kraft banning Macklemore from Gillette Stadium over 'Free Palestine' comments.
Zach Bryan made his position known without saying a word.
The country music superstar walked onto the stage at Gillette Stadium Friday night wearing a shirt that said "Free Palestine."

His shirt appeared to some to be a pointed message at the venue owned by New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who recently barred Macklemore from performing at the stadium over what Kraft described as the rapper's "broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery."
ED SHEERAN CONCERTGOERS WARN ARTISTS ABOUT SHARING POLITICAL VIEWS: 'YOU'RE GOING TO ALIENATE' FANS
Country music star Zach Bryan took the stage at Gillette Stadium in a "Free Palestine" shirt weeks after venue owner Robert Kraft barred Macklemore from performing there. (Scott Legato/Getty Images)
Members of Bryan's band also appeared to wear clothing supporting the Palestinian cause.
Bryan is scheduled to return to Gillette Stadium Saturday night for the second show of his two-night run.

Bryan's shirt immediately ignited a debate online, with social media users split over whether the singer was making a courageous political statement or bringing politics into a concert where fans simply came to hear music.
ED SHEERAN SAYS HE TRIED TO ‘BUILD A BRIDGE’ OVER MACKLEMORE TOUR SPOT BEFORE VENUES SAID NO
Zach Bryan wore a shirt that said "Free Palestine" during his concert at Gillette Stadium, home of the New England Patriots. (Lorne Thomson/Redferns)

One supporter celebrated the move, writing, "A great decision by Zach Bryan and his crew. I’m sure they will have to pay a price, but a courageous statement to help the conservative crowds see the light."
ED SHEERAN APOLOGIZES FOR MACKLEMORE BACKLASH, ENCOURAGES UNITY AT FIRST CONCERT SINCE FALLOUT
Another commenter, while clearly disagreeing with Bryan's position, defended the singer's right to make the statement.
"Listen I don’t agree with his political view on this but he has the right to wear the shirt. He didn’t stand there & preach his politics. It’s a shirt. He sang songs what he’s suppose to do"
Others disagreed with Bryan’s statement.

Another comment said, "Zach Bryan played Gillette Stadium Friday night in a ‘Free Palestine’ shirt. That’s Robert Kraft’s stadium. Last month Kraft barred Macklemore there over his ‘free Palestine’ remarks, citing antisemitic rhetoric. Kraft should cancel tonight’s show. Same standard he held Macklemore to."

Macklemore was kicked off Ed Sheeran's stadium tour over his "Free Palestine" remarks. (Getty Images)

Macklemore announced his own Free Palestine Tour after being dropped from the remaining U.S. dates of Ed Sheeran's tour. (Getty Images)

title: People who live to 100 have 3 drinks in common, longevity expert says
summary: Dan Buettner highlights how blue zones residents drink water, black coffee and red wine with resveratrol to support long-term health goals.
story: Red wine gets plenty of criticism, but it still appears in some blue zone diets. Coffee may also support healthy aging. Yet the top longevity drink is much simpler, according to longevity researcher Dan Buettner.

In the world’s "blue zones" — regions such as Sardinia, Italy, and Okinawa, Japan, known for unusually high concentrations of long-lived residents — researchers have studied dietary and lifestyle habits for clues to healthy aging and longevity.
In a recent video post, longevity researcher Dan Buettner highlighted three beverages commonly consumed in blue zones — and studies offer some clues about how each may affect health and longevity.
No. 1: Purified water
Buettner ranked water first among his three longevity drinks.
FILTERED WATER AT SPECIFIC AGES COULD ADD MONTHS TO YOUR LIFESPAN DECADES LATER, NEW STUDY FINDS

"The indisputable, best thing you can drink to live to 100 [is] water," he stated. "People in blue zones are drinking six to seven glasses of water. You want to make sure it is purified water. Water helps lower your blood pressure, helps keep your blood thin and keeps you hydrated."
Research from the National Institutes of Health indicates that proper hydration helps prevent cellular degradation, lowers the risk of chronic heart conditions and supports healthy aging. (iStock)

Research from the National Institutes of Health has linked better hydration with healthier aging, including lower risks of chronic disease and premature death, although researchers noted that the findings do not prove cause and effect.
Other health experts note that adequate water intake supports kidney function, helps regulate blood pressure and keeps blood circulating effectively.
Coffee consumption has been associated with lower rates of diabetes and Parkinson's disease. (iStock)
No. 2: Black coffee
Coffee consumption is another daily habit highlighted by Buettner, who said it is associated with lower rates of diabetes and Parkinson's.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Drink it black, one to two cups a day, quit by noon, it'll help you live longer," he added.
Routine coffee intake has been associated with reduced risks of type 2 diabetes and neurological conditions. (iStock)

Coffee contains antioxidants and polyphenols, plant compounds that have been studied for their potential anti-inflammatory effects. Routine coffee consumption has also been associated with lower risks of type 2 diabetes and neurological conditions.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Limiting added sugars and heavy creams can help avoid extra calories, while consuming caffeine earlier in the day may reduce its impact on sleep.
No. 3: Red wine
Residents in blue zone areas, like Sardinia, often consume small amounts of red wine during meals.
Buettner acknowledged that red wine's place in a longevity-focused diet is "controversial."
"I'm very well aware of all the negative press wine is getting lately, but it's consumed in the Blue Zones, and it seems to add years to life," Buettner said. (iStock)
"I'm very well aware of all the negative press wine is getting lately, but it's consumed in the blue zones and it seems to add years to life."

Red wine contains plant compounds such as resveratrol and flavonoids, which have been studied for their potential cardiovascular effects. However, experts have increasingly questioned whether any benefits attributed to red wine outweigh the known risks of alcohol.

Alcohol consumption has been linked to numerous health risks, including an increased risk of at least seven types of cancer, according to the U.S. Surgeon General.

People with underlying health conditions or those taking medications should consult a healthcare professional before making significant dietary changes.

title: Alan Alda reveals unexpected weapon in his battle against Parkinson's disease
summary: Alan Alda, now 90, reveals how humor and acceptance help him cope with Parkinson's disease, calling the condition "just a hobby" he lives with.
story: Dr. Chadrick Lane, a neuropsychiatrist and director of the geriatric and neuropsychiatry clinic at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, Texas, said humor can be a helpful wellness tool for those navigating the Parkinson's journey.
Alan Alda is sharing his surprising method of coping with Parkinson’s.

The actor, 90, best known for portraying Captain Benjamin Franklin "Hawkeye" Pierce in the CBS wartime sitcom "M*A*S*H," was diagnosed with the degenerative motor disease in 2015 and publicly shared the news in 2018.
The diagnosis came after the actor learned that his own behavior of acting out dreams could be an early Parkinson's symptom.
DAD JOKES MAY BE GOOD FOR YOUR BRAIN IN ONE SURPRISING WAY, EXPERTS SAY

"I had a symptom, which at the time was not that well-known: Acting out your dreams," he said in an Oct. 4 interview with CBS News. "I had a dream that somebody was attacking me. And I picked up a sack of potatoes and threw it at 'em. What I was really doing was throwing a pillow at Arlene, my wife."
Alda identified humor as his way of coping with the frustrations and limitations of the disease.
The actor, pictured with the cast of "M*A*S*H," was diagnosed with the degenerative motor disease in 2015 and publicly shared the news in 2018.  (Getty Images)

While he acknowledged the frustrations of the physical effects and limitations of Parkinson’s, he said "the best way to deal with anything that's a little bit of a problem is to find out what's funny about it and laugh at it."

In one example, he shared that when he has trouble controlling the computer mouse while composing an email, he personifies his condition as "Dr. Parkinson," moving his hand all over the screen and deleting things.
"I don't let Parkinson's define me," Alda said, joking that he sees the disease as "just a hobby."
PARKINSON’S PATIENT’S YEARS-LONG TREMOR VANISHES WITHIN MINUTES OF NEW ULTRASOUND TREATMENT
Rather than wishing he didn’t have the condition, the actor said he aims to accept his current reality.
"I really think reality is my friend," he said. "I don't want to wish it away. I can't wish it away. I can't hope for a better future. I gotta accept what is."
Arlene Alda and Alan Alda attend AARP The Magazine's 19th Annual Movies For Grownups Awards at Beverly Wilshire on Jan. 11, 2020, in Beverly Hills, California. (Getty Images)
Although Alda acknowledged that everyday tasks, such as buttoning his shirt, have become difficult, he said he treats each one like a "puzzle" to solve.

"I do hate it, but the only thing that's helpful is: What haven't I tried? And pretty soon, you get the feeling, 'If I keep looking for new ways to try this, I'll get a solution.' It's a puzzle. Will I be able eventually to put my socks on? The last time I put my socks on was a tremendous moment to celebrate!"
SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISING BRAIN BENEFIT OF LAUGHTER: 'IT'S A MENTAL WORKOUT'

Dr. Chadrick Lane, a neuropsychiatrist and director of the geriatric and neuropsychiatry clinic at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, Texas, agreed that humor can be a helpful wellness tool for those navigating the Parkinson's journey.

"Humor involves cognitive reframing, this idea of looking at a circumstance through different angles — not necessarily changing the reality that one is in, but shifting the meaning and the emotional weight of the situation," an expert said. (iStock)

"Humor involves cognitive reframing, this idea of looking at a circumstance through different angles — not necessarily changing the reality that one is in, but shifting the meaning and the emotional weight of the situation," Lane, who has not treated Alda, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
When something feels frightening or distressing, such as a medical diagnosis, creating some "psychological distance" can make a "big, big change" in perspective, he added.
Connection is another important component of humor, Lane noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Humor is often shared. It brings us together," he said. "We are meant to share our lives with others. The importance of having a sense of belonging and humor can be a glue in that way, bringing us closer with others so that one does not go on the journey alone."
"Humor is often shared. It brings us together."
Lane shared that he has witnessed the power of humor and connection in his own practice as he cares for people living with Parkinson's disease.
"One of the wonderful things that I've seen in those settings is that, just like Mr. Alda, people crack a joke, [it] brings them a smile."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The neuropsychiatrist also noted that Alda’s acceptance of his condition is "enormously empowering."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It's the idea of saying to oneself, what are the choices that I can make in the moment?" Lane told Fox News Digital. "Rarely do we ever have control over our entire day and certainly not our entire life, but we often do have control over what we choose in the moment."
"Our sense of agency is an important part of our emotional well-being."

title: New York declares measles disaster emergency as cases surge in Pennsylvania
summary: Kathy Hochul declared a statewide New York emergency as 108 measles cases spread from Pennsylvania, expanding who can administer MMR vaccines.
story: Officials are warning some travelers may have been exposed to measles at select areas inside the Philadelphia International Airport as cases rise in Pennsylvania.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a statewide emergency on Monday over a measles outbreak spreading from Pennsylvania.
It is the first time an emergency declaration has been issued since measles began surging in the U.S. in 2025.
Pennsylvania has reported 977 measles cases and five deaths as of Oct. 2, with most cases centered in rural communities. Meanwhile, New York has reported 108 cases.
WORLD’S MOST CONTAGIOUS VIRUS HITS MAJOR US AIRPORT AS OFFICIALS WARN OF POSSIBLE EXPOSURE
"No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease," Hochul said in a statement.
Kathy Hochul, governor of New York, speaks during a public safety announcement in New York on Friday, Jan. 30, 2026. (Angelina Katsanis/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The U.S. is having its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 cases reported, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
PENNSYLVANIA COMMISSIONER ACCUSES SHAPIRO OF 'DECEPTIVE' MEASLES DEATH FRAMING AS RFK JR BLASTS DEM GOVERNOR
Hochul also issued an executive order expanding the number of health professionals who are approved to administer measles vaccines.

A measles alert sign hangs outside the entrance to the Cohen Children's Medical Center, where the state health department confirmed that a baby tested positive and that there is a possibility of exposure to others at the facility, in New Hyde Park, New York, on March 14, 2025. (REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton)

The order allows registered nurses to order tests for suspected measles and pharmacists to vaccinate children as young as 2. It also requires all MMR vaccinations to be reported to state or New York City immunization registries within 72 hours, while waiving adults’ consent for such reporting.
DOCTOR SHORTAGES ARE HURTING RURAL PATIENTS. LET PHARMACISTS HELP THEM HEAL

The Pennsylvania and Philadelphia health departments, as well as the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, reported last month that they are "working closely to ensure potentially exposed infants receive a preventative antibody product to prevent or lessen severe disease and to take steps to prevent the further spread of measles" amid the outbreak.

Sherry Andrews, right, holds 13-month-old Jaqi Herrera’s hand after administering the first MMR vaccine dose to Herrera at the City of Lubbock Health Department in Lubbock, Texas, on February 27, 2025. (Reuters)
Philadelphia Health Commissioner Dr. Palak Raval-Nelson wrote that measles exposures are "a reminder of how important it is for all of us to be up to date on our vaccinations."
MEASLES DEATHS MAY HAVE BEEN 'FABRICATED,' RFK JR CLAIMS AFTER CORONER RAISES QUESTIONS

The health department advised that anyone who has been exposed who is not immune, is unsure of their vaccination status, is an infant, is pregnant and not immune, or is immunocompromised should contact their doctor.
Girl gets checked by a doctor for measles. (iStock)

"Some people may still be eligible for treatment after exposure that can prevent measles or reduce the severity of illness," the department wrote. "Anyone who develops symptoms should call ahead before visiting a healthcare facility and tell the provider about the possible measles exposure."
MEASLES-INFECTED TRAVELER MAY HAVE EXPOSED PASSENGERS AT LAX AND NEARBY HOTEL, HEALTH OFFICIALS WARN
Measles is a highly contagious virus that can be fatal in one to three patients per 1,000 cases, data shows.

The virus can cause long-term health problems, including pneumonia and brain swelling.
Nearly 20% of individuals who contract measles are hospitalized.

title: 10 rules for living longer, seeing your grandkids grow up and enjoying your retirement savings
summary: Dr. Michael Hall shares his 10 basic longevity rules for healthy aging, from sleep and movement to purpose and social connection, in his new book.
story: Dr. Michael Hall, a Miami Beach longevity physician and author of the new book "Infinite Youth" has identified what he calls the "10 commandments of longevity," which he believes can help people extend their healthiest years.

As scientists increasingly investigate how everyday habits may influence health and aging, one longevity doctor says the keys to a longer, healthier life don't require expensive supplements, elaborate biohacks or cutting-edge treatments.

Dr. Michael Hall, a Miami Beach longevity physician and author of the new book, "Infinite Youth," has identified what he calls the "10 commandments of longevity," which he believes can help people extend their healthiest years.
Hall said the principles were shaped by nearly two decades in longevity medicine and by observing health and aging across cultures around the world.
LONGEVITY DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR AGING WELL, BEYOND PRICEY BIOHACKS

"These are core elements that are not peptides, they're not NAD," Hall told Fox News Digital. "It's not that you've got to buy a fancy thing on Amazon." Instead, he said, "you start out with the basics and you maintain them consistently."
The keys to a longer, healthier life don't require expensive supplements, elaborate biohacks or cutting-edge treatments, says a longevity doctor. (iStock)
"If you’re embracing some of these things, you are doing exactly what you need to do — and these don’t cost anything."
No. 1: Guard your attention

The content that people repeatedly consume — particularly when it’s fear-based or negative — can shape their behavior, according to Hall. He sees protecting attention as part of protecting health, emphasizing the importance of being intentional about what people consume mentally.
"What you put in your mind, you need to be very careful about," he said. "What you think, you become."
ONE SIMPLE LIFESTYLE CHOICE COULD HELP YOU LIVE LONGER, SAYS LONGEVITY EXPERT
No. 2: Honor sleep
A recent study identified a "sweet spot" of about six to eight hours of sleep per day, which researchers linked to healthier aging and lower risks of premature death and disease.
Sleep is when the body recovers and the brain "resets," yet technology and poor sleep habits increasingly interfere with that process, according to Hall.

Dr. Michael Hall, a Miami Beach longevity physician and author of the new book, "Infinite Youth," has identified what he calls the "10 commandments of longevity," which he believes can help people extend their healthiest years. (Dr. Michael Hall)
"Sleep is probably one of the most important things that we just don’t talk about enough," he said.
The expert pointed out that the body’s circadian rhythm responds naturally to light and darkness, while screens, artificial light and late bedtimes can disrupt that cycle.
"The bed is really for sleep and sex," Hall added.
No. 3: Move daily
A September 2026 study found that highly active older adults maintained high levels of aerobic fitness into their 60s, 70s and 80s, despite some normal age-related decline.
"Movement is life," Hall agreed. He recalled seeing older adults remain highly active during his time working in New Zealand and Sri Lanka, including women in their 90s who were still mobile and fit.
3 COMMON FACTORS MAY BE SECRETLY SPEEDING UP THE AGING PROCESS, EXPERT SAYS
Hall’s own routine includes walking, swimming, cycling and resistance work.
For everyday movement, he particularly recommends walking and squatting, which engage large muscle groups and help maintain strength and mobility.
No. 4: Preserve strength
Muscle strength helps support bones, posture and mobility, and may help reduce frailty and fall risk later in life, according to the longevity expert.
"You need to maintain that good, healthy posture and strength throughout your life," Hall said.
Muscle strength helps support bones, posture and mobility and may help reduce frailty and fall risk later in life. (iStock)
He connected loss of movement and strength with weakening muscles, bones, tendons and ligaments, potentially increasing fall risk as people age.
"If you’re moving, you’re preserving strength, you’re maintaining your bones, because they go together," Hall said.
No. 5: Eat real food
For optimal longevity nutrition, Hall recommends choosing minimally processed foods, with a focus on simple preparation, portion control and awareness of what goes into meals.
"Food is medicine, food is fuel, food is life," Hall said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
While Hall said he cooks his own meals, primarily chooses fresh foods and largely avoids foods that come "out of a bag or a box," he emphasizes portion control rather than complete deprivation.
"I don’t care what it is you love, you can have a bite," he said.
No. 6: Embrace purpose
Having a mission gives people something beyond themselves to invest in, contributing to emotional well-being and a meaningful life, according to Hall.
"It’s the most important part of being human," he said. "Our mission … is our purpose."
Hall recommends choosing minimally processed foods, with a focus on simple preparation, portion control and awareness of what goes into meals. (iStock)

That purpose does not have to come from an extraordinary calling, Hall suggested. Whether someone is a physician, firefighter, baker or coffee shop owner, serving others can provide a sense of meaning.
"If you’re just serving yourself, you aren’t going to be a happy person," he added.
No. 7: Cultivate meaningful relationships
"No one ages well alone," Hall said. "You cannot live alone. You’re not designed to be atomized living in a box alone."
Research published in October 2026 in PLOS One found that loneliness was associated with a higher risk of death at one, three and five years.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Hall also pointed to companionship, family and meaningful relationships as important parts of his own life.
"Having people around you who appreciate you, who you can relate to, who can have a conversation with, have a laugh with, it’s so important," he said.
No. 8: Welcome challenge
A 2025 study of more than 10,000 older adults with cognitive impairment found that greater participation in cognitively stimulating activities was associated with a lower risk of death over time.
"We’re needing to be challenged … as an individual and as a community and as society," Hall said.
No. 9: Remain curious
Continuing to learn, explore and seek out new experiences could play a role in healthy aging, research has found.
"No one ages well alone," the expert said. "You cannot live alone. You’re not designed to be atomized living in a box alone." (iStock)
Hall similarly believes curiosity helps people remain engaged with the world as they get older.
"Curiosity allows us to explore and to always be aware there’s something more," he told Fox News Digital. "You’re never going to know everything. So you’re always on the quest."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Curiosity has driven much of Hall’s travel and work around the world, he said, noting that getting older shouldn't mean stopping the pursuit of new experiences.
"We were children, and we never really grew up, by the way — we just get older in our bodies."
No. 10: Keep the funnel wide
In his book, Hall describes healthy aging as keeping the body's metaphorical "funnel" as wide as possible for as long as possible.
He sees aging as a gradual narrowing of that funnel, with increasing physiological stress as the body loses some of its ability to maintain optimal function.
"We were children, and we never really grew up — we just get older in our bodies."
Keeping the funnel wide, he said, means supporting overall health and resilience through the fundamental habits outlined in his other commandments.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Ultimately, Hall said his goal is not simply to help people accumulate more birthdays, but to make those additional years healthier and more meaningful.
"I’m selling healthspan as much as I possibly can," he said. "Your best years of your life, the best living you can possibly have, sharing with others and making society better."

title: Alzheimer’s risk linked to compound found in popular joint health supplements
summary: University of Florida researchers found glucosamine users with mild cognitive impairment were 25% more likely to progress to dementia in a new study.
story: Alzheimer's Association VP Rachel Conant joins 'Fox News Live' to discuss policy hurdles blocking access to breakthrough Alzheimer's treatments.
Many older adults turn to glucosamine to manage aging joints, but for individuals with mild cognitive impairment, the supplement could be linked to faster progression to Alzheimer’s disease.

To investigate how glucosamine affects dementia risk and mortality, University of Florida researchers analyzed medical records of patients with mild cognitive impairment, tracked laboratory mouse models and examined healthy versus Alzheimer’s-affected human brains.
The study, which was published in Nature Metabolism, focused on glycosylation, a natural process where brain cells attach small chains of sugar to proteins.
7 NEW DEMENTIA RISK FACTORS REVEALED — INCLUDING ONE MILLIONS STRUGGLE WITH

"You can think of these sugar chains as the labels and fittings on a machine part — they help a protein fold correctly, get shipped to the right place in the cell and connect with its partners," senior author Ramon Sun, Ph.D., professor of biochemistry and molecular biology in the College of Medicine at University of Florida, told Fox News Digital. "The right amount is essential."
Many older adults turn to glucosamine to manage aging joints, but for individuals with mild cognitive impairment, the supplement could be linked to faster progression to Alzheimer’s disease. (iStock)
What is glucosamine?

"Glucosamine is a naturally occurring compound of sugar and an amino acid group that is a fundamental structural building block in the body," Neil Levin, senior nutrition education manager of Now, a manufacturer of glucosamine supplements in Illinois, told Fox News Digital.

Glucosamine is concentrated in cartilage, the connective tissue that cushions joints, and is a component of larger molecules that help give cartilage its strength, elasticity and ability to retain water, he added.
"Support for aging joints is the primary reason people take glucosamine as a dietary supplement," Levin said.
ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TESTS MAY PREDICT SYMPTOMS YEARS IN ADVANCE, BUT EXPERTS URGE CAUTION
The body uses an internal "checkpoint" that naturally regulates how many of these sugar chains it produces, according to Sun.

Supplemental glucosamine bypasses that "front gate" entirely — like a delivery truck pulling straight up to the loading dock, instantly boosting the supply of raw material used to make the sugar chains, the expert added.

Glucosamine is concentrated in cartilage, the connective tissue that cushions joints, and is a component of larger molecules that help give cartilage its strength, elasticity and ability to retain water. (iStock)

In the study, researchers analyzed thousands of patients with dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, as well as those with mild cognitive impairment, and then narrowed the group to those who were taking glucosamine.

For those with mild cognitive impairment, taking the supplement didn't change their risk of death, but it did make them 25% more likely to progress to dementia. However, among individuals who already had dementia, glucosamine users had a higher mortality compared to similar non-users.
POPULAR DRUGS FOR BONE HEALTH LINKED TO SIGNIFICANTLY LOWER ALZHEIMER'S RISK
The researchers also examined brain tissue to understand what might be driving the association. "We found an excess of sugar chains on proteins in the Alzheimer’s brain," Sun said.

Many of those proteins help nerve cells communicate, but the excess sugar chains may interfere with how they function, Sun said. He compared the effect to coating a key in too much wax — it is still the same key, but no longer fits the lock properly.
"A brain affected by dementia and a healthy brain are different biological environments, and we shouldn't assume a supplement behaves the same way in both."
Glucosamine is one of the materials cells use to make these sugar chains, according to Sun.
Researchers also tracked how glucosamine was processed in mice, comparing its effects on healthy brains with those affected by Alzheimer’s-like disease.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"In our experiments, normal mice given glucosamine showed no increase in these sugar chains and no change in a memory test," Sun said.
"But in mice with Alzheimer's-like disease, where the production line was already running too hot, glucosamine increased the sugar chains further and worsened performance on a memory test."
Study limitations
The researchers relied on medical records, which may not capture every supplement a patient was taking.

"Health records tell us what was documented, not everything a person took," Sun said. "Over-the-counter supplements are not always recorded, and records don't reliably capture dose, brand or how consistently someone took it."

Researchers analyzed thousands of patients with dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, as well as those with mild cognitive impairment, and then narrowed the group to those who were taking glucosamine. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci, File)
An observational study looking at past records can find a signal, but can't prove one.

Glucosamine users may also differ in factors such as arthritis, pain, mobility, frailty and medication use, Levin noted. The records also did not establish the exact supplement, dose, duration or consistency of use.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"The finding should therefore be treated as a safety signal that warrants controlled human research, but it did not — could not — reach a conclusion that glucosamine causes Alzheimer’s disease," Levin said.
The next step is a well-designed, double-blind clinical trial to evaluate the impact of glucosamine on cognitive decline in patients with dementia.
The study did not examine cognitively healthy people and does not suggest glucosamine poses a risk to those who take it for joint health. (iStock)

"For now, the evidence isn't strong enough to recommend any supplement for slowing [Alzheimer’s] disease, which is why doing this research properly, including the clinical trial we've called for, matters," Sun said.
The study did not examine cognitively healthy people and does not suggest that glucosamine poses a risk to those who take it for joint health.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"A brain affected by dementia and a healthy brain are different biological environments, and we shouldn't assume a supplement behaves the same way in both," Sun said.
He emphasized the importance of consulting with a doctor before starting or stopping a supplement.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"If you or a family member has a diagnosis of cognitive impairment or dementia and takes glucosamine, it's reasonable to bring it up at the next visit, as part of an ordinary conversation about what's in the medicine cabinet," the doctor advised.

title: 7 everyday mistakes could be quietly damaging your vision, eye doctor warns
summary: An NYU ophthalmologist reveals how sun exposure, eye rubbing, dehydration and poor sleep may silently accelerate aging in the eyes and impact vision.
story: NYU Langone ophthalmologist Dr. Douglas Lazzaro explains how factors like sun exposure, poor lighting, dehydration, diet and sleep can affect aging eyes — and how outine exams can help detect and prevent vision-impacting conditions.
As Americans live longer, experts say everyday habits may be taking a toll on eye health earlier than expected.
Dr. Douglas Lazzaro, professor of ophthalmology at NYU Langone Health, warned that several everyday habits may be silently affecting eye health.
Age-related eye conditions include glaucoma, which damages the optic nerve, and cataracts, a clouding of the eye’s lens that can block light and blur vision.
POPULAR ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION DRUG LINKED TO EYE DISEASE THAT CAN CAUSE IRREVERSIBLE VISION LOSS
While genetics and aging remain major drivers of many eye diseases, avoiding the following common mistakes may help slow their progression and protect vision, Lazzaro told Fox News Digital.
No. 1: Not protecting eyes from the sun
While exposure to sunlight is beneficial for overall metabolic health and longevity, failing to protect the eyes from the sun may lead to accelerated damage.
Failing to protect the eyes from the sun may lead to accelerated damage. (iStock)
Lazzaro pointed to research suggesting that long-term ultraviolet exposure may contribute to macular degeneration and the progression of cataracts.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS FACE NUMEROUS LAWSUITS OVER RARE 'EYE STROKE' LINKED TO VISION LOSS
In the doctor's own practice, cataracts are appearing five to 10 years earlier than they did three decades ago, which he believes may be linked to ultraviolet light exposure.
He recommends wearing sunglasses in bright, sunny conditions to help protect the eyes, including the lens and retina.
No. 2: Reading in poor light
Reading in poor lighting can increase eye strain and make it harder to focus, particularly with age, according to Lazzaro.
Straining the eyes to see or read something puts stress on the optic nerves, the eye doctor said. (iStock)

"As we get older, our eyes have more difficulty seeing under certain lighting conditions," he told Fox News Digital, noting that older adults may have more difficulty adjusting to darker environments.
"If you're going be reading, and it's not a bright, sunny day outside, or you're not inside with bright lights, you should increase the lighting," he recommended.
No. 3: Not eating a healthy diet
Research suggests that a nutritious diet may protect eye health by reducing the risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease, both of which can affect vision.
"Diet is important," Lazzaro said. "There's certainly a lot of known data about poor diets [contributing] to poor cardiovascular health, and that same thing can apply with the eye."
DIET CHANGE TIED TO ‘YOUNGER’ BIOLOGICAL AGE IN OLDER ADULTS AFTER 4 WEEKS
High cholesterol and high blood pressure can worsen diabetic eye disease, even when patients may not realize those conditions are affecting their vision, according to the doctor.
Researchers are also exploring whether gut health may influence retinal health, although that connection is still emerging.
No. 4: Not staying hydrated
Another condition that becomes increasingly common with age is dry eye, in which a lack of tear production and oil secretion causes red, itchy, irritated eyes.
This condition can be exacerbated by lifestyle factors like dehydration, Lazzaro noted.
People who don't sleep well have fluctuations in their circulation at night, which can impact eye health. (iStock)

Staying hydrated helps keep the cornea properly moisturized, he said. "We always tell our patients, particularly in the summer, if they're going out on a hot day … make sure to hydrate, because not only will it dry out the body … but it can dry out your corneas."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
No. 5: Getting poor sleep

Getting adequate sleep helps support overall health, and there’s "good evidence" that patients who don’t sleep well, particularly those with sleep apnea, may experience increased eye pressure, according to Lazzaro.

People with sleep apnea also appear to face higher rates of glaucoma and certain vascular eye conditions, similar to their increased cardiovascular risk, the doctor said. "They also have an increased incidence of vascular phenomena in the eye … People who don't sleep well have fluctuations in their circulation at night."
No. 6: Rubbing the eyes

Eye rubbing is considered a risk factor for keratoconus, a progressive eye disease where the cornea begins to dome and bulge out in a cone shape, although experts' opinions differ on whether it can directly cause the disease, according to Lazzaro.
The eye doctor "strongly" advises against rubbing the eyes. (iStock)
Patients with keratoconus often rub their eyes frequently, he noted, and repeated rubbing can potentially change the shape of the cornea — one reason he "strongly" advises against the habit.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
No. 7: Delaying routine eye doctor visits
Because glaucoma often develops without symptoms, a comprehensive eye exam is frequently the only way to detect it early, Lazzaro said.
Glaucoma is known as a "silent disease" that can lead to blindness, the doctor noted. (iStock)
Glaucoma is known as a "silent disease" that can lead to blindness, the doctor noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Its nickname is 'the silent thief of sight,'" he said. "Sometimes the only way you know you have glaucoma is by going to the ophthalmologist. It’s a disease that we see with increasing frequency as we get older."

Lazzaro recommends that adults get annual eye exams, rather than waiting until age-related vision changes begin. Presbyopia — the gradual loss of the ability to focus on nearby objects — commonly develops in middle age and often leads to the need for reading glasses.
"The only way you know you have glaucoma is by going to the ophthalmologist."
"Patients will come in at some point, usually between 40 and 50, and say they can't see up-close anymore; it happened overnight," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Annual visits should also include a scan for skin cancer and eyelid tumors, which occur more frequently with age, the doctor advised.

Sun exposure may contribute not only to cataracts and macular degeneration, but also to cancers of the eyelid, Lazzaro said. "Most of them can be removed locally without a big problem if diagnosed early," he added.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Subtle change in how you speak could be early sign of dementia risk, new research suggests
summary: A new Drexel University study of 833,417 participants links voice disorders to a 58% higher likelihood of developing dementia or cognitive impairment.
story: Harvard researchers found that people who engaged in moderate amounts of resistance training had a lower risk of dying from several major causes, including heart disease and neurological disease.
New research suggests that voice disorders, including shifts in vocal pitch, volume or clarity, could indicate a higher probability of developing dementia or cognitive impairment in the future.

A study involving 833,417 participants aged 50 and older examined the connection between a voice disorder, hearing loss, or both with the chance of developing cognitive impairment or dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease, beginning a year after the voice disorder and hearing loss diagnoses.
The findings from the study, conducted by a team at the Drexel University College of Medicine in Philadelphia, were published in the Journal of Voice.
EVERYDAY TASK MAY HELP DETECT EARLY DEMENTIA SIGNS BEFORE DIAGNOSIS, STUDY FINDS

Results showed that participants with a voice disorder but no hearing loss had a 58% increased likelihood of developing dementia or cognitive issues in the future — whereas participants with a voice disorder and hearing loss had a 104% chance.

For all participants with voice disorders, with or without hearing loss, there was a 29% increased probability of developing dementia or cognitive impairment, whereas those with only hearing loss had a 27% greater risk.
New research indicates that voice disorders can increase the likelihood of developing dementia in the future. (iStock)

"We found the strongest link with dementia among patients experiencing a voice disorder and hearing loss," said Robert Sataloff, a professor and chair at the Drexel University College of Medicine, Science Alert reported.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
"Importantly, we found that those with a voice disorder and no hearing loss were at greater risk than patients who experience hearing loss only," he added.
Examples of voice disorders include laryngitis, vocal cord paralysis, vocal cord lesions and spasmodic dysphonia (laryngeal dystonia), among others, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
Voice disorders and hearing loss may discourage people from social interaction, which can play a role in dementia development. (Getty Images)
Regardless of the possible correlation between vocal issues and dementia, researchers noted that seeking treatment for a voice disorder could also benefit a patient’s brain.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Hearing loss and trouble speaking could discourage individuals from socializing with others, and studies have shown that social engagement can stimulate the brain and play a role in warding off dementia.
Sataloff said that it’s "only natural" for voice disorders and hearing loss to be connected to cognitive impairment.
Studies have linked hearing loss to an increased risk of dementia. (iStock)
Those who experience pain or discomfort when talking or singing might "participate less often in brain-supporting social or other engaging activities," he noted.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Despite the study's findings, having a voice disorder doesn’t necessarily mean that future cognitive impairment is absolutely certain.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Additionally, it’s not guaranteed that vocal issues indicate the beginning of a decline in brain function or the onset of dementia or Alzheimer’s.
Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: 10-minute fitness habit can help adults over 40 maintain muscle and stay strong
summary: CEO Carl Daikeler compares metabolism to a furnace: Muscle is the coal and cardio stokes it, urging a balance of strength training and cardiovascular work.
story: BODi co-founder Carl Daikeler reveals why building muscle matters more with age, how just 10 minutes of daily strength work can be effective, and why a little discomfort now can make everyday life easier later.
Adults over 40 may not need to spend hours in the gym to maintain muscle, preserve mobility and stay strong.
According to Los Angeles fitness entrepreneur Carl Daikeler, just 10 minutes of targeted resistance exercise each day can help preserve muscle, mobility and long-term function.

Daikeler, 63, who has spent 28 years leading BODi, the fitness brand formerly known as Beachbody, says his approach to exercise stems from a practical desire to stay healthy without having to be a dedicated fitness enthusiast.
4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS

"I don't like to eat healthy, I don't like to work out," Daikeler told Fox News Digital at the Strong New York conference in September. "I'm just constantly trying to figure out how I can hack my way without having to overturn my life to become one of these diehard health and fitness people, because I'm never going to become that."
While resistance training builds muscle and strengthens bones and connective tissue, cardiovascular exercise challenges the heart and lungs, helping to maintain overall fitness. (iStock)
For adults looking to stay healthy in midlife, Daikeler recommends what he considers a "minimum effective dose" — short, targeted resistance workouts at home instead of lengthy gym sessions.
"Ten minutes a day, and you can establish and build and maintain muscle," he said.
WANT TO AGE BETTER? RESEARCHERS SAY 4-MINUTE ROUTINE MAY HELP PREVENT DANGEROUS FALLS

Federal physical activity guidelines say that adults should perform muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups at least two days per week, in addition to regular aerobic activity.

Rather than doing a full-body workout every day, Daikeler recommends rotating muscle groups — focusing on the chest one day, upper body the next, then legs and glutes — to build consistency without requiring lengthy gym sessions.
"Ten minutes a day, and you can establish and build and maintain muscle."
"Do that consistently, and you're going to find your strength return, your muscles return, your joints will start to respond appropriately," he said.

The 10-minute approach can be especially valuable for people taking GLP-1 medications, who may be trying to preserve muscle mass and bone density while losing weight but may feel intimidated by traditional gyms, Daikeler said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
For individuals seeking more significant weight loss, he recommends extending daily activity to 20 or 30 minutes, incorporating a balance of strength training and cardiovascular exercise.
The balancing act
Daikeler cautioned against focusing exclusively on either cardio or resistance training, noting that different exercise types serve distinct functions in the body.

"Your body's like a furnace," Daikeler said. "The coal in that furnace is muscle. So you want to build muscle. But then you want to stoke that coal, and that's cardio. So, you need a balance of both things."
Establishing a healthy routine requires accepting short-term daily physical discomfort to ensure long-term comfort and mobility in everyday life, the expert said. (iStock)
While resistance training builds muscle and strengthens bones and connective tissue, cardiovascular exercise challenges the heart and lungs, helping to maintain overall fitness, he said.
Shifting focus to function
As adults age, Daikeler says the primary motivation for maintaining physical activity should shift away from aesthetic goals and toward functional mobility and independence.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Reflecting on his personal experience visiting his father in an assisted living facility, Daikeler observed how residents struggled with basic movement and balance.
Short daily resistance workouts can help adults over 40 maintain muscle, mobility and overall strength, the expert said. (iStock)
Many residents relied on walkers and canes, and often stopped walking before talking to one another because they feared tripping over cracks in the pavement, he recalled.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"This is no longer about my abs," Daikeler added. "I need to work out in order to be able to walk and talk at the same time into my 90s ... It's no longer about aesthetics and vanity. It's really about mobility."
Maintaining healthy physical habits means accepting daily short-term discomfort to protect long-term independence, Daikeler noted.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"If I do 20 minutes of discomfort, the rest of the day is awesome," he said, adding that the goal is to consistently incorporate resistance training, cardio and flexibility work into a daily routine.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Silent heart threat found in adults under 30 with no known cardiovascular disease
summary: Silent artery plaque was detected in over half of healthy adults in the REACT study, yet traditional cardiovascular risk scores missed many of those cases.
story: Dr. Jason A. Gluck, vice chair of the Heart & Vascular Institute and system chief of cardiology at AtlantiCare in New Jersey, discusses a recent study that found stroke incidence has more than doubled among young adults.
A buildup of artery-clogging plaque may begin much earlier than many people realize, new research has found.

About one in 13 adults ages 18 to 29 already had silent atherosclerosis, the hardening of the arteries from plaque, despite having no known cardiovascular disease, while more than half of all healthy adults in the study showed signs of plaque somewhere in their arteries, according to a major new international study.
Researchers from Denmark and Spain used advanced imaging to examine more than 16,800 adults ages 18 to 70 with no known cardiovascular disease.

They found plaque in 57.1% of participants, with prevalence increasing steadily with age, from about one in 13 adults under 30 to roughly nine in 10 adults ages 60 to 70, according to the research published in The New England Journal of Medicine in August.
EVERYDAY HABIT LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DYING FROM HEART DISEASE

Atherosclerosis occurs when fatty deposits, cholesterol and other substances build up inside arteries, according to experts. The process often develops silently over many years before causing a heart attack or stroke.
A new study found signs of silent artery plaque in some healthy young adults with no known cardiovascular disease. (iStock)

"For decades, we have estimated cardiovascular risk using factors such as age, blood pressure and cholesterol," Dr. Borja Ibáñez, a cardiologist and scientific director of Spain's National Center for Cardiovascular Research (CNIC), said in a statement.
"This study shows that we can now go one step further and detect the disease directly before it causes a heart attack or stroke."
COMMON CHOLESTEROL DRUG LINKED TO LOWER DEMENTIA RISK WHEN STARTED EARLY

The new findings come from the first phase of the ongoing international REACT study, which is mapping how common silent artery plaque is across adulthood. In the next phase, researchers will test whether earlier detection can improve heart disease prevention.
Researchers are studying whether earlier detection of artery plaque could improve heart disease prevention. (iStock)

"Until now, preventive decisions have been based on an estimate of risk, but we did not know whether the disease was already present," Henning Bundgaard, professor of cardiology at Rigshospitalet in Copenhagen, said.
"REACT shows that atherosclerosis can be detected decades before clinical manifestations appear and provides the most comprehensive atlas of the evolution of the disease across adult life."
MAN GOES TO DOCTOR TO PROVE HE’S ‘IN PERFECT SHAPE’; TEST REVEALS SHOCKING DIAGNOSIS
The study also revealed that men tended to develop plaque five to 10 years earlier than women, while women experienced their steepest increase between ages 40 and 60.
Knowing your blood pressure, cholesterol and other heart health risk factors can help reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, experts say. (iStock)

Researchers also found that commonly used cardiovascular risk scores only identified a small proportion of people who already had silent atherosclerosis, suggesting some cases may go undetected using traditional risk assessments alone.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
While the researchers believe portable ultrasound could eventually help identify hidden plaque earlier, they said further clinical trials are needed.
The findings should encourage people to take heart health seriously but not to panic, experts note.
Researchers say heart disease prevention should begin early, even before symptoms appear. (iStock)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Finding plaque doesn't mean someone is about to have a heart attack, but finding it gives us an opportunity to address a patient's risk factors," Dr. Sirisha Vadali, a cardiologist at HonorHealth Women’s Heart Health in Arizona who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.
"We shouldn't wait for symptoms to start paying attention to heart health. Feeling healthy doesn't necessarily mean your arteries are free of plaque."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
She cautioned that the study alone does not establish that screening everyone will directly prevent heart attacks or strokes.
Healthy lifestyle habits, including avoiding tobacco, staying active and eating a nutritious diet, can help protect heart health, experts say. (iStock)
Vadali stressed that the findings do not mean everyone under 30 should undergo artery screening, saying decisions about additional testing should be based on a person's individual risk factors.

She recommended avoiding tobacco, staying physically active and eating a diet rich in vegetables, fruits, beans, whole grains, nuts and fish while limiting saturated fat and excess sodium to help protect heart health.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital has reached out to the researchers for comment.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: One group of married Americans is having more sex — and happier marriages
summary: The Institute for Family Studies research finds regular churchgoers report more frequent sex and greater sexual satisfaction than nonreligious spouses.
story: Jessica Steinman, a Los Angeles-based marriage therapist, discusses new findings that married couples who regularly attend church report having more frequent sex and greater sexual satisfaction than those who attend less often or not at all.

Married couples who regularly attend church report having more frequent sex and greater sexual satisfaction than those who attend less often or not at all, according to a new report from the Institute for Family Studies (IFS) in Charlottesville, Virginia.

Researchers analyzed findings from multiple datasets, including the 2026 IFS Religion and Family Survey of 3,125 married adults ages 18–54, the long-running nationally representative General Social Survey and a separate survey of 1,219 alumni of FOCUS, a Catholic campus ministry.

Regular churchgoers reported having more frequent sex than less religious or non-religious married adults, with regularly attending Catholics reporting some of the highest levels of sexual frequency. The association remained even after accounting for demographic differences.
COMMON MARRIAGE HABIT COULD QUIETLY KILL YOUR SEX LIFE, EXPERT WARNS
Among married adults ages 20 to 54, 62% of regular churchgoers reported having sex at least once a week, compared with 48% of nonreligious spouses, according to the report.

In addition to frequency, sexual satisfaction was also higher among church attendants. Catholics and Protestants who regularly attended religious services were more likely to rate their sex lives positively than those who attended less often or had no religious affiliation.
Married couples who regularly attend church report having more frequent sex and greater sexual satisfaction than those who attend less often or not at all, according to a new report. (iStock)
Daily prayer was linked to greater sexual satisfaction among married Catholics and Protestants, though it was not associated with more frequent sex.

Among churchgoers, 55% of Catholics and 45% of Protestants rated their sex lives as "excellent" or "very good," compared with 45% of nominal Catholics, 35% of nominal Protestants and 40% of religiously unaffiliated respondents.
‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT

Those who viewed marriage as a permanent commitment were more likely to report both frequent and satisfying sex. That belief, along with shared values, was also strongly associated with overall marital quality.
Study limitations
Because the analysis was observational, it cannot determine whether religious practice directly causes better marital or sexual outcomes, the authors acknowledged.
Additionally, the marital outcomes were self-reported, and other unmeasured differences between religious and non-religious respondents could have influenced the results.

Regular churchgoers reported having more frequent sex than less religious or non-religious married adults, with regularly attending Catholics reporting some of the highest levels of sexual frequency. (iStock)
Differences in factors such as age and length of marriage could also make it challenging to strike comparisons with the broader population.
The study was funded by FOCUS, the Fellowship of Catholic University Students.
Marriage therapist reacts

Jessica Steinman, a licensed marriage and family therapist and certified sex addiction therapist in Los Angeles, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential relationship between religious activity and the quality of a couple’s sex life.

"When we think of people who are really involved in religion … we might think they're not having a lot of sex or that they're having very constricted views on their sex lives," she said. "And this article and research show that's changing."
WHY COUPLES SHOULD FLIRT WITH EACH OTHER EVERY DAY — PLUS THE ‘RED FLAG’ TO AVOID

People who actively participate in a shared spiritual or religious life may also feel more connected to one another as partners, according to Steinman, who is also the chief clinical officer for No Matter What Recovery in Los Angeles, Chicago and Austin.
The rituals and shared practices associated with religious life likely play a role in strengthening that connection, the expert suggested. (iStock)

"If they're showing up and looking at things outside themselves — things that are spiritual, things that are religious, things that are having them look inward, things that are having them look into larger morals and values within their marriages and partnerships — I think they're going to possibly have happier marriages and partnerships," the therapist said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
They may also be more vulnerable and open with one another, which could contribute to a more active sex life, she added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The rituals and shared practices associated with religious life likely play a role in strengthening that connection, the expert suggested.
Religious couples who attend church together may also be more vulnerable and open with one another, which could contribute to a more active sex life, an expert noted. (iStock)

"Certain religious settings are really focused on rituals and traditions," Steinman said. "And if you're looking at partnership and marriage … engaging in sexual connection and sexual intimacy can really become a ritual itself."
The research highlighted what has been described as an ongoing "sex recession" during which people are not engaging in sexual intimacy as much as they once did.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Regardless of religious affiliation, Steinman encourages people to find ways to connect with their partners.
"Get off the phones, get off of the internet, turn the TV off and start really connecting with your partner," she advised.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Steinman suggested that partners engage with one another and build connections that go deeper than simply asking, "How was your day?"
That can include building emotional openness and discussing how partners want to connect sexually, she said.

title: Taking daily supplement may help preserve muscle as you age — even without exercise
summary: New research in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition links daily creatine to memory gains and sarcopenia prevention.
story: Jacob Zemer, a New York-based fitness coach who primarily trains clients ranging from 35 to 55 years old, said there are several reasons that adults start losing muscle as they get older.

Daily creatine supplementation could help middle-aged and older adults preserve lean muscle mass, gain strength and support cognitive function, whether it's paired with exercise or not, according to a study published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition.
The 12-week study, conducted by researchers at Texas A&M University’s Exercise & Sport Nutrition Lab, evaluated 64 men and women ages 45 to 65.

Participants were divided into non-exercise and exercise-plus-diet groups, then randomly assigned to take either 10 grams of creatine monohydrate per day — administered in two 5-gram doses — or a placebo.
ONE MUSCLE PROTEIN MAY HOLD THE KEY TO STAYING STRONGER AS YOU AGE, STUDY FINDS

Creatine is a naturally occurring compound that helps cells regenerate adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the primary energy source for cellular activity in both muscle and brain tissue, according to Cleveland Clinic.
Creatine monohydrate is a dietary supplement that helps muscles produce quick energy during activities like strength training.

A 12-week study in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition found that taking 10 grams of creatine monohydrate daily helped middle-aged and older adults increase lean muscle mass and strength. (iStock)

Adults naturally lose muscle mass and strength as they age, a condition known as sarcopenia. While dieting can accelerate that muscle loss, the new study found that creatine monohydrate helped counter the effect.
FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG

Adding creatine to an exercise and diet intervention resulted in greater reductions in body fat percentage, better preservation of lean body mass, and marked improvements in upper- and lower-body strength compared to a placebo.

Even among participants who did not engage in exercise or dietary changes, daily creatine supplementation increased lean tissue mass and improved muscular strength and endurance, according to the study.
When combined with a resistance training and weight-loss program, creatine supplementation enhanced fat loss while preserving lean body mass. (iStock)

"The fact that you can increase lean muscle mass even without exercise is remarkable, especially as we age," New York-based fitness coach Jacob Zemer told Fox News Digital. "Between the physical and mental benefits, most people should be considering creatine supplementation."
The expert, who was not involved in the study, noted that even participants who did not exercise saw an increase in their bench press and leg press.
"The fact that you can increase lean muscle mass even without exercise is remarkable."
Zemer said the findings suggest creatine may help build actual muscle tissue that generates strength, rather than simply increasing the amount of water stored in muscle cells.
Beyond physical performance, the researchers found that the 10-gram daily dose of creatine supported improvements in select tests of memory and cognitive processing.
While creatine offers clear physical and cognitive benefits as adults age, experts emphasize that supplementation enhances — but does not replace — the primary benefits of regular exercise. (iStock)

"My main takeaway from the study is that the benefits of creatine extend far beyond just athletes and bodybuilders," Zemer said. "Creatine continues to be the most scientifically studied and validated supplement on the market."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
However, the trainer emphasized that supplementation should not replace regular physical activity.
"Just because you can increase lean muscle mass by taking creatine without exercise does not mean that it is optimal or a replacement for exercise," Zemer cautioned.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"The benefits of exercise will always supersede those of creatine alone, and when the two are combined, they are both enhanced."
Even without an exercise routine, participants who supplemented with creatine saw gains in lean tissue mass, upper- and lower-body strength, and markers of glycemic control. (iStock)
The study authors noted several limitations to their findings.

Participants chose whether to join the exercise or non-exercise groups before being randomly assigned to receive either creatine or a placebo, which could have introduced lifestyle differences between the groups.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Additionally, because the study lasted just 12 weeks and included only healthy adults, researchers don't yet know whether the benefits would be long-term or whether they would apply to people with serious metabolic or neurological conditions.

For those considering taking creatine, Zemer advised consulting a healthcare professional to determine whether it's right for them, then choosing a reputable brand, staying hydrated and taking it consistently.

The study authors noted several limitations, including participant self-selection into exercise groups, exploratory cognitive endpoints, and a 12-week timeframe that leaves long-term adaptations unexamined. (iStock)

"Recommended minimum dosages for creatine are typically 3 grams for women and 5 grams for men," he said. "This study used higher dosages. Creatine is about consistency rather than when you take it, so find a time you can consistently take it daily."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
According to the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, creatine is generally considered safe for healthy adults, although some people may experience bloating, stomach discomfort or water retention.
Experts recommend talking with a healthcare provider before beginning supplementation, particularly for those with kidney disease or other chronic health conditions.

title: Men are hiding potentially deadly disorder amid pressure to build the 'perfect' body
summary: Sylvester Stallone's bulimia revelation spotlights a crisis experts say is surging among men and boys driven by looksmaxxing and musculature ideals.
story: Brian Pollack, a licensed clinical social worker and certified eating disorders specialist at Hilltop Behavioral Health in Summit, New Jersey, specializes in treating males who struggle with eating disorders, which he said is "highly underreported."
Days after Sylvester Stallone revealed his own history with bulimia, experts are highlighting a growing but often overlooked rise in eating disorders among men.
The Academy Award-nominated actor, 80, revealed during an interview with The New York Times that he developed an "obsession" with eating habits while prepping for his role in the 1982 movie "Rambo."

Stallone said he took pains to appear more "animalistic," drawing inspiration from jaguars and cats. "It became an obsession. Really bad. It got to the point where I became bulimic," he said during the interview.
SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH STRUGGLE BEHIND HIS FAMOUSLY RIPPED PHYSIQUE

Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder marked by episodes of binge-eating — consuming a large amount of food while feeling a loss of control — followed by purging behaviors such as vomiting, excessive use of laxatives or diuretics, fasting or excessive exercise, according to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH).
Experts are highlighting a growing but often overlooked rise in eating disorders among men. (iStock)

Brian Pollack, a licensed clinical social worker and certified eating disorders specialist at Hilltop Behavioral Health in Summit, New Jersey, specializes in treating males who struggle with eating disorders, which he said is "highly underreported."

According to the National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Associated Disorders (ANAD), about 30 million Americans experience an eating disorder during their lifetime, and roughly one-third are male.
What's driving the trend?

"Guys with eating disorders just present differently — for some men, it's about musculature … they continue to build muscle because they are afraid that they are weak, they want their muscles to align," Pollack told Fox News Digital. "We also see people who want to be so lean and pencil-thin that they don't eat whatsoever."
The expert, who has not treated Stallone, compared today's body-image pressures on boys and men with the beauty ideals many girls and women faced during earlier decades.
MEN FACE NEW PRESSURE TO STAY ‘HOT’ AS THEY AGE — AND IT’S NOT JUST ABOUT LIVING LONGER

"We’re seeing this extreme need for perfection and musculature — and that is leading to bulimia right now," he told Fox News Digital. "It’s particularly in our adolescent boys, who are consuming a lot of information about the ideal of masculinity in the eyes of society at large."
Societal expectations of masculinity can make it harder for men to identify and express feelings of vulnerability or distress, according to Pollack.
With binging, there is a loss of control over food — and purging is a way to get back in control, the expert noted. (iStock)
"Bulimia, especially, is about control," he said. "And what is it that men want? They want to be in control on a superficial level."
With binging, there is a loss of control over food — and purging is a way to get back in control, Pollack noted.
COMMON GYM SUPPLEMENT COULD HELP FIGHT DEPRESSION, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
The increase in bulimia and other eating disorders among men may also be driven by a desire to emulate celebrities.

"There's a big trend right now called ‘looksmaxxing,' where boys are harming themselves in pursuit of an ideal appearance, including undergoing cosmetic procedures to alter their jawlines," Pollack said. "It’s getting very scary out there, actually."
Warning signs

For many men, it may not be easy for others to recognize that they are struggling with bulimia or other eating disorders, as the binging and purging behaviors are usually done in secret, Pollack said.
"They're hidden," he said. "People are ashamed of them at times."

Some men become fixated on restrictive eating patterns, the expert said, including following strict ketogenic diets, consuming excessive amounts of protein, or eating only foods they consider "clean," such as organic, whole-food or non-GMO products. (iStock)
One red flag, he said, is if a loved one begins purchasing increasing amounts of supplements, such as creatine, or performance-enhancing substances such as human growth hormone.
People with eating disorders may exhibit compulsive behaviors around both exercise and eating, including working out for multiple hours every day and carefully calculating every aspect of their diet.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Some men become fixated on restrictive eating patterns, Pollack said, including following strict ketogenic diets, consuming excessive amounts of protein or eating only foods they consider "clean," such as organic, whole-food or non-GMO products.
In some cases, the obsession becomes so extreme that men may avoid eating foods prepared elsewhere or outside their strict standards.
The expert said men often don't have the vocabulary to talk about emotional distress, making eating disorders harder to identify. (iStock)

Pollack said some people may have "cheat days" where they visit fast-food restaurants and eat as much as they can, in an attempt to satisfy an "intense urge" stoked by restriction. "They binge, and we often see people hiding in the bathroom within 45 minutes after meals."

Another warning sign is escalating use of laxatives or diuretics, with some people taking increasingly large amounts because smaller doses no longer produce the desired effect of feeling "emptied" or "in control."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Pollack emphasized that bulimia and other disorders are experienced among men at all ages, from middle school and high school through college and adulthood.
"This is real, and men are afraid to talk about it," he said. "There's a real issue."

Bulimia is known to have life-threatening health impacts. "Just on a baseline level, with someone who purges, we see electrolyte imbalances, along with kidney and liver damage," an eating disorders specialist said. (iStock)
The expert said men often don't have the vocabulary to talk about emotional distress, making eating disorders harder to identify.

Instead, Pollack recommended asking questions about body goals — such as whether someone is trying to "sculpt your body" or "make sure that you have a six-pack" — and whether those pursuits are helping them avoid confronting difficult emotions.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Health effects
Bulimia is known to have life-threatening health impacts. "Just on a baseline level, with someone who purges, we see electrolyte imbalances, along with kidney and liver damage," Pollack said.
The expert shared that he has seen people go into cardiac arrest because prolonged malnutrition and repeated purging had severely damaged their hearts.
Bulimia patients may face expensive dental work, he added, due to severe erosion of their tooth enamel.
Esophagus issues, such as acid reflux and GERD, may also develop due to purging.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Long-term medical issues can range from treating heartburn with over-the-counter medication to facing life-threatening issues, Pollack said.
"It's a very serious scenario."
