iRobot Roomba 115X Combo Robot Vacuum & Mop

This robot vacuum suctions up dirt and debris, and it has a built-in mop that scrubs floors to leave them shiny. It’s designed with sensors that map your home to detect and avoid obstacles, and it connects to the Roomba Home app so you can select cleaning modes, create cleaning schedules, adjust suction level and more. You can also set keep-out and no-mop zones where needed, like on area rugs. The appliance comes with a charging dock, reusable microfiber mopping pad and edge sweeping brush.
Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition 32GB

We named the Paperwhite Amazon’s best Kindle because of its extra-long battery life that lasts up to 12 weeks. It also has a front light that automatically adjusts depending on your environment, helping you see the glare-free screen clearly. The Kindle Paperwhite is water-resistant, and you can charge it via the USB-C port or wirelessly with a charging dock that’s sold separately.
Amazon Smart Plug

Once you connect devices like lamps, fans and small kitchen appliances to the Amazon Smart Plug, you can control them through an app or via voice commands. The app also lets you set timers, schedules and routines — for example, I connect my Christmas lights to this smart plug and create a schedule for them so they turn on at 10 a.m. and turn off at 10 p.m. The plug is compact to keep your second outlet free.
Shark Navigator Lift-Away Upright Vacuum (NV352)

I rely on this corded vacuum to get rid of dirt, dust and hair on hard floors and carpets in my three-pet home. It has powerful suction, a multi-stage washable HEPA filter to trap allergens and a swivel steering system that makes it easy to navigate. My favorite part of the vacuum is the detachable pod, which I carry around my home and use the extended reach tool to clean above door frames, under furniture and on stairs. Interchangeable wide upholstery and crevice attachments for the extended reach tool are included.
KitchenAid Ribbed Soft Silicone Oven Mitt (2-Pack)

These were one of my best purchases during last year’s Prime Big Deal Days. Their ribbed silicone exterior helps me grip hot pots and pans, and they’re heat-resistant up to 500 degrees Fahrenheit, according to the brand. The material is also water-resistant, so I don’t worry about spills or splashes. The inside of the mitts are lined with cotton, making them soft against my skin.
Ugg Adalee Throw Blanket

Prepare for the cozy season ahead by adding Ugg’s faux fur blanket to your couch or bed. It’s double-sided, so it feels soft against your skin no matter how you use it, and it’s roomy enough for two people to share. While Ugg recommends dry cleaning the blanket, you can also machine wash it on cold, according to the brand.
Colgate Optic White Pro Series High Impact White Toothpaste (3 Pack)

Colgate’s toothpaste is made with 5 percent hydrogen peroxide, a bleaching ingredient that helps remove stains from teeth and make your smile less yellow. There’s also cavity-fighting fluoride in its formula. The minty whitening toothpaste is safe for daily use and doesn’t cause tooth sensitivity, according to the brand.
Apple AirPods Pro 3

Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 made our list of the best earbuds, and I use mine every day while listening to music on runs, taking calls and blocking out noisy city streets. They’re comfortable and secure in my ears even when I get sweaty — they come with five interchangeable ear tips so you can find the right fit. The AirPods have three listening modes, including active noise cancellation, hours of battery life with the included charging case and advanced features like heart rate sensing during workouts, hearing aid mode and live language translation.
Cascade Platinum Plus Dishwasher Pods

The most boring essentials on your shopping list are often the best deals to take advantage of during Prime Big Deal Days — you’ll need to restock eventually, so you might as well do it when items are discounted. Cascade’s dishwasher pods are a perfect example. They come in a pack of 62, and with the discount applied, you’re only paying about 0.28 per pod. Each one has soap inside that gets rid of grease and food residue, and it cleans your dishwasher’s filter, too.
Samsonite Freeform 2-Piece Luggage Set

I’ve beat up my Samsonite luggage while traveling over the years, but it still works perfectly, looks great and, perhaps most importantly, fits all my stuff. You get a matching expandable carry-on and checked bag with this set, both of which are lightweight and made with hard, protective exteriors. The suitcases have spacious interiors with elastic straps, a divider and a pouch for organization, plus they’re designed with smoothly gliding wheels, a built-in ID tag, a height-adjustable handle and a TSA-approved lock.
Urevo Auto Incline 12% Walking Pad

Urevo makes some of our favorite walking pads, and this model has features experts told us to look for while shopping, like multiple speed and incline levels, as well as a quiet motor. You can connect it to an app that lets you pick programs, control the settings and enroll in challenges to stay engaged. The brand says the walking pad is slim and compact enough to fit under most standard office desks.
LifeStraw Personal Water Filter

Take LifeStraw’s Personal Water Filter on hikes and camping trips, or put it in your emergency kit. You use it like a straw, and its built-in filter removes over 99 percent of bacteria, parasites and microplastics from water, according to the brand. You can use it to filter up to 1,000 gallons of water before needing a new one.
Top October Prime Day deals on household essentials and groceries
Dawn Platinum Powerwash Dish Spray Bundle

I’m very picky about dish soap because I don’t have a dishwasher, and out of all the options I’ve tested, Dawn Powerwash Spray is hands-down the best one. It easily removes dirt and grime from my dishes without pre-soaking, and it leaves them literally sparkling. Also, since the soap works without water, I don’t turn my faucet on until I’m ready to rinse. Beyond washing dishes, you can use Dawn’s spray on laundry stains, kitchen surfaces, appliances and grills, according to the brand. This starter kit comes with four bottles of liquid and one reusable sprayer head.
Premier Protein Shake, Chocolate (12 Pack)

Premier Protein’s shakes are ideal for snacking on the go. Each one has 30 grams of protein, no added sugar and 160 calories, according to the brand, plus they’re gluten-free. They come in over a dozen creamy flavors, like chocolate, vanilla, cookies and cream, cafe latte and pumpkin spice, almost all of which are currently on sale.
Hefty Ultra Strong 13-Gallon Trash Bags

These trash bags are multi-layered and slightly stretchy to prevent leaks and rips while you fill them to the brim, and they have a drawstring closure to keep everything inside once full. They’re also made with baking soda and added fragrance to neutralize odors. You get 80 13-gallon bags in this pack.
Tide Odor + Oxi Laundry Detergent Pods 63-pack

These Tide Pods don’t just clean clothes. The detergent inside each one also fights odors, pre-treats and removes stains, protects colors and boosts scents, according to the brand. I use them for all my laundry, including sweaty workout clothes and my pets’ beds, and I’ve never had an issue with them not dissolving, even in cold water. You get 63 Tide Pods in this pack, which come in a resealable container.
Scrub Daddy Scrub Mommy Sponges

The dual-sided Scrub Mommy is the only sponge I buy. Its scrubber side is soft in warm water yet firm in cold water to get rid of stuck-on grime, while its sponge side is always soft and highly absorbent to create suds. The circular sponges are easy to hold, and the smiley face in the center is purposeful: You can put your fingers in the eyes for a secure grip and put utensils through the mouth to wipe them down. The Scrub Mommy is odor-resistant, scratch-free and dishwasher-safe.
Energizer AA and AAA Batteries (48 Count)
I always buy batteries when they’re on sale so I never run out at home. This pack comes with 24 AAs and 24 AAAs, and they last for up to 10 years in storage, according to the brand.
Top October Prime Day tech deals
Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+

You can monitor visitors and deliveries at all times with Blink’s video doorbell. It connects to the brand’s app, letting you livestream head-to-toe video (including in night vision) and audio, as well as speak to people. The doorbell runs on two AA batteries, comes with a mounting kit and you can install it wire-free. There’s also a Blink subscription available for an additional fee, which gives you access to features like in-app person detection and motion-activated notifications.
Anker Nano Power Bank

Never worry about a dead phone or earbuds again with Anker’s Nano Power Bank, which has a built-in folding USB-C connector, eliminating the need for a cable. It fits in the palm of your hand and weighs 3.5 ounces, so you can put it in any bag or even your pocket. The Nano comes with a charging cable when you need to refill its battery, or you can connect it directly to a block.
Amazon Fire TV Stick HD

Turn any TV into a smart TV with Amazon’s Fire Stick, which you simply plug into an HDMI port to use. It lets you stream entertainment from your favorite platforms and watch live TV in HD. The Fire Stick comes with a remote that lets you control the TV via buttons or voice commands. It’s also compact so it won’t block other ports.

Medicube Toner Pads

Exfoliating with Medicube’s Zero Pore Pads every other night has transformed my skin in the past year. The pads are soaked in a serum made with AHAs and BHAs, ingredients that have made my skin noticeably softer, smoother and clearer. There’s two sides to the pads: you use the textured one first to remove dead skin cells, then the soft one to soothe. The pads come with a tweezer, preventing you from touching those inside the container with dirty hands.
Grace & Stella Under Eye Patches Variety Pack

I wear these under eye patches almost every day to depuff the area under my eyes before putting on my makeup or after taking it off. They’re made from a cooling gel material and soaked in serum made from ingredients to target different concerns, like vitamin C for brightening and peptides for moisturizing. The masks come individually packed, and this set comes with 18 pairs across six types: brightening, restoring, firming, illuminating, energizing and moisturizing.
Crest 3D Whitestrips

If you’re not a fan of thread floss or floss pickers, using a water flosser is another way to get rid of plaque. Amika’s dry shampoo came highly recommended to us by numerous hair stylists. They say the rice starch in its formula effectively absorbs moisture from the scalp and reduces odors to extend time between washes, while sea buckthorn berry nourishes the hair. It also blends into hair easily, is lightweight and adds volume and body.

The Casper Sleep Original Pillow is a NBC Selected staff-favorite product, and many of us rest our heads on it every night. It’s stuffed with a down alternative material, has a breathable cotton cover and gets its medium-soft feel from a two-layer design: the inner layer is firmer to offer support, while outer layer is plush for extra comfort. It has a strong brew setting if you like your coffee extra flavorful, and it’s designed with a 42-ounce removable water reservoir that’s easy to refill. The machine is compact, making it ideal for small spaces, and you can remove the drip tray to fit tall travel mugs.

Use the built-in measuring cup on the lid to portion out kernels, pour them into the popper and microwave it for about three minutes. You can also put butter on the lid, which has holes that let it melt onto the popcorn. Plus, once your snack is done cooking, you can use the popper as a serving bowl.

title: How the shooting death of a Houston father is igniting Latino politics in Texas
summary: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was fatally shot on his way to work by an ICE officer, after authorities say Salgado Araujo used his vehicle as a weapon. The community is demanding justice.
story: HOUSTON — As the sun set on a late September evening, a voice rose over the din of traffic at the roadside memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the 52-year-old husband and father fatally shot here by immigration authorities three months ago.
Sitting on barbershop steps, Berta Lopez, a nearby resident, alternately sang, recited prayers and cried for a man she never met.

“It was unjust — he was killed unjustly! The family is deeply hurt, his wife, his children. They are like family to us. And why don’t they show the people who did the killing? Why don’t they show them? Why don’t they release the names of the people who killed Lorenzo? Why don’t they expose them?” she said in Spanish.

In tears, Lopez said that after more than a year of intensive operations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Salgado Araujo’s killing was a clarifying moment. The government, she said, saw those who weren’t U.S. citizens as less than nothing. She was tired of it.

“Just because we’re Hispanic, shouldn’t we hold our heads high? No, God doesn’t want us hanging our heads in shame. He wants all of us, his children, to hold our heads up high,” Lopez said. “God doesn’t care about papers.”

Lopez’s hurt and anger were reflected in NBC News interviews with more than three dozen Houston-area Latinos, elected officials, activists and political strategists. They reveal a distraught community whose members feel degraded by the messages they hear out of Washington, D.C., during President Donald Trump’s second term. They said they have been terrorized by the constant stories of those detained, many wrongly, and left to languish. They were aghast that the government was sending immigrants to countries they had never heard of.

Many said Salgado Araujo’s shooting death crystallized their feelings of powerlessness. Most Latinos were better versed in the details of the incident than in the names and backgrounds of those running for some of the highest-profile offices in their state.
Their refrains were in the same vein: That could have been my dad, my brother, my uncle, my son — or me.

title: Police knew who her rapist was. The law kept them from prosecuting him for the attack.
summary: After a certain point in some states, there’s no way to hold a perpetrator accountable for sexual assaults.
story: Dana Beatty survived a horrific rape that took decades to solve.

After 34 years, authorities were finally able to identify the masked intruder who pressed a knife to her neck, wrapped her face in tape, lashed her to a bed and assaulted her for hours on Aug. 1, 1989. DNA evidence pointed to a local doctor who turned out to be someone Beatty knew. He was the husband of her best friend.

But Beatty’s assailant couldn’t be charged with rape. Authorities told her that the statute of limitations for the crime — which was six years in Ohio at the time of the assault — had long since run out, and a 2015 update to the state’s statute didn’t revive the case.
“Disbelief” is how Beatty, 67, described her reaction to the development.
“I do not understand why there would even be a statute of limitations,” she told “Dateline” in her first interview about the issue. “I don’t understand what the value in that is.”

What happened to Beatty highlights an issue faced by adult survivors of sexual violence across the country: More than 30 states have statutes of limitations for the most serious charges of sexual assault — a crime that is generally described as rape but is prosecuted under different names in different states, according to data gathered this year by the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network, a nonprofit that tracks the issue and advocates for victims.

The data, which was verified and analyzed by NBC News, shows that time limits vary dramatically from state to state. Some states impose statutes of limitations of a decade or less with few exceptions, while others eliminate time limits entirely in some circumstances.
Calls for change
Several legal experts and advocates believe statutes of limitations for all or many such types of assaults should be eliminated.
Ayesha Bell Hardaway, a former prosecutor who is a professor of law at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio, is alarmed by the dramatic variation across the country.

“It should cause anyone to have some concern about whether or not there would be accountability,” she said. “If you have individuals who are able to perpetrate crimes in the ‘right’ location, where if you get past six years of looking over your shoulder there’s no way you would be held accountable, that is quite alarming.”

To Stefan Turkheimer, vice president of public policy with RAINN, the variations can leave survivors agonizing over “math problems” instead of seeking justice or dealing with the aftermath of a crime that has devastating consequences.

“They should be able to concentrate on their own healing rather than a race to the courthouse to see whether or not the doors will be locked for them,” he said. “It is an unfair situation that when so many survivors come forward, they find that the time limit for justice has expired and that there’s nothing that they can do and that this person that harmed them will continue to go free.”

Beatty immediately reported the rape to authorities, and investigators spent years trying to solve the crime. They even investigated a local police officer who early on was considered a potential suspect, according to Charlie Beaver, a former Cincinnati police detective.
But that officer had a “perfect” alibi, Beaver said, and investigators were unable to identify her attacker.

Margaret Drew, an associate professor of law at the University of Massachusetts who specializes in gender violence, said it’s not unusual for survivors to take years to report what happened to them. She said she was struck by the “ambivalence” some legislatures display about rape survivors through statutes of limitations.

“We now know that sexual assault is a significant, life-changing event for the survivors and has serious psychological and physical consequences,” she said. “Why doesn’t everyone just agree to remove the statute of limitations?”

In interviews with NBC News, legal experts and advocates echoed that point. Some said there should be no time limits on any case involving nonconsensual sex; Hardaway said they should be eliminated for the most severe sexual assault charges, which can include the use of force or the threat of force or cases in which victims are incapacitated.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

But Nathan Rouse, an assistant professor of law at the University of South Carolina, cautioned that statutes of limitations act as deadlines for authorities to act on allegations. That can be crucial, he said, because investigations and prosecutions have historically been “sluggish, delayed or fully abandoned” for those victims.
“Discarding deadlines altogether is not a way to incentivize timely prosecutions of sexual assault cases,” he said.
Factoring in DNA evidence

Some who support eliminating time limits pointed to DNA evidence as a crucial tool that has transformed investigations and prosecutions. DNA, they said, can blunt evidentiary issues like faded memories, unavailable witnesses or lost evidence.

Such issues — along with what Turkheimer described as “court efficiency” — are the reasons statutes of limitations exist, they said. But no state has a time limit on the most serious crime, murder. And most states have eliminated them for certain sexual assault crimes involving children, according to Turkheimer.

Renee Williams, CEO of the National Center for Victims of Crime, said, “I don’t know why most states would not say, if there’s DNA, it blows the statute of limitations out of the water” for sexual assault prosecutions.

While nearly a dozen states eliminate time limits if DNA evidence is used to identify a suspect, six offer limited extensions of five years or less. In Iowa, the statute of limitations for the most serious rape charge — first-degree sexual abuse — is 10 years. An extra three years can get added if DNA evidence comes into play.

In Montana, the statute of limitations for aggravated sexual intercourse without consent — that state’s most serious rape charge — is five years, with a one-year DNA extension. The time limit is 10 years for the lesser crime of sexual intercourse without consent.

According to the Legislative Services Division of Montana’s Legislature, lawmakers created the aggravated charge in 2017 but never addressed the crime’s statute of limitations in committee hearings. It isn’t clear why. But the time limit automatically became five years — the “catchall” period for most felony crimes in the state, according to the division.

Seven other states and Washington, D.C., have statutes of limitations of 10 years or less and no DNA exceptions that extend the clock. In some states, these charges are misdemeanors or lower-level felonies. But in North Dakota, one of the most serious sex crimes has a time limit of seven years that can be paused only if the accused isn’t a resident of the state.
Such “tolling” provisions are common in state statutes. They pause the time limit in certain circumstances and often apply to all felony crimes.
Question of justice, not math

In Ohio, authorities initially believed they could pursue a rape charge against the man who assaulted Beatty, according to Jeff Smallwood, a Cincinnati police detective. While the statute of limitations for the crime was just six years in 1989, it was extended to 20 years in 1999, then again to 25 years with an additional five-year extension for DNA evidence in 2015.

When Smallwood approached the prosecutor’s office, he recalled, they believed that even though they were outside the 25-year window, the five-year DNA extension would kick in because of biological evidence recovered from Beatty’s dress.

Using genetic genealogy, the investigators determined the DNA was that of Frederick Tanzer, a doctor who in 1989 was the husband of Beatty’s best friend. Authorities were preparing to make an arrest, Smallwood said, when the prosecutor’s office came back with bad news.
A misreading of the law meant that because the original statute of limitations had already run out, the DNA extension didn’t apply.
“They say, ‘We made a mistake,’” Smallwood recalled. “‘We are unable to prosecute this case.’”

A spokeswoman for the Hamilton County Prosecutor’s Office said the attorney who now leads the office wasn’t involved in the process, so it’s “impossible” to know how it unfolded. Turkheimer said the apparent mistake illustrates how the complexities of statutes of limitations can undermine the fundamental premise of the justice system.
“The reality is these should be questions of justice, but they’re often complicated math problems,” he said.

Because investigators in Ohio couldn’t pursue a rape charge, they reached out to federal authorities for help. Using a coffee cup that Tanzer threw out, the investigators confirmed Tanzer’s DNA was found on Beatty’s dress. And they began examining other possible crimes that Tanzer could be charged with, including allegations that he’d drugged his ex-wife and had nonconsensual sex with her, federal prosecutors wrote in a pretrial detention filing.

But those, too, were ruled out because, at the time of the alleged assaults, there was an exemption in Ohio law that barred spouses from being prosecuted for rape. (In an interview with “Dateline,” Tanzer declined to discuss the allegations.)
Such spousal exemptions once existed in every state, but few remain, Turkheimer said. Ohio eliminated its spousal rape exemption in 2024.
Last-ditch plan for prosecution
Authorities next developed what Smallwood described as a last-ditch plan to prosecute Tanzer — a ruse that could catch him lying about the rape. Then, he could be prosecuted for that lie.

After having made up a story about how authorities were investigating a police officer suspected of raping Beatty and covering it up, Smallwood said, they planned to approach Tanzer not as a suspect, but as a witness. They’d ask whether he knew anything about the attack.
The tricky part, said Julie D. Garcia, a federal prosecutor in Ohio’s Southern District, is that Tanzer could have refused.
“Everyone has a right to remain silent,” Garcia said. “And he would have been well within his rights to say: ‘I don’t want to talk to you. Close the door.’”
But Tanzer talked. And he lied.

He told them he didn’t speak with Beatty on Aug. 1, 1989, nor did he go to her apartment or have sex with her, a recording of the interview shows. On Dec. 11, 2024, Tanzer was arrested on suspicion of making false statements to a federal agent, and he later pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to 15 years in prison this year.
In the interview with “Dateline,” he admitted raping Beatty and said he was “working on the why.”

To Hardaway, the former prosecutor, authorities did the best they could in bringing the federal charges. But the case, she said, was the “perfect example” of why statutes of limitations shouldn’t apply to a crime like rape — especially when the suspect’s identity is unknown.

“These types of crimes have an enormous impact on those who are not able to protect themselves,” she said. “To be in a place where there isn’t a recognition of that from the legislatures and a more uniform approach to sexual assault crimes, I think, is very telling about the priorities of our nation.”
For Beatty, eliminating statutes of limitations wouldn’t just deliver the appropriate punishment to criminals, she said.
“To me, that would be relief,” she said. “True relief.”

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at https://www.rainn.org/get-help.

title: ‘A Skydance Corp.’: David Ellison immediately puts his stamp on Warner Bros.
summary: LOS ANGELES — On Tuesday, as some employees at Warner Bros.
story: LOS ANGELES — On Tuesday, as some employees at Warner Bros. logged onto their laptops, they were met by a logo that signaled a changing of the guard.
SKYDANCE, written in all caps, underlined.
Similar branding was also quietly added below the famous Warner Bros. water tower in Burbank, California, where the studio’s storied lot is located, and at the company’s New York City office.
The message was clear for all to see: The $110 billion Paramount-Warner merger of two Hollywood giants closed Tuesday, and CEO David Ellison isn’t taking any time to dwell on the past.

“We’re proud to write this next chapter with you,” Ellison and newly tapped co-CEO Ynon Kreiz wrote in a roughly 1,000-word memo to employees, which was titled “Day 1,” a copy of which was shared with NBC News.
“Now the real work begins. Let’s go!”

Ellison’s emphasis on rebranding and moving forward signals an effort to put his own stamp on Hollywood at a moment of significant industry change. But that push will likely come with consequences that could affect the industry as a whole, with some worried what greater corporate control could mean for the future of entertainment and media.

The merger blends two historic film studios (Paramount and Warner Bros.), two popular streaming platforms (Paramount+ and HBO Max) and two news organizations (CBS News and CNN) under the leadership of the 43-year-old Ellison, son of Oracle chief Larry Ellison, who is a close ally of President Donald Trump.
Larry Ellison is personally backing the deal with tens of billions of dollars of his own fortune.

title: Trump says he plans to speak with Putin about possible pneumonic plague case in Russia
summary: Trump has said that the U.S. was willing to help Russia, where the death of a staffer at an anti-plague lab has sparked global public health concerns.
story: President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the pneumonic plague, after the death of a female staffer at a Russian anti-plague lab that’s sparked public health fears worldwide.
Asked whether he had spoken with Putin about the matter, Trump told reporters on the White House South Lawn that he had a “call scheduled” and that it would take place “very soon.”
The Russian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump’s remarks.
Trump had told reporters Monday that he was willing to help Russia, calling the pneumonic plague “a rough disease.”
“I hate to see them having it,” Trump said. “Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we’re always willing to help.”
A Russian health watchdog said last week that Darya Shipilova, 28, a staffer at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, had died from a “pneumonia of undetermined” origin.
The watchdog concluded that plague was not found among the staffer’s contacts, saying only that they found two cases of Covid and one of rhinovirus.
Add to Google
Add to Google

A State Department official told NBC News earlier Tuesday that the U.S. had been in contact with the Russian government regarding the incident since as early as Friday, following reports of Shipilova’s death.
For Subscribers
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Russia should share more information with the world, but asked the public not to jump to conclusions.
For Subscribers

“Maybe, you know, there’s nothing there. Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know,” Rubio told reporters during a news conference in Iceland. “But I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate about what this might or might not be or what this is or what this isn’t.”
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Tuesday it was aware and monitoring reports of the death, which it called “a suspected case of pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region of Russia.”

“At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC wrote on X.

title: U.S. resident charged with helping Canadian school shooter in rampage that killed 8
summary: A 30-year-old Washington state resident was charged with providing assistance to a teenager who killed eight people in Canada, including schoolchildren, U.S. prosecutors said Tuesday.
story: A 30-year-old Washington state resident was charged with providing assistance to a teenager who killed eight people in Canada, including schoolchildren, U.S. prosecutors said Tuesday.

James Cody Bryant, who the FBI said identifies as female, was arrested Tuesday and is charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country in connection with the Feb. 10 shootings in the British Columbia town of Tumbler Ridge, officials said.

Prosecutors said Bryant had been in contact over Discord with the shooter, who killed five children and a teacher at a secondary school as well as two other people. He gave the shooter advice, money and offered to help livestream the killings, the U.S. Justice Department said.
Bryant ”had been in repeated contact” with the shooter, Neil Floyd, acting U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington, said at a news conference Tuesday.

Bryant ”had the information and ability to alert law enforcement, and even discussed that possibility with the shooter — but chose not to,” Floyd said. “Instead, he encouraged and offered assistance to a murderer.”

About 2 p.m. Feb. 10, Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, who was born male but had been transitioning to female for six years, killed her mother and 11-year-old stepbrother in the small town of Tumbler Ridge, officials said,

She then went to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School and killed five children — three 12-year-old girls and two boys, one 12 and the other 13 — and a teacher, authorities said. Van Rootselaar then died by suicide.
The rampage was one of the deadliest shootings in Canada’s history. In addition to those killed, two other children were shot and suffered serious injuries, officials said.
Bryant attempted to talk Van Rootselaar out of the attack or reconsider several times but did not tell law enforcement about the plan and offered to livestream it, the U.S. Justice Department said.

The two met on the former random video chat service Omegle around three years before the shooting and kept in contact through Discord, an online communication service, said W. Mike Herrington, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Seattle office.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
There is no indication the two ever met in person, he said.

The back-and-forth messages on Discord cited in the complaint have a conversational and friendly tone. At one point, Bryant writes, “You believe me when I promise I won’t snitch on you, right?” At another point, Bryant tells Van Rootselaar, “if you are uncertain, maybe take it as a sign.”
On the day of the shootings, after Van Rootselaar killed her mother and stepbrother, she had trouble starting her car, Floyd said.
“Bryant provided advice and offered assistance on how to get the car started so that JVR could proceed to the school and kill children,” Floyd said, using the initials for the shooter’s name.
The charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country carries up to life in prison.
Bryant was in custody Tuesday, officials said. Online federal court records did not show an attorney representing Bryant Tuesday afternoon.
The shooting was livestreamed on Twitch, but only for about 20 seconds before it shut off, officials said.
Twitch said an account appearing to belong to Bryant’s was the only account that saw it, according to the criminal complaint.
Herrington, of the FBI, said the shooter wanted maximum views, but didn’t have much of a social media presence.

“Without Bryant’s misplaced loyalty and willingness to operate the livestream, we don’t ultimately know if the shooter would have gone through with the crime,” Herrington said. “We certainly know that the shooter was concerned that not enough people would see the livestream.”
Elija Rain, assistant commissioner of the British Columbia RCMP, said that the impact of the shooting was widespread.
“The people of Tumbler Ridge experienced a tragedy that forever changed the lives of families, friends, students, educators, first responders and the entire community,” he said.

title: Sally Yates, former acting attorney general who defied Trump, to lead Cornell investigation
summary: A longtime federal prosecutor, she became known in 2017 for refusing to enforce President Trump’s ban on travelers to the U.S. from predominantly Muslim countries.
story: Sally Yates, whose career in the Department of Justice spanned about three decades, will lead an independent review on how Cornell University responds to sexual harassment, assault and misconduct on campus, the university announced Tuesday.
The decision comes in the wake of national outrage over allegations made by a former Cornell student last month that she was gang-raped and plied with drugs at a fraternity in 2024.

New York Attorney General Letitia James is also investigating the allegation. A spokesperson said staff from the attorney general’s office have “spoken with the Tompkins County District Attorney, Jane Doe’s attorney, and several candidates for outside counsel to support the investigation.”
The independent probe headed by Yates will look into how the university responded to those allegations and whether the school followed its policies and procedures, according to the university.

More broadly, the review will examine Cornell’s policies and practices spanning from prevention to response. It will include how reports are investigated, how disciplinary decisions are handled, and how students are supported, the university said. The investigation will also look into the role and response of campus police, and its coordination with other law enforcement agencies and prosecutors. Yates did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“Sally Yates brings extraordinary experience, independence and judgment to this work,” Anne Meinig Smalling, the chair of the university’s Special Committee of the Cornell University Board of Trustees, said in a statement.
An attorney for one of the Chi Phi members who was accused of sexual assault, Gillio Lopes, said they welcome the independent investigation.

“Sally Yates has tremendous experience as a prosecutor and investigator, and she and her team should have access to the full record and the freedom to follow the facts wherever they lead,” Attorney Andrew Miltenberg said.
Lopes denies sexually assaulting the former student and disagreed with the Title IX finding, he said. Attorneys for several of the other men have denied wrongdoing or disputed Doe’s account.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Yates is a longtime federal prosecutor who became known in 2017 for refusing to enforce President Donald Trump’s ban on travelers to the U.S. from predominantly Muslim countries. Currently a partner at the law firm King & Spalding, she also previously investigated allegations of abuse and misconduct at U.S. Soccer.

Yates was named the deputy U.S. attorney general, the second-highest ranking in the Department of Justice, with bipartisan support in 2015. During that tenure under former President Barack Obama, Yates wrote a memo directing prosecutors to focus on individual wrongdoers in corporate cases. The memo followed the fallout of the 2008 financial crisis, where corporations were forced to pay fines but many individual executives were not prosecuted.

Yates was also the former acting U.S. attorney general for 10 days in 2017 before she was fired for refusing to defend Trump’s travel ban. Trump’s order at the time created an early flashpoint of protest against his aggressive immigration policies.

The White House said at the time that Yates had “betrayed the Department of Justice by refusing to enforce a legal order designed to protect the citizens of the United States.” The statement added that “Ms. Yates is an Obama Administration appointee who is weak on borders and very weak on illegal immigration.”

Yates penned an op-ed in The New York Times in July 2017, after her firing, writing that Trump was “attempting to dismantle the rule of law, destroy the time-honored independence of the Justice Department, and undermine the career men and women who are devoted to seeking justice day in and day out, regardless of which political party is in power.”
For Subscribers
“If we are not careful, when we wake up from the Trump presidency, our justice system may be broken beyond recognition,” she wrote.
For Subscribers

Yates began her career in the DOJ in 1989 at the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia, where she was an assistant U.S. attorney. That office covers 46 counties and includes Atlanta. In 2010, Obama appointed her to lead the office, making her the first woman to do so.
She has also previously led investigations into sexual misconduct.
In 2022, Yates led an independent probe into U.S. Soccer that resulted in a damning report.

“Our investigation over the past year has revealed a league in which abuse was systematic. Verbal and emotional abuse and sexual misconduct occurred at multiple teams, was perpetrated by several coaches and affected many players,” she said at the time.
U.S. Soccer said that the findings were “heartbreaking and deeply troubling” and that they would work to thoroughly address the recommendations.

“The abuse described is inexcusable and has no place on any playing field, in any training facility or workplace,” U.S. Soccer President and former U.S. Women’s National Team member Cindy Parlow Cone said at the time.

In Cornell’s announcement on Monday, it said that Yates and her team have been asked to “examine Cornell’s overall approach to preventing and responding to sexual misconduct, identify where we are doing things well and where we can do better, and recommend changes that will help make our community safer.”
The university said it would share the results of the review along with any recommendations with the Cornell community.

title: Why Democrats may need a gut check on their midterm ambitions: From the Politics Desk
summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki writes that some Democrats fear the party’s election expectations are getting too rosy. Plus, Ben Kamisar dives into one big factor working in the GOP’s favor.
— Adam Wollner
Why Democrats may need a gut check on their midterm ambitions
Democrats have had an extraordinary run of good news with less than a month until Election Day.
Polls show President Donald Trump’s approval rating in free fall amid growing angst over his handling of the economy and the Iran war. Key groups, like Latinos, are abandoning Republicans in droves.
Prognosticators increasingly shifting race ratings in Democrats’ direction has spurred a litany of headlines about the potential prizes awaiting the party.
Can they snag a Senate seat in Kansas? What about South Carolina? In addition to the Texas Senate contest, can Democrat Gina Hinojosa knock out Republican Gov. Greg Abbott?

“I’ve been trying to tell yall: Don’t sleep on Mississippi,” the longtime Democratic strategist James Carville posted on X last week, referring to the Senate race in a state Trump carried by 23 points two years ago.
As crunch time hits these campaigns, Democrats have critical questions before them: Should they reach for the stars? Or are they getting starry-eyed?
We’ve all been here before. A poll-driven media cycle that paints a far rosier picture for one party (Republicans in 2022) or another (Democrats in 2024).
One Democratic national strategist working on races across the country said the party needs to pump the brakes on its optimism.

“The Senate is far from secure,” said the strategist, who was not authorized to comment publicly. “We should remain aggressive in Maine and Michigan, single-digit presidential states that are not yet secure organizationally.”

The Democrat, who added that Alaska’s Senate race is also worth sustained investment, noted that Republicans have an enormous spending advantage in many of the contests that will determine which party wins the majority. (More on that below.)

There are other reasons Democrats should proceed with caution. While Latino voters are swinging away from Republicans, there are still big questions around whether they will turn out for the other side.
That goes for other critical voting blocs, too. Despite deep dissatisfaction with Trump, as well as notable energy on the left this year, the Democratic Party as a whole is still receiving low marks.
And as polling shows depressed Republicans may sit it out, there’s also a pivotal group of undecided voters who in the end could come back to the GOP, particularly in red states.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Still, it is Republicans who are on the defensive with four weeks to go. Last week, a top GOP super PAC canceled its remaining ad buys in the North Carolina Senate race, a sign that Democrats are on track to flip the seat. The group, Senate Leadership Fund, has also begun directing money to Senate contests in deep-red Kansas and South Carolina.
And if Democrat James Talarico weren’t a threat, Republicans wouldn’t have, in September alone, dumped $122 million into a state Trump won by nearly 14 points in 2024.
“It’s a toss-up race right now. It’s 50-50,” a Republican working on Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign said.

But the bottom line is to win the Senate, Democrats need a net gain of four seats, including at least two that Trump won by double-digits in 2024. And they’d need to stretch even further into Trump territory if they aren’t able to unseat longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins in Maine or defend seats in battlegrounds like Michigan and New Hampshire.
The Democratic strategist put it succinctly: “We should sleep on Mississippi.”
☀️ Related read: Florida Democrats try to regain their mojo after years of Republican dominance, by Matt Dixon
Republicans fight red-state midterm chaos with hundreds of millions in late money

Republicans are swamping House and Senate races with an unprecedented flood of late ad spending as the party tests whether hundreds of millions of dollars can buy it some reprieve from the eroding political environment that’s threatening longtime GOP states and districts.

Since the start of September, Republicans have made more than $700 million worth of new advertising bookings in congressional races alone, according to an NBC News analysis of data from AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm. That’s new money on top of what had already been committed to those races in ad reservations made over the summer.
By comparison, Democrats booked more than $430 million in new ad reservations across those races last month.

The disparity is greatest in the battle for the Senate majority, where almost 7 of every 10 newly booked advertising dollars are coming from Republicans.  The gap is smaller in the House, where a bit less than 6 in 10 of those new ad dollars are coming from the GOP.

title: Eva Marie Saint, star of ‘On the Waterfront’ and ‘North by Northwest,’ dies at 102
summary: Eva Marie Saint, the Oscar-winning star best known for playing a New Jersey dockworker’s grieving sister in the Elia Kazan drama “On the Waterfront,” has died.
story: Eva Marie Saint, the Oscar- and Emmy-winning star best known for playing a New Jersey dockworker’s grieving sister in the Elia Kazan drama “On the Waterfront” and an elegant government agent in the Alfred Hitchcock thriller “North by Northwest,” died Tuesday. She was 102.
Saint’s death was confirmed by her representative, Jeff Sanderson, who attributed it to natural causes and said she was “surrounded by family and loved ones.”
Saint was one of the last surviving luminaries of the Golden Age of Hollywood, revered by generations of cinephiles for the understated complexity of her most celebrated performances.

In a career that started in the early 1950s and spanned more than seven decades, Saint appeared in 20 feature films. She was a prolific television performer, collecting five Emmy nominations and winning one for the 1990 miniseries “People Like Us.”

Saint collaborated with some of the most fabled performers and filmmakers of the classical era. She co-starred with Marlon Brando, Cary Grant, Paul Newman, Gregory Peck and Elizabeth Taylor in movies from giants like Hitchcock, Kazan, Vincente Minnelli and Otto Preminger.

The entertainment industry changed dramatically during Saint’s life, but she persevered through each new chapter with a smile and a sense of humor, even appearing as Clark Kent’s adoptive mother in “Superman Returns,” released in 2006.
“You know how to stay young? Go with the flow,” Saint told Turner Classic Movies (TCM) in 2014.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Eva Marie Saint was born on July 4, 1924, in Newark, New Jersey. She started acting while she was a student at Bowling Green State University, graduating in 1946. She then launched her career as a radio actor in New York City and took classes at the city’s famed Actors Studio.

In the late 1940s and early 1950s, Saint appeared on small-screen programs such as “Actors Studio” and “The Prudential Family Playhouse.” She was applauded for her turn in a 1953 televised version of Horton Foote’s “The Trip to Bountiful,” starring Lillian Gish, an icon of silent cinema.

Gish proved to be one of the key mentors in Saint’s young life. In an interview with TCM, Saint recalled what Gish would say to younger actors fretting about their future: “It’s today and tomorrow, and don’t get cranky.”
In 1951, Saint married Jeffrey Hayden, who went on to become a prolific television director and producer. (He died in 2016 at the age of 90.)
Saint’s big-screen breakout came when she was cast in Kazan’s “On the Waterfront,” now considered one of the landmarks of midcentury American drama.
She played Edie Doyle, sister of a slain Hoboken dockworker and the conflicted love interest of washed-up prize fighter Terry Malloy (“I could’ve been a contender!”), played by Marlon Brando.

Brando, as she later recalled, seemed at once “really adorable” and somewhat intimidating during the production of “Waterfront.” He was possessed of such an intense acting talent, she told TCM, that “I felt that he could see right through me.”

Saint’s feature film debut earned her an Academy Award for best supporting actress at the ceremony in 1955, two days before she gave birth to her first child. Frank Sinatra called out her name, and the visibly pregnant Saint took the stage to deliver a brief acceptance speech.
“I may have the baby right here,” she said with a laugh. “But I would love to thank Elia Kazan, and Sam Spiegel, Marlon Brando, Karl Malden, Boris Kaufman, all the longshoremen. Thank you.”

The same year she won an Oscar, Saint was nominated for an Emmy for her work in the TV version of Paddy Chayefsky’s play “The Middle of the Night.” The following year she received another Emmy nod for her turn in a TV musical production of Thornton Wilder’s “Our Town.”

Saint’s film career flourished, too. She co-starred with Bob Hope in “That Certain Feeling,” picked up a Golden Globe nod for her role in Fred Zinnemann’s addiction drama “A Hatful of Rain” and appeared alongside Montgomery Clift in Edward Dmytryk’s “Raintree County.”

But then came arguably the best-known part of Saint’s screen career: Eve Kendell, a steely double agent who gets swept up in a convoluted espionage plot and romance with a dashing Madison Avenue executive (Cary Grant) in “North by Northwest.”

In the role, Saint was asked to convey equal parts competence and vulnerability, seductiveness and fear. She pulled it off with aplomb. In the film’s deliriously suspenseful climax, Eve tries to fend off villainous operatives atop Mount Rushmore and nearly falls off the mountain.
In actuality, the actor raced around on a 30-foot recreation of Mount Rushmore inside a Culver City soundstage. Still, the action set piece was not exactly easy to shoot.

“I had just given birth two weeks before to our second child,” Saint recalled in a 2000 interview with the Oklahoman. “So, there I was, climbing around. I thought: Oh my, I have no fear of heights, but I don’t climb mountains.”
But then she realized she “wasn’t nervous, and Cary was older than I, and I thought: Oh, if he can do it, I can do it,” she told the publication.

In the years to come, Saint tried her hand at various genres, from the historical epic (Preminger’s “Exodus”) and domestic melodrama (Minnelli’s “The Sandpiper”) to a memorable Cold War comedy (“The Russians Are Coming! The Russians Are Coming!”).

In the 1970s, Saint reduced her feature film commitments and started to appear more frequently in intimate made-for-television films and miniseries, including “The First Woman President” and “Fatal Vision.”

In an interview with The Associated Press published in 2014, Saint said she continued to savor the challenge of acting but envied the plum roles handed to veteran British performers such as Judi Dench and Maggie Smith.
“We don’t have quite that attitude in Hollywood,” she said. “You reach a certain age and you’re so proud that you’re walking and breathing and loving and working and all of that at 90.”

Saint’s last big-screen credit was in the 2014 fantasy romance “Winter’s Tale,” co-starring Colin Farrell and Jessica Brown Findlay, of “Downton Abbey.” Saint recalled that Farrell gifted her five dozen roses on the final day of shooting.
Saint is survived by her two children, Darrell and Laurette; four grandchildren, Eli, Tyler, Molly, and Stella; and two great grandchildren, Arlo and Finley.

title: A ‘super’ El Niño sets an ocean temperature record as aid groups prepare for the worst
summary: Sea surface temperatures have spiked to record levels in the tropical Pacific this fall, a sign that El Niño continues to strengthen.
story: “Godzilla.” “Super.” “Very strong.”
There’s no shortage of superlatives to describe the El Niño pattern brewing in the tropical Pacific Ocean, with grave consequences expected in many corners of the world.
So far, data continues to back up the hype.

Sea surface temperatures have spiked to record levels in the tropical Pacific this fall, a sign that the pattern continues to strengthen. In the region where the El Niño trend is typically measured, temperatures are 6.1 degrees Fahrenheit higher than normal.

In its latest update, the National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Agency said the pattern was strengthening and that there was a 90% chance of a “very strong event” this fall and winter, with a 75% chance of becoming a historic event larger than any El Niño since 1950.

The index data NOAA uses to characterize El Niño suggests this season’s event is the second-biggest anomaly on record for the months of July through September, even when the influence of global warming on temperatures is not factored into the equation.
“It feels like super El Niño is appropriate,” said Abby Frazier, a climatologist and professor of geography at Clark University.

The children’s aid organization UNICEF said Tuesday its analysis suggests hundreds of millions of children could be exposed to dangerous conditions as a result of the climate pattern, which raises the risk of intense precipitation in some areas and drought in others.

“With over 347 million children living in areas expected to experience drier or wetter conditions because of El Niño, we must act now to protect communities and children,” UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell said, adding that El Niño was expected to increase water shortages, malnutrition and disease outbreaks.
Southern California faces coastal erosion concerns
The University of Chicago’s Climate Impacts Lab estimates that El Niño will raise global average temperatures enough to cause 451,000 excess-heat deaths worldwide.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern that happens when winds near the equator slacken and the upwelling of cold water to the surface of the eastern Pacific Ocean stalls. The pattern typically drives up global average temperatures, causes marine heat waves off the U.S. West Coast and dampens the Atlantic hurricane season. El Niño is associated with intense rainfall and storms in the Southeast and warm conditions in the Pacific Northwest that can rob the region of its snowpack and water supply.

Scientists expect El Niño to batter the U.S. West Coast and cause unusual beach erosion, because storms are sending strong waves toward the shore, where sea levels are already rising because coastal waters are warmer than usual and therefore taking up more space.

El Niño’s influence is most obvious in the winter, because it often shifts the normal flow of the jet stream, the high-altitude air current that encircles the Northern Hemisphere and drives weather patterns. El Niño usually pushes the jet stream southward, scrambling weather patterns.

Some regions will likely suffer drought; others will be deluged with extreme rainfall and flooding. Now is the time to prepare for water restrictions in some locations and to watch rainfall forecasts in others, Frazier said. Expect those effects to ripple through agricultural economies — goods like rice, coffee and chocolate could be affected as growing conditions are affected.
“This could have cascading impacts through supply chains and other things, so it could impact the prices that we pay in the grocery store for some of our food,” Frazier said.
The signs of El Niño’s presence are growing more plain. The U.S. had a historically mellow Atlantic hurricane season, while powerful hurricanes raced across the Pacific, fueled by warm seas.
“The number of storms that have formed and have impacted, especially Hawaii, has been really incredible this year,” Frazier said.
Meanwhile, unusual marine species — including whale sharks, sea snakes and nesting turtles — have been spotted off the California coast, farther north than what water temperatures typically allow.
And earlier this summer, NASA satellites could tell that the height of seas had actually grown taller near the equator, a sign that the ocean water was growing warmer and expanding in volume.

title: Christa Pike is awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
summary: The Tennessee woman who survived an execution attempt last week is conscious, speaking and receiving medical care, in a development her attorneys described as “unprecedented.”
story: The Tennessee woman who survived an execution attempt last week is conscious, speaking and receiving medical care, in a development her attorneys described as “unprecedented.”

In a Tuesday statement, attorneys for Christa Pike said she remains handcuffed and shackled despite having sustained significant injuries to her arms after two injections of pentobarbital failed to kill her.
The statement described her prognosis as unclear.

“At a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” attorneys Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason said. “We are incredibly grateful to the first responders and the medical team at the hospital who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her. We also want to thank thousands from all over the world who sent messages offering prayers and support for Christa.”
The statement said the attorneys will speak at a news conference Wednesday.
Prison officials administered the injections Wednesday in an attempt to execute Pike for the 1995 murder of her classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 at the time of the killing.
After the injections failed to kill her, Pike was hospitalized and placed on a ventilator as staff members worked to clear the pentobarbital from her system, her attorneys have said.
For Subscribers
Pike, 50, would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
For Subscribers

Gov. Bill Lee ordered an independent review of the failed execution last week and paused all executions for the rest of the year. Pike’s attorneys have said they believe problems with the IV lines may have caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
On Saturday, Lee announced the resignation of Frank Strada, the state’s top prison official.

In a statement, Strada said he believed the state Department of Correction had carried out its responsibilities “in accordance with the established protocol.” But stepping aside, he added, was in the “best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward.”

title: Freddie Jackson, R&B star who sang ‘You Are My Lady,’ dies at 70
summary: Jackson’s silky voice earned him two Grammy nominations and a slate of platinum and gold records.
story: Freddie Jackson, whose smooth vocals swept an entire generation off its feet, died Monday night, his family announced on Instagram. He was 70.
“Freddie was more than a legendary voice. He was a kind, generous soul who loved his fans, his family, his friends, and his music with everything he had,” his family wrote.
“For decades he gave us the songs that became the soundtrack to our love stories, our celebrations, and our most treasured memories,” the post went on. “That gift will live on forever.”
His hit 1985 single “You Are My Lady” became one of the most recognizable songs at weddings and engagements and any time a romantic mood needed to be set.
“To everyone who ever sang along, danced, or felt something when Freddie took the stage: thank you. You were family to him, and he carried your love with him always,” his family said on social media.
No cause of death was given.
Jackson announced in 2024 that he had been diagnosed with kidney disease and planned to partner with the National Kidney Foundation to spread awareness.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Jackson said that after much thought and reflection, he was finally able to speak publicly about his deeply personal journey.
“This journey has been challenging, but I am not facing it alone,” he said. “My close friends, my manager and music family, and all of you are here with me keeping me going.”
The foundation said it was deeply saddened to learn of his death and praised him for his courage during the darkest of times.
“His battle with kidney disease touched many lives, and his courage will not be forgotten,” the foundation said in a social media statement.

One in 7 Americans have chronic kidney disease, which can lead to weak bones and heart disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Nine out of 10 people don’t know they have it.

Jackson was born in Harlem, New York, and learned to sing gospel music before he graduated to more adult themes. His silky voice earned him two Grammy nominations and a slate of platinum and gold records, Rolling Stone reported.
In 1989, The New York Times wrote that he was “one of black pop’s most elegant performers, a singer who can turn a heartbreak ballad into a world view.”
“My music is for people who like to hold hands in concert,” he told the Times.
“If people could diminish some of their hate, the chaos and trouble in life wouldn’t be so strong,” he added. “At my shows, I see people who don’t know each other end up talking to each other.”

title: Dolly Parton’s estate alleges nephew used barbed wire and caution tape to avoid being summoned
summary: She’s Alive, the entity that manages and protects Parton’s professional property, is suing Bryan Seaver, accusing him of threatening the late music icon’s legacy.
story: Barbed wire, yellow caution tape and “no trespassing” signs.

Attorneys for the estate of Dolly Parton claim that Bryan Seaver, the late country music icon’s nephew, used these items to barricade his property in an attempt to avoid being served with a lawsuit accusing him of threatening to destroy Parton’s legacy.

The revelation came to light on Monday in court filings in which lawyers for the estate included images showing a “no trespassing” sign in Seaver’s front yard, and barbed wire and yellow caution tape wrapping the handrails leading to his front door.
The photos were part of a court filing urging the judge overseeing the case to deny Seaver’s request for additional time to retain an attorney ahead of a temporary injunction hearing set for Friday.

The legal ordeal between Seaver and She’s Alive, the entity in charge of managing and protecting Parton’s professional property and business, began two weeks ago, when the estate filed a civil complaint against the nephew. Seaver is the person the late star had handpicked to announce her death from cancer.

She’s Alive, which is led by Parton’s longtime manager Danny Nozell, accused Seaver of waging a successful “campaign of threats” against its employees and business partners — causing many of them to quit their jobs, according to the complaint.

The complaint included text messages and emails from Seaver. In one message he threatens to “set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or f------ pay me.”
For Subscribers
She’s Alive also claimed it was forced to hire private security for its remaining personnel, including at their homes, as a result of the threats.
Court records state Seaver used to work for private military contractors before providing security services for Parton and her properties through his company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services.
Court records still do not list an attorney for Seaver. On Tuesday, he did not respond to an email seeking comment.
For Subscribers

Seaver said in a recent text to The New York Times that his messages were twisted, writing, “This is a contrived out-of-context explanation of how this went down and it is being done in an effort to solidify me as some sort of opposition to her brand in her legacy.”
She’s Alive removed Seaver from his security role about a week before filing its lawsuit, saying his “terrorizing conduct made their continued retention untenable.”

Seaver was eventually served via email after She’s Alive unsuccessfully “tried to serve the summons, Verified Complaint, and injunction paper on Mr. Seaver on three occasions,” according to court records.

Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles, the judge overseeing the case, granted a temporary restraining order on Sept. 22 after reviewing text messages from Seaver that directed harmful threats “toward identifiable existing business relationships rather than merely expressing generalized dissatisfaction,” according to her ruling.
Seaver also boasted about “his access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate against persons whom he perceived to have acted against his family,” the ruling stated.

The temporary restraining order intends to stop Seaver from talking with or being within 1,000 feet of any She’s Alive employees, attorneys and business partners. It is also meant to keep him from interfering with the estate’s business relationships.
The legal battle has gained national attention over the past few weeks after it offered initial signs of discord in a carefully managed estate process for one of the nation’s most beloved artists.

Parton, who died Aug. 25, was a country music giant, philanthropist and cultural icon. She distinguished herself by writing hundreds of songs — including timeless hits like “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors” and “I Will Always Love You,” which earned over 100 million worldwide sales and more than 1 billion online streams.

title: California couple with 21 children, most born via surrogates, charged in ‘house of horrors’ abuse case
summary: A Southern California couple who had 21 children, most of whom were birthed by different surrogate mothers, lied to the surrogates and then subjected the children to vicious beatings and punishments, authorities said.
story: A Southern California couple who had 21 children, most of whom were birthed by different surrogate mothers, lied to the surrogates and then subjected the children to vicious beatings and punishments, authorities said.

Silvia Zhang and Guojun Xuan were arrested Tuesday after authorities served a search warrant at their Arcadia mansion as part of a child abuse investigation. They have been charged with conspiracy to commit child abuse and witness intimidation.

Xuan also faces one felony count of child abuse, one felony count of accessory after the fact, and five felony counts of dissuading a witness. Zhang also faces one count of accessory after the fact and four counts of dissuading a witness.
“This house could only be described as a house of horrors for these incredibly young children,” Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said at a Tuesday news conference.

Authorities began investigating the couple last year after a 2-month-old child was brought to the hospital with head injuries. Hochman, citing a criminal complaint, alleged that a nanny struck the baby in the head on May 4, 2025.
Xuan and Zhang did not seek medical attention until days later, he said, noting that the baby has since recovered.
During the investigation, authorities learned that Xuan and Zhang were running a surrogacy ring out of their home and hired surrogates throughout the country.
Hochman said the couple often lied to the women about why they wanted children or how many children they already had.

“One surrogate in particular … was paid for both a first and second surrogacy,” he said. “She was told initially Zhang was a single mother struggling to conceive when she agreed to act as a surrogate. That was a false statement.”
The woman was paid up to $75,000 per surrogacy, the district attorney said.
The couple failed to tell another woman who was 7 months pregnant that they already had 16 other children, he said.
“Another surrogate, they said they were seeking the miracle baby, and they paid that surrogate $135,000,” Hochman said.
Over the years, the children were allegedly abused while Xuan and Zhang watched on 32 motion-activated cameras they set up around the home, Hochman said.
He described three rooms the couple called “learning rooms,” where the children would spend hours seated at desks under the supervision of various nannies.
“Each one of these defendants monitored the nannies’ discipline of the children that were happening in the three learning centers,” the district attorney said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
He said during one incident, a nanny had forced a child “to maintain a horse stance” and Xuan could be seen on video laughing.
“In another situation, defendant Xuan entered one of the learning centers while a nanny was striking a child, and instructed the nanny to strike the child harder,” he said.
Hochman alleged that Xuan also beat a child across the child’s bare buttocks and struck the child’s head.

“Defendant Xuan also lifted the child into the air by one arm, while continuing to strike him and repeatedly struck the child’s head from side to side with sufficient force that the child’s body lurched into alternating directions with the blows,” he told reporters.
He said the children were punished, physically abused and beaten “on a daily basis.”
One room in the home did not have cameras. Hochman said the children would be taken into the room and could be heard “screaming from inside.”

The couple is accused of trying to cover up the alleged abuse by instructing the children to lie, according to Hochman. During a meeting after the 2-month-old was taken to the hospital, the couple allegedly told the nannies not to leave visible marks on the children.
“This case is unprecedented,” Hochman said. “It is horrific, and the physical abuse, beating, and punishment that these very young children received is despicable.”
Los Angeles County Sheriff Robert G. Luna said the children were subjected to “horrific abuse.”
Fifteen children were removed from the home last year, and another six were found to be in the care of family and friends.
Xuan and Zhang are expected to be arraigned Tuesday. Prosecutors are seeking $100 million bail.
An arrest warrant was previously issued for one of the nannies seen on video violently shaking the 2-month-old baby. The nanny has not been arrested.

title: I’m a John Steinbeck Expert. This Is What I Really Think of Netflix’s ‘East of Eden’
summary: Two John Steinbeck experts unpack East of Eden and explain why they like the depiction of Cathy.
story: “Take it From Me” is a TODAY series where experts use their wisdom to explain trends or make recommendations within their fields.
Jeffrey Yeager sat down to watch the Netflix adaptation of the book he’s spent his career studying.

The vice president of the International Society of Steinbeck Scholars went into “East of Eden,” the seven-episode series directed and written by Zoë Kazan, with a “skeptical eye.” The show premiered just one day earlier, but he’d already heard chatter about how “it’s different than the book.”
Seven episodes later, he was won over by Kazan’s interpretation, which came over 60 years after her grandfather Elia Kazan directed the 1955 film adaptation.
“I came out very pleased. I thought it was fantastic,” Yeager tells TODAY.com.

“East of Eden” was the book Steinbeck considered his epic. At over 600 pages, the book is long enough to contain the origin stories of two sets of brothers, both loosely based on the Genesis story of Cain and Abel. The sprawling book, spanning the Civil War era to World War I, also maps out how two families came to live in California’s Salinas Valley; the Hamiltons and the Trasks.
Both the book and its characters are concerned with good and evil, free will and fate.
“Do our genes dictate who we are? Do our genes dictate the path we have in life, or do we have freedom in who we become?” Yeager summarizes the questions “East of Eden” asks.

Cal Trask (Joseph Zada in the show) is particularly consumed by these questions the more he finds out about his mother, Cathy Ames (Florence Pugh), and wonders if he’s destined to carry her less-than-golden legacy.
Steinbeck experts say Cathy’s nuanced depiction in Kazan’s “East of Eden” is what makes it so remarkable.

“I like the opening episode, and I like the fact that (Kazan) sets out the themes really clearly in terms of Cathy and the meditation on good and evil,” Susan Shillinglaw, a professor of English at San Jose State University who served as the university’s director of the Steinbeck Center for 18 years, tells TODAY.com.

In “East of Eden,” Steinbeck likens Cathy to a monster, writing in his introduction of the character, “The face and body may be perfect, but if a twisted gene or a malformed egg can produce physical monsters, may not the same process produce a malformed soul?”
According to Yeager, Cathy, in the book, is depicted as the “epitome of evil,” and “somebody who’s just missing something that is key to being human.”
Certainly, Cathy does evil things in both the TV show and book, including killing her own parents and attempting to kill the father of her twins (and that’s not all).
But Kazan says she set out to understand where Cathy’s monstrousness came from, reframing her childhood to include sexual assault.

Take the situation with her teacher as another example of how the show casts a different light on Cathy. In the book, she clearly manipulates a teacher to the point that he takes his own life. “But in the show, the teacher is trying to abuse her, and then she takes advantage of the situation,” Yeager says.
Rather than being wicked, Yeager says Pugh’s Cathy is “trying to redefine morality in her own way.”
Yeager applaudes Pugh’s performance, which shuffles between “reptilian eyes” and scenes that can draw empathy.

“I feel like the show can’t make its mind up on where it wants to go (with Cathy), and in some ways, that makes the show richer than the novel. It makes us think more about that character. How does evil come into the world?” Yeager says.
“The whole point of ‘East of Eden’ is to engage readers in an assessment of who Cathy is.”
For Shillinglaw, the show’s changing interpretations of Cathy are right in line with the legacy of the book.

“The whole point of ‘East of Eden’ is to engage readers in an assessment of who Cathy is,” Shillinglaw says. “She’s like the white whale in ‘Moby Dick.’ You have to keep looking at her. What does she mean? What is her purpose in the book?”
Yeager, after watching all seven episodes, wishes more attention had been given to the Hamiltons, the family Steinbeck based on his own.
“The Hamilton family was Steinbeck sort of tracing his lineage, and I can see why that wouldn’t be important for the story the show was trying to tell,” Yeager says.

He praises Hoon Lee’s “emotionally charged performance” as Lee, Aron and Cal Trask’s caretaker who plays an important role in healing the family at the end of the show. He’s also the voice of the story’s most overarching lesson: Timshel, a Hebrew word that’s translated to allow for free will in the triumph over evil, rather than fate.

For Shillinglaw, who taught a course on Steinbeck, says the conversations around “East of Eden” were always her favorite, and anticipates more brought on by the show, currently No. 1 on Netflix in the U.S.
“Students just found (the book) fascinating, and it was because of Cathy — what she meant and her legacy.”

title: ‘Days of Our Lives’ Star Robert Kelker-Kelly Dies at 62
summary: Longtime soap star Robert Kelker-Kelly, best known for portraying Bo Brady on “Days of Our Lives,” has died at age 62.
story: Longtime soap star Robert Kelker-Kelly, best known for portraying Bo Brady on “Days of Our Lives,” has died at age 62.
Kelly died on Oct. 3 in Missouri, according to a statement to NBC News by Kathleen Diebold Hargrave, the division director of the Office of the Regional Medical Examiner in St. Charles, Mo.
The cause of death is not available at this time, according to the statement. The timeline for death certification is normally 12 weeks, per the medical examiner’s office.
TMZ was first to report the news.
The Witchita, Kansas, native launched his daytime television career when he originated the role of Sam Fowler on “Another World” from 1987 until 1990.
He began playing rebel-turned-police detective Bo Brady on “Days of Our Lives” in 1992 after Peter Reckell, the actor who originated the role nearly a decade before, left the series.
Kelker-Kelly’s character was embroiled in a love triangle alongside Hope Brady, played by Kristian Alfonso, and Billie Reed, played by Lisa Rinna.

Rinna made headlines earlier this year when she detailed her challenging behind-the-scenes relationship with Kelker-Kelly in her memoir, “You Better Believe I’m Gonna Talk About It: A Candid New York Times Bestselling Memoir of Hollywood, Aging, and Owning It All.”
Kelker-Kelly left “Days of Our Lives” when Reckell resumed the role of Bo in 1995.
Kelker-Kelly returned to “Another World” from 1996 to 1998 to play professional race car driver Bobby Reno, who was later revealed to be Dr. Shane Roberts.
The actor next took on the role of Stavros Cassadine on “General Hospital,” appearing in more than 40 episodes from 2001 to 2014.
Kelker-Kelly won a Soap Opera Digest Award in 1994 for outstanding lead actor and another the following year for hottest soap couple, which he shared with Rinna.
Kelker-Kelly was married to fellow “Days of our Lives” star Miriam Parrish from 1997 until 2013, according to IMDB.

title: Anna Camp Is Nearly Unrecognizable on TODAY After Dramatic Hair Transformation
summary: Anna Camp traded in her blond hair for brown hair and showed off the new look in a TODAy appearance on October 6.
story: The blonde look that was Anna Camp’s signature in everything from “True Blood” to “Pitch Perfect” over more than 15 years has given way to her “brunette era.”

The actor had some fans doing a double take when she first revealed her new hair on Instagram in September. She also showed off the brunette look on TODAY Oct. 6 to promote her new HGTV show, “A Very Haunted Renovation.”
“The same but different.. brunette era loading now 🧉” Camp wrote on Instagram Sept. 7.
Fans were on board with the dramatic change from the blonde look she has worn as a vampire, snobby sorority sister, “Scream 7” horror queen and blonde twins on “You.”
“Beautiful! I mean you look good either way, blonde or brunette. 🤎” one fan commented.
“I mean… gorgeous either way! ❤️” another wrote.
“Looks great!” another commented.
One fan asked Camp what color her natural hair is.
“A little lighter than this!” she replied.
Camp, 44, still has the platinum blonde look on her new HGTV show, which features a renovation competition at one of America’s most haunted homes.
In keeping with the haunted theme, the actor will also be returning to the stage in a production of “2:22 A Ghost Story” at the Lucille Lortel Theatre in New York City in October.
“I like the spooky stuff and Halloween’s coming up, so it’s my season, I’m excited,” she said on TODAY.

title: Jenna Bush Hager Says Her October 2026 Book Club Pick Is By an Author on Her ‘Mt. Rushmore of Writers’
summary: The October Read With Jenna book club pick for October 2026 is Partita by Barbara Kingsolver.
